The lecture of this chapter (figures built as it is explained)

We start this chapter with machines whose joints are moved by motors: an industrial arm that welds, moves or assembles. We build on chapter 8, where we described a system of rigid bodies with constraints, degrees of freedom and generalized coordinates, and derived the equations of motion from virtual work. From chapter 2 we have the rotations of coordinate axes written as matrices, and the determinant. This chapter applies that knowledge to one family of machines.

The chapter's name has three words. The word robot comes from the Czech word robota. The Czech playwright Karel Čapek introduced it in his play Rossum's Universal Robots in 1920 (SPONG, introductory chapter, which translates robota as worker, while more precisely it means serf labour, hard forced work). Today it names a machine that works with some degree of autonomy under computer control. We show the other two words, kinematics and dynamics, on such a machine, an arm that welds (figure 27.1).

We put the arm together from the ground up. On the ground stands the base, which does not move. On it, at the point \(O\), is the first motor, which turns the first rigid bar. At the other end of this bar, at the point \(B\), is the second motor, which turns the second bar. We call the bars links (členi), and the places \(O\) and \(B\), where a link turns against its neighbour, joints (zglobi), as in an elbow. At the end of the second link is the tip of the torch \(E\). Before we run the motors, let the arm lie stretched and horizontal, and we draw it so in grey dashes. Then the first motor turns the first link by the angle \(q_1\), which we measure from the horizontal to the new direction of the link. The second motor turns the second link by the angle \(q_2\), which we measure from the dashed extension of the first link to the new direction of the second, because the second motor sits on the first link and turns against it. We draw the new position of both links in orange. In front of the arm stands the workpiece, a piece of sheet metal on a stand, and on it the seam \(S\) is marked, the place that has to be welded.

Kinematics (kinematika, Greek kinema, motion) is the description of positions and motion of bodies without forces. On the left part of figure 27.1 it asks where the tip \(E\) is when we know the rotations \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). On the middle part it asks where and how fast the tip moves while the motors turn. What drives the arm is not its concern. Dynamics (dinamika), which we met as a word in chapter 8, adds forces and moments. On the right part of the figure the same arm carries the weights of its links, \(m_1g\) and \(m_2g\). We draw them as arrows pointing down from the middle of each link, where the centre of gravity of a uniform bar is. Without the motors the weights would turn the arm downward and it would fall. The motor in the joint \(O\) therefore turns the first link with the torque \(\tau_1\), and the motor in the joint \(B\) turns the second link with the torque \(\tau_2\). We draw them as curved arrows around the joints, because a torque turns and does not push: a torque (navor) is the moment (definition 2.37) with which the motor acts on the link about the axis of the joint. Dynamics asks what the torques must be for the arm to stay at rest or to move as we want. The chapter's name therefore gives the order of work, positions first, then forces.

Why does this matter? A robot that welds a car body must bring the tip of the torch \(E\) to the seam \(S\) without any link hitting the workpiece. Whoever knows only the motor rotations does not know where the tip is. Whoever knows only the wanted point \(S\) does not know what rotations it requires. There are also positions in which the arm can no longer move its end in some direction at all, however strong the motors are. The middle part of the figure shows one: the arm is stretched, both links lie on one line. The links are rigid bars that do not get longer, and two bars joined at a joint reach farthest when they are in line. The tip is therefore at a distance from the joint \(O\) equal to the sum of the two link lengths, and in no position does it get farther. All points at that distance lie on a circle about \(O\), which we draw in grey dashes, and the tip is on it. Outward, across the circle, no motor can move it, so we crossed out the arrow in that direction. Along the circle the tip can still move, which the blue double arrow shows. Finally we have to choose the motors. What torques they must manage we compute from the equations of motion.

The chapter promises five things, and each can be seen on figure 27.1. First, we will be able to say how many numbers fix the position of the arm (for this arm they are the angles \(q_1\) and \(q_2\)) and which points the end of the arm can reach at all (up to the edge of its reach). Second, we will write the position of every link with matrices, so that the position of the end of the arm \(E\) is a product of matrices that we can read link by link, the first, then the second. Third, we will solve the reverse task, which joint rotations give a given point such as the seam \(S\), and show when a solution exists and how many there are. Fourth, we will connect the joint speeds with the speed of the end of the arm, then the forces at the end with the torques needed in the joints, and so find the positions where mobility is lost, as in the crossed-out direction of the stretched arm. Fifth, from chapter 8 we will derive the equations of motion of the arm, which connect the weights, the torques and the motion, and show which properties they always have.

27.1 Robot chains, joints and workspace (robotske verige, zglobi in delovni prostor)

An industrial arm consists of a few rigid bars that motors turn against each other, with a tool or a gripper at the end. The robot must know where this tool is when it knows the motor angles, and the other way round, what angles a given point demands. Three questions stand before us. How many numbers do we need to say in what position the whole arm is? Where is the end of the arm when we know these numbers? Which points can the end of the arm reach at all? The first two are questions of kinematics (kinematika), the description of the positions and motion of bodies without forces. The third is a question about the extent of the motion. In this section we answer the first and the third for a planar arm, and we finish the second in the later sections of this chapter, where the positions of bodies are written with matrices. Forces and the equations of motion come later still.

The chapter builds on chapter 8: configuration, constraints, degrees of freedom and generalized coordinates are derived there, and here we only use them.

Model. The model of the arm has idealizations, which we list in advance, each with what it would spoil in a real arm. Figure 27.2 shows each in its own tile: top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right.

  1. The links are rigid (definition 1.11): they do not bend and do not vibrate. For short thick links this is fine, for long thin ones it is not. An aluminium tube \(1\) m long with a diameter of \(50\) mm and a wall of \(3\) mm, clamped at one end, sags under a load of \(50\) N at the other end by \(Fl^3/(3EI) = 1{,}9\) mm (equation (5.57) with \(E = 70\) GPa and \(I = 1{,}23 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^4\), the numbers are our choice, NumPy), while the rigid model gives \(0\) mm. By that much the gripper is elsewhere than the model says. Flexible links are treated in chapter 28.
  2. The joints are ideal (definition 8.3), hence without friction. Besides, they have no backlash, and the rotation is not limited. A real joint has a limited angle, and its backlash gives an error at the gripper.
  3. The motors give only forces and moments in the joints. Their own masses and inertias are not in the model. How much this matters is told by section 27.8: a motor behind a gear with the ratio \(r : 1\) adds the inertia \(r^2 J_{\mathrm{m}}\) to the link, where \(J_{\mathrm{m}}\) is the moment of inertia of the motor, so at \(r = 100\) it is \(10^4\,J_{\mathrm{m}}\), which is not small.
  4. The base stands still (so the robot is not on a vehicle), and the chain of links is open, as the definition below says.

We first picture the arm in space. Figure 27.3 shows its scheme.

We start at the floor. The base (podlaga) stands and never moves, we call it link \(0\). On it sits the first joint (zglob), where the first link (člen) can turn against the base. At the other end of the first link is joint \(2\), which carries link \(2\), and so on to joint \(3\) and link \(3\). At the end of the last link is the end effector (prijemalo). There the robot acts on an object, which is why it is called an end effector. We know the word link from a chain: a link of a chain holds its neighbour, and every link of the arm is joined to its two neighbours in a joint, so the structure is called a chain. A joint is a place where two links touch and can move, as in an elbow. The base is called so because it carries everything else.

Figure 27.3 is the scheme of every arm in which each link holds only the next one. An arm in which the links close into a loop appears in example 27.5.

Definition 27.1 Serial manipulator (serijski robot)

Let \(n \ge 1\) be an integer. A serial manipulator (serijski robot) with \(n\) joints is a system of \(n + 1\) rigid bodies (definition 1.11), the links \(0, 1, \dots, n\), and \(n\) joints \(1, \dots, n\) with the following properties:

  1. Link \(0\), the base (podlaga), stands still.
  2. Joint \(i\) connects link \(i - 1\) to link \(i\) and to no other link.
  3. The end effector (prijemalo) is a chosen point of link \(n\), which we denote \(E\).

The chain is open (open chain), because each link is connected only to the previous and the next one, link \(0\) only to the next, link \(n\) only to the previous. The links do not form a loop.

Source: SPONG section 3.1 (PDF p. 98): "A robot manipulator with \(n\) joints will have \(n + 1\) links", the links are numbered from \(0\) and joint \(i\) connects link \(i - 1\) to link \(i\). The base stands still, same page. The notion of the end effector is in SPONG section 1.1.4 (PDF p. 29). The wording "open chain" and the requirement of links without a loop are our explanation.

What are the joints like? Figure 27.5 shows two kinds. A human elbow has one motion, like a door on hinges: two parts turn about one axis, this is a revolute joint. We know another one from a telescopic aerial or a drawer that is pulled out: a displacement along one line, this is a prismatic joint.

The shoulder, however, we move in three directions, like a ball in a bowl. SPONG section 3.1 (PDF p. 98) shows that this is nothing new: a ball joint with two degrees of freedom and a wrist with three can be thought of as a succession of joints with one degree of freedom and links of length zero between them. The arrow with the equals sign between the two halves says that the right picture shows the same motions as the left. So in this chapter we always assume joints with one degree of freedom. Two kinds suffice.

On the left of figure 27.5 is the revolute joint. Link \(i - 1\) carries the axis of the joint. We look along it, so it is drawn as a circle with a dot. As long as the joint is not turned, link \(i\) lies in the extension of link \(i - 1\), dashed grey. When it turns, it is orange. Every point of link \(i\), for example the point \(P\), then moves on a circle about the axis, and we measure the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\) between the lines of the two links, which is zero in the initial position. On the right is the prismatic joint. The guide is part of link \(i - 1\). The slider of link \(i\) is dashed grey in the initial position. When it slides along the guide, it is orange, and it does not turn. We measure the displacement \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\) between the mark on the guide and the mark on the slider, which were at the same place in the initial position.

Definition 27.2 Revolute and prismatic joint (vrtljivi in drsni zglob)

Let joint \(i\) connect links \(i - 1\) and \(i\) of a serial manipulator (definition 27.1). The joint is revolute (vrtljivi zglob, symbol R) if every point of link \(i\) moves relative to link \(i - 1\) on a circle about the same line, the joint axis (os zgloba), which is fixed to link \(i - 1\). The joint is prismatic (drsni zglob, symbol P) if every point of link \(i\) moves relative to link \(i - 1\) on a line parallel to the same line, the joint axis, and link \(i\) does not turn. Both joints are ideal (definition 8.3), hence without friction. Besides, they have no backlash, and the angle or displacement is not limited. A joint has one degree of freedom, because one number determines the position of link \(i\) relative to link \(i - 1\), an angle or a displacement, which the next definition calls the joint variable.

Source: SPONG section 1.1.1 (PDF p. 27) and figure 1.4 (PDF p. 28): the revolute joint is like a hinge and allows a relative rotation, the prismatic joint allows a linear relative motion, symbols R and P. The statement that all points move on circles or lines is ours. The source gives no reasons for the names: revolute is from "revolve" (to turn), for prismatic we explain the name by the prismatic shape of a slider that stays aligned in its guide, which is our explanation and not from the source.

The names have a reason: the revolute joint revolves, in Slovenian vrtljivi, the prismatic one slides, drsni. An angle or a displacement is written as a number. The next definition says how.

Definition 27.3 Joint variable (spremenljivka zgloba)

Let joint \(i\) be a revolute or prismatic joint of a serial manipulator. For a revolute joint we choose on the two links lines perpendicular to the joint axis that are parallel and equally directed in some reference position of the joint, and we choose the direction in which the angle counts as positive. The joint variable (spremenljivka zgloba) \(q_{\mathrm{i}} = \theta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is then the angle, in radians (definition 8.8), by which the line of link \(i\) turns relative to the line of link \(i - 1\) from the reference position. For a prismatic joint we choose marks on the two links on the axis that are at the same place in a reference position, and a direction of the axis. The variable \(q_{\mathrm{i}} = d_{\mathrm{i}}\) is then the displacement of the mark of link \(i\) from the mark of link \(i - 1\) along the axis, in the chosen direction, in metres. The numbers are collected in a column \(\vek q = (q_1, \dots, q_{\mathrm{n}}) \in \mathbb{R}^n\), which we also call the configuration of the robot in joint coordinates.

Source: SPONG section 1.1.2 (PDF p. 28) and equation (3.1) of section 3.1 (PDF p. 98): \(q_{\mathrm{i}} = \theta_{\mathrm{i}}\) for a revolute and \(q_{\mathrm{i}} = d_{\mathrm{i}}\) for a prismatic joint, and the vector \(\vek q\) determines the position of every point of the rigid links. The choice of the reference lines, which fixes the zero and the sign, is our wording. In the section on the Denavit-Hartenberg notation the frame of the link will fix the zero and the sign.

In this section the letter \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\) always means the displacement of a joint and the letter \(\theta\) the angle of a joint. In chapter 8 the letter \(\theta\) is the angle of a pendulum, here it is the angle in a joint. The variables \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) have the same name and the same role as the generalized coordinates of chapter 8. For a planar chain with revolute joints lemma 27.4 will show this. For chains with prismatic joints and for chains in space we quote it from SPONG section 1.1.2 (PDF p. 28), where the number of joints determines the number of degrees of freedom, and we do not prove it here.

For a planar arm we can see everything in one picture. Arm \(A\) is a planar arm with two revolute joints whose axes are perpendicular to the plane (an RR arm). Its links have the lengths \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m, like the double pendulum of example 8.50. The masses of the links, which we shall need at the equations of motion, are our choice and not from a source: \(10\) kg and \(5\) kg, the links are homogeneous thin bars.

Let us draw the arm as we see it. We draw the axes \(x_0\) and \(y_0\) through a chosen point of the base, they are the axes of a fixed coordinate system labelled \(0\), because it is fixed to link \(0\). The base is below them. At the origin is joint \(O\), the first revolute joint. From it goes link \(1\) of length \(l_1\), which is turned from the axis \(x_0\) by the angle \(q_1\). This angle is also the variable of joint \(1\), because the base is at rest and the line of link \(0\) has the direction of the axis \(x_0\). At the end of the link is joint \(B\), and from it goes link \(2\) of length \(l_2\). Its angle \(q_2\) is measured from the extension of link \(1\), drawn dashed, because that is the line of link \(1\) at joint \(2\) from which the joint counts the rotation. At the end of link \(2\) is the end effector \(E\). Where is it? The position of a point on a link we know from lemma 8.41: a point of a rigid body with the initial vector \(\vek r_0\) from the point \(O\) of the body is, after a rotation \(\varphi\), at the position \(\vek o + \mat R(\varphi)\vek r_0\).

Link \(1\) has its point \(O\) at the origin and the rotation \(\varphi_1 = q_1\), the point \(B\) is at the vector \(\vek r_0 = (l_1, 0)\) from it. Link \(2\) has the point \(B\) and the rotation \(\varphi_2 = q_1 + q_2\), because link \(2\) turns by \(q_2\) against link \(1\), which is already turned by \(q_1\). The end effector is at \(\vek r_0 = (l_2, 0)\) from \(B\). So

\[\vek b = l_1\begin{pmatrix} \cos q_1 \\ \sin q_1 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek e = \vek b + l_2\begin{pmatrix} \cos(q_1 + q_2) \\ \sin(q_1 + q_2) \end{pmatrix} . \tag{27.1}\]

For \(q_1 = 30°\) and \(q_2 = 60°\) we get \(\vek b = (0{,}866;\ 0{,}500)\) m and \(\vek e = (0{,}866;\ 1{,}000)\) m: the second link has the rotation \(\varphi_2 = 90°\) and points vertically up, as the figure shows, which was drawn from exactly these numbers. The end effector is at the coordinates \(0{,}866\) m from the axis \(y_0\) and \(1{,}0\) m from the axis \(x_0\) (numbers from NumPy).

Did we compute the same as for the double pendulum? Let us check on figure 27.7.

For the double pendulum (example 8.50) the links hang from the point \(O\). The angles are measured from the downward vertical, \(\theta_1 = \pi/6\) and \(\theta_2 = \pi/3\). In the axes of the pendulum, \(x\) to the right and \(y\) up, the point \(B\) is at \((0{,}5000;\ -0{,}8660)\) m and the end \(E\) at \((0{,}9330;\ -1{,}1160)\) m. To read the pendulum as an arm we turn the axes: let the axis \(x_0\) point down and the axis \(y_0\) to the right. Together with the perpendicular axis \(z\) out of the plane of the drawing they form a right-handed system. The horizontal coordinate of the pendulum is then the coordinate \(y_0\), and the vertical one is \(-x_0\). The pendulum angles in this system are the rotations of the links from the axis \(x_0\), that is \(\varphi_1 = 30°\) and \(\varphi_2 = 60°\), and the joint variables are \(q_1 = 30°\) and \(q_2 = \varphi_2 - \varphi_1 = 30°\), the angle from the dashed extension of the first link. Equation (27.1) gives \(\vek b = (0{,}866;\ 0{,}500)\) m and \(\vek e = (1{,}116;\ 0{,}933)\) m, these are the distances of the point \(B\) and the point \(E\), read along the axes \(x_0\) and \(y_0\). In the axes of the pendulum these are \((0{,}500;\ -0{,}866)\) m and \((0{,}933;\ -1{,}116)\) m, as in chapter 8 (NumPy). The relative angle \(q_2 = \theta_2 - \theta_1\) is chosen there as the second generalized coordinate (step 3 of example 8.50), here it is the variable of the second joint.

Why are the two numbers \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) enough to write the position of every point of the arm? Let us count on figure 27.8.

On the left are the links of arm \(A\) without joints, free in the plane \(xy\). Link \(1\) needs three numbers: the coordinates \(x_1\), \(y_1\) of the point \(O_1\) and the rotation \(\varphi_1\). Link \(2\) needs three as well. Together that is \(3 + 3 = 6\) numbers. A joint is a pin that holds two points together. The first pin fixes \(O_1\) to the origin: the gap between the origin and \(O_1\) has a horizontal part \(f_1\) and a vertical part \(f_2\), and both must be zero. The second pin fixes \(O_2\) to the end of link \(1\): this gap too has two parts, \(f_3\) and \(f_4\). Each pin takes two numbers, because a gap in the plane has two directions, and a pin does not hinder the rotation. What remains is \(6 - 2 - 2 = 2\). On the right the arm is assembled: the pins \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) are inserted, only the angles \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) are still free, and from them we get the rotation of the second link \(\varphi_2 = q_1 + q_2\). The lemma says the same for \(n\) links and adds what the counting alone does not show: that no pin equation repeats another and that the angles can really be chosen freely.

Lemma 27.4 Joint variables of an open planar chain are generalized coordinates (spremenljivke zglobov odprte ravninske verige so posplošene koordinate)

Let a chain consist of \(n\) rigid links moving in the plane \(xy\) and \(n\) revolute joints with axes perpendicular to this plane, open by definition 27.1. The point \(O_{\mathrm{i}}\) of link \(i\) is the centre of joint \(i\). The point \(O_{\mathrm{i}+1}\) is the point of link \(i\) at the distance \(l_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) from \(O_{\mathrm{i}}\) that lies, in the position with the angle \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), on the axis \(x\) from \(O_{\mathrm{i}}\). Link \(0\) stands still, its point \(O_1\) is at the origin. Let \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) be the rotation of link \(i\) by lemma 8.41, \(\varphi_0 = 0\), so that the joint variable is \(q_{\mathrm{i}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{i}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{i}-1}\). Then:

  1. The configuration of the chain (definition 8.42) has \(N = 3n\) numbers, the constraints of the joints are \(m = 2n\) independent scleronomic holonomic constraints (definition 8.43), and the number of degrees of freedom is \(n\).
  2. The joint variables \(q_1, \dots, q_{\mathrm{n}}\) are generalized coordinates of the chain (definition 8.46) at every \(\vek q \in \mathbb{R}^n\), not only near a chosen position, with the map \(\vek X\) given by equation (27.2) below.
Proof

We must show that the constraints of the joints give \(2n\) independent equations, and that the angles \(q\) are mapped to a configuration by a map whose columns have \(n\) pivots.

  1. Link \(i\) has by definition 8.42 three numbers, \((x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{i}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{i}})\), where \((x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{i}})\) is the position of the point \(O_{\mathrm{i}}\) (left in the figure for \(n = 2\)). Link \(0\) stands still and is not in the configuration. So \(N = 3n\).
  2. Joint \(1\) holds \(O_1\) at the origin: \(f_1 = x_1 = 0\) and \(f_2 = y_1 = 0\) (gap to the origin). Joint \(i + 1\) (\(i = 1, \dots, n - 1\)) holds \(O_{\mathrm{i}+1}\) at a point of link \(i\). By lemma 8.41 this point is at the position \(\vek o + \mat R(\varphi)\vek r_0\) with \(\vek r_0 = (l_{\mathrm{i}}, 0)\), so \(f_{2\mathrm{i}+1} = x_{\mathrm{i}+1} - x_{\mathrm{i}} - l_{\mathrm{i}}\cos\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) and \(f_{2\mathrm{i}+2} = y_{\mathrm{i}+1} - y_{\mathrm{i}} - l_{\mathrm{i}}\sin\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). For \(i = 1\) these are the parts of the gap between the end of link \(1\) and \(O_2\). Altogether there are \(m = 2n\) constraints, none contains time.
  3. We number the coordinates so that \(x_1, y_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}\) are the first columns of the \(2n \times 3n\) matrix \(\partial\vek f/\partial\vek x\). Of these, the constraint \(f_{2\mathrm{i}+1}\) contains only \(x_{\mathrm{i}+1}\) with the coefficient \(1\) and \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the constraint \(f_{2\mathrm{i}+2}\) only \(y_{\mathrm{i}+1}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{i}}\), and all nonzero entries are on the diagonal or below it. The matrix of these \(2n\) columns is lower triangular with ones on the diagonal. The reason can be seen in the figure: each pin attaches the new point \(O_{\mathrm{i}+1}\) to the link before it, so its gap contains the new coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{i}+1}\), \(y_{\mathrm{i}+1}\) and besides them only the numbers of the previous link. Elimination of the lower rows gives the identity matrix, so it has \(2n\) pivots (definition 8.21) and the constraints are independent (definition 8.43).
  4. By definition 8.46 the number of degrees of freedom is \(n = N - m = 3n - 2n\) (for \(n = 2\) these are the angles \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) that remain of the six numbers). This is point 1.
  5. Let \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} = q_1 + \dots + q_{\mathrm{i}}\) (which follows from \(q_{\mathrm{i}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{i}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(\varphi_0 = 0\), for arm \(A\) this is \(\varphi_2 = q_1 + q_2\)) and
    \[x_1 = y_1 = 0 , \quad x_{\mathrm{i}+1} = x_{\mathrm{i}} + l_{\mathrm{i}}\cos\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} , \quad y_{\mathrm{i}+1} = y_{\mathrm{i}} + l_{\mathrm{i}}\sin\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} . \tag{27.2}\]
    The map \(\vek X(\vek q) = (x_1, y_1, \varphi_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\) is continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (sums and derivatives of sine and cosine, theorem 8.13) and satisfies the constraints by step 2: we insert \(x_{\mathrm{i}+1} - x_{\mathrm{i}} = l_{\mathrm{i}}\cos\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) into \(f_{2\mathrm{i}+1}\) and get zero.
  6. The matrix \(\partial\vek X/\partial\vek q\) has in the rows of the angles \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) (for arm \(A\) the row of \(\varphi_2 = q_1 + q_2\) has two ones) a square lower triangular matrix \(\mat L\) with \(L_{\mathrm{ij}} = 1\) for \(j \le i\) and \(L_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) otherwise. We put these rows at the top (a row swap is allowed by definition 8.21). In step \(k\) of the elimination row \(k\) equals row \(k\) of the identity matrix: at the start it has ones in the columns \(1, \dots, k\), and in each step \(j < k\) we subtract from it row \(j\), which is then row \(j\) of the identity matrix. Its one in column \(k\) is the pivot. So the elimination finds a pivot in each of the \(n\) columns, as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 8.47. Since the square matrix \(\mat L\) has \(n\) pivots by the same steps, it is invertible by lemma 8.22. This is the third requirement of definition 8.46, the first two hold by step 5. This is point 2, at every \(\vek q\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. SPONG section 1.1.2 (PDF p. 28) says that the configuration of a robot is given by the vector of joint variables and that the number of joints determines the number of degrees of freedom. The coordinates of chapter 8 are example 8.50, where \(n = 2\).

What did we show? For an open chain we can choose all \(n\) joint variables freely, and every choice gives an admissible position, with no hidden constraint between them. Why are the joint variables \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) relative angles and not absolute angles \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\)? The motor in joint \(i\) turns link \(i\) against link \(i - 1\), and the sensor in the joint also tells only \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\). The same chain could be described by the \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\), since \(\mat L\) is invertible, but the motor does not grip these angles. For arm \(A\) we have \(n = 2\), \(N = 6\) and \(m = 4\). The matrix \(\partial\vek f/\partial\vek x\) has four pivots at \(\vek q = (30°, 60°)\) and also at \(q_1 = 0\), the matrix \(\partial\vek X/\partial\vek q\) has two, and the product \((\partial\vek f/\partial\vek x)(\partial\vek X/\partial\vek q)\) is the zero matrix, as lemma 8.48 demands (SymPy).

The lemma says "open", and that condition is used. Let us see what happens when it is missing.

Example 27.5 Closed chain: toggle mechanism D (zaprta veriga: mehanizem D)

Take mechanism \(D\) of example 8.49: bars \(AB\) and \(BC\) of length \(a = 0{,}5\) m, joint \(A\) is fixed, the end \(C\) slides on a horizontal guide. On the left of the figure is the mechanism. The chain has four links: the base with the guide, the bar \(AB\), the bar \(BC\) and the slider. The joints are the revolute joint \(A\) between the base and \(AB\), the revolute joint \(B\), the revolute joint \(C\) between \(BC\) and the slider, and the prismatic joint between the slider and the base. The chain returns to the base, it is closed, and definition 27.1 excludes it.

  1. The joint variables by definition 27.3 are: \(q_1\), the angle of the bar \(AB\) from the guide, \(q_2\), the angle of the bar \(BC\) against the extension of \(AB\) (\(q_2\)), \(q_3\), the angle of the bar \(BC\) from the guide, and \(d = x_{\mathrm{C}}\). Step 4 of example 8.49 gives \(\varphi_2 = -\varphi_1\) and \(x_2 = \tfrac32 a\cos\theta\), hence \(x_{\mathrm{C}} = x_2 + \tfrac a2\cos\varphi_2 = 2a\cos\theta\), and so \(q_1 = \theta\), \(q_2 = \varphi_2 - \varphi_1 = -2\theta\), \(q_3 = -\theta\) and \(d = 2a\cos\theta\). At \(\theta = 30°\) we have \((q_1, q_2, q_3, d) = (30°, -60°, -30°, 0{,}866\ \text{m})\), at \(\theta = 20°\) it is \((20°, -40°, -20°, 0{,}940\ \text{m})\).
  2. These are four joint variables but one single degree of freedom: step 5 of example 8.49 found five independent constraints on six configuration numbers. The variables cannot be coordinates, because by definition 8.46 there are \(n = 6 - 5 = 1\) of them, not four. Lemma 27.4 says nothing here, because the chain is not open. We can choose only one, \(q_1\), the others depend on it.
  3. Where in the proof of the lemma does this show? The bars \(AB\) and \(BC\) are an open chain with two joints, and the lemma gives it the coordinates \((q_1, q_2)\), since at a free end \(C\) everything is possible. The end \(C\) must lie on the guide, which is an additional constraint \(g(q_1, q_2) = a\sin q_1 + a\sin(q_1 + q_2) = 0\) (the height of the point \(C\)). This constraint is not one of the joint constraints of step 2 of the proof, it links the angles of the two joints. Because of it the constraints are no longer triangular as in step 3.
  4. At \(q = (30°, -60°)\) we have \(g = 0{,}25 - 0{,}25 = 0\), the end is at \((0{,}866;\ 0)\) m, on the guide. At \(q = (30°, 30°)\) we have \(g = 0{,}25 + 0{,}433 = 0{,}683\) m, the end \(C'\) is at \((0{,}683;\ 0{,}683)\) m and is not on the guide. At \(q_1 = 30°\) the constraint \(g = 0\) has only the solution \(q_2 = -60°\) (besides the folded position \(q_2 = 180°\), which we leave out, as in chapter 8), so \(q_2\) is not free.
  5. The matrix of derivatives of the constraint is the row \(\partial g/\partial\vek q = (a\cos q_1 + a\cos(q_1 + q_2),\ a\cos(q_1 + q_2)) = (0{,}866;\ 0{,}433)\) m at \(q = (30°, -60°)\), and it has one pivot. One independent constraint, the end \(C\) on the guide, so \(2 - 1 = 1\) degree of freedom, as in chapter 8.

Source: The mechanism and its numbers are from example 8.49. The conclusion about the closed chain and the constraint \(g\) are ours.

The example says what "open" means in the model. In a closed chain, such as the mechanism of a piston engine, the joint variables are not all independent, and we treat this in chapter 23. An open planar chain with \(n\) revolute joints has exactly \(n\) independent variables (lemma 27.4). That this also holds with prismatic joints and in space we quote from SPONG section 1.1.2 (PDF p. 28) without proof.

Now we can answer the third question from the start of the section: how far does the end of the arm reach?

Definition 27.6 Workspace (delovni prostor)

Let \(E\) be the end effector of a serial manipulator whose joint variables \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) can take values from sets \(S_{\mathrm{i}} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), for an ideal revolute joint from all real numbers, for a prismatic joint from an interval limited by the stroke of the guide. The workspace (delovni prostor) is the set of positions of the point \(E\) that we get when \(\vek q\) runs through all values of \(S_1 \times \dots \times S_{\mathrm{n}}\). The position of \(E\) is a function of the column \(\vek q\), as equation (27.1) is for arm \(A\).

Source: SPONG section 1.1.4 (PDF p. 29): the workspace is the total volume swept out by the end effector when the manipulator executes all possible motions, constrained by the geometry of the manipulator and the mechanical constraints on the joints. SPONG splits it into the reachable workspace and the dexterous workspace, the points that the end effector can reach with an arbitrary orientation. We use the reachable workspace and do not define the dexterous one, because we write the orientation of a link only in the next section.

The name workspace has a reason: it is the space in which the robot can work. For arm \(A\) we compute it completely, it is the annulus in the figure below.

The answer and the way to it we read on two figures. Figure 27.10 shows the answer, the blue annulus around the joint \(O\). Figure 27.11 shows how the arm reaches one chosen point of the annulus.

In the figure the arm \(A\) is in the axes \(x_0\), \(y_0\) with its end at the point \(\vek p\). The blue segment is the distance \(r = |\vek p|\) of the end from \(O\). With the links it forms the triangle \(OBE\), which has at \(B\) the angle \(q_2\) between the extension of the first link and the second link. The proof reaches the point in two moves, as if we set the arm with our hands. First it chooses the \(q_2\) that gives the right distance: the distance of the end from \(O\) depends only on how much the arm is bent at the joint \(B\), not on where the arm points. The dashed grey arm has this \(q_2\) and \(q_1 = 0\). Its end \(\vek w\) is already at the distance \(r\), but in the wrong direction, at the angle \(\alpha\) instead of the angle \(\psi\) of the point \(\vek p\). Then it turns the whole arm by \(q_1 = \psi - \alpha\), and the end arrives at \(\vek p\).

Lemma 27.7 Workspace of the RR arm (delovni prostor roke RR)

Let an RR arm have the lengths \(l_1 > l_2 > 0\), revolute joints with no limit on the angle, and the end effector \(E\) at the end of the second link. Then its workspace is the closed annulus

\[\{\,\vek p \in \mathbb{R}^2 : l_1 - l_2 \le |\vek p| \le l_1 + l_2\,\} ,\]

where \(|\vek p|\) is the distance of the point from the joint \(O\). For \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m this is the annulus between \(0{,}5\) m and \(1{,}5\) m with the area \(2\pi = 6{,}2832\) m\(^2\).

Proof

We must show two things: that the position of the end effector always lies in the annulus, and that every point of the annulus is reached by some choice of \(q_1\), \(q_2\). For the first we compute the distance from equation (27.1), for the second we find the angles.

  1. Let \(\vek e(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)\). By equation (27.1), \(\vek p = l_1\vek e(q_1) + l_2\vek e(q_1 + q_2)\), the path from \(O\) along both links to the end.
  2. The squared distance is \(|\vek p|^2 = l_1^2(\cos^2 q_1 + \sin^2 q_1) + l_2^2(\cos^2(q_1 + q_2) + \sin^2(q_1 + q_2)) + 2l_1l_2\big(\cos q_1\cos(q_1 + q_2) + \sin q_1\sin(q_1 + q_2)\big)\). The first two brackets are \(1\) (lemma 8.11, point 1). The third is \(\cos q_2\): the addition formulas (corollary 8.16) with \(\alpha = q_1 + q_2\) and \(\beta = -q_1\), together with the oddness of sine and the evenness of cosine (lemma 8.11, point 4), give \(\cos q_2 = \cos(q_1 + q_2)\cos q_1 + \sin(q_1 + q_2)\sin q_1\). Hence
    \[|\vek p|^2 = l_1^2 + l_2^2 + 2l_1l_2\cos q_2 . \tag{27.3}\]
    The angle \(q_1\) dropped out: the distance \(r\) depends only on the angle \(q_2\).
  3. Since \(-1 \le \cos q_2 \le 1\) (lemma 8.11, point 1), we have \((l_1 - l_2)^2 \le |\vek p|^2 \le (l_1 + l_2)^2\). Both sides are squares of nonnegative numbers, because \(l_1 > l_2\), so lemma 1.29 gives \(l_1 - l_2 \le |\vek p| \le l_1 + l_2\). In the figure the largest distance is at the extended arm, the smallest at the folded one.
  4. Conversely. Let \(\vek p\) be a point with \(r = |\vek p|\) and \(l_1 - l_2 \le r \le l_1 + l_2\), so \(r > 0\). Let \(c = (r^2 - l_1^2 - l_2^2)/(2l_1l_2)\). From \(r^2 \ge (l_1 - l_2)^2\) it follows that \(c \ge -1\), and from \(r^2 \le (l_1 + l_2)^2\) that \(c \le 1\). By definition 8.10, point 1, there is \(q_2 \in [0, \pi]\) with \(\cos q_2 = c\).
  5. Let \(\vek w = (l_1 + l_2\cos q_2,\ l_2\sin q_2)\), the end of the arm with this \(q_2\) and \(q_1 = 0\). With the addition formulas (corollary 8.16), \(l_1\vek e(q_1) + l_2\vek e(q_1 + q_2) = \mat R(q_1)\vek w\) for every \(q_1\), where \(\mat R(q_1)\) is the matrix of lemma 8.41. By equation (27.3) for this \(q_2\), \(|\vek w|^2 = l_1^2 + l_2^2 + 2l_1l_2c = r^2\), so \(|\vek w| = r > 0\).
  6. By step 2 of the proof of lemma 8.41 there are angles \(\psi\) and \(\alpha\) with \(\vek e(\psi) = \vek p/r\) and \(\vek e(\alpha) = \vek w/r\). Let \(q_1 = \psi - \alpha\). Then \(\mat R(q_1)\vek w = r\,\mat R(\psi - \alpha)\vek e(\alpha) = r\,\vek e(\psi) = \vek p\) (addition formulas). The point \(\vek p\) is reached.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. SPONG section 3.3.1 (PDF p. 109-110) treats the same planar two-link arm with Denavit-Hartenberg matrices, it does not compute the workspace there. The proof and the cosine formula are ours.

The proof also shows how a point is reached. For \(\vek p = (0{,}866;\ 1{,}000)\) m we have \(r = 1{,}3229\) m, \(c = 0{,}5\), so \(q_2 = 60°\). The vector \(\vek w = (1{,}25;\ 0{,}433)\) m has the polar angle \(19{,}1°\), the point \(\vek p\) has the polar angle \(49{,}1°\), so \(q_1 = 49{,}1° - 19{,}1° = 30°\), as at the start (SymPy and NumPy).

Where did the assumption enter that the joint rotation is not limited? In step 4, which takes \(q_2\) anywhere between \(0\) and \(180°\), and in step 6, which takes an arbitrary \(q_1\). A real arm has a limited angle. If joint \(B\) allows only \(q_2\) between \(-150°\) and \(150°\), then by equation (27.3) the smallest distance is \(\sqrt{1 + 0{,}25 + \cos 150°} = 0{,}620\) m instead of \(0{,}5\) m (NumPy): the hole in the middle is larger, but the outer edge stays. The axes \(x_0\) and \(y_0\) cross at \(O\), from where both radii are measured.

In figure 27.10 the annulus around joint \(O\) is the workspace, and the two radii are the distances \(l_1 - l_2 = 0{,}5\) m and \(l_1 + l_2 = 1{,}5\) m. The outer edge is reached by the stretched arm with \(q_2 = 0\) (by equation (27.3) \(r = l_1 + l_2\)), the inner edge by the folded arm with \(q_2 = 180°\).

The annulus is not a disc. What is in the middle? Let us look at a point that lies near \(O\) but is not on it. The point \(U\) at the distance \(0{,}3\) m from \(O\) is unreachable: it would be reached if \(\cos q_2 = (0{,}09 - 1 - 0{,}25)/1 = -1{,}16\), which is less than \(-1\), so no such position exists. The inner radius \(0{,}5\) m is therefore a real obstacle: an arm with a longer first link cannot fold the second link so that the end comes closer than \(l_1 - l_2\). If the links were equally long, \(l_1 = l_2 = 1\) m, then by equation (27.3) \(|\vek p|^2 = 2 + 2\cos q_2\) and \(|\vek p|\) would reach zero at \(q_2 = 180°\): the hole disappears, the workspace is a disc of radius \(2\) m and area \(4\pi = 12{,}566\) m\(^2\). Step 6 of the proof would then fail at \(r = 0\), because the angle \(\alpha\) does not exist, but in that case the point \(O\) is reached at every \(q_1\) with \(q_2 = 180°\). For \(l_1 < l_2\) the hole stays too: by equation (27.3) \(|\vek p|^2 \ge l_1^2 + l_2^2 - 2l_1l_2 = (l_2 - l_1)^2 > 0\), and the same proof with \(l_2 - l_1\) in place of \(l_1 - l_2\) gives the annulus between \(l_2 - l_1\) and \(l_1 + l_2\). For \(l_1 = 0{,}5\) m and \(l_2 = 1\) m the end comes no closer to the point \(O\) than \(0{,}5\) m (NumPy). So there is a hole exactly when the two lengths differ, and its radius is \(|l_1 - l_2|\). The condition \(l_1 > l_2\) in the lemma only simplifies the notation, it does not cause the hole.

We checked the two radii of the annulus by tabulation: on a \(361 \times 361\) grid of the angles \(q_1\), \(q_2\) the smallest distance of the end is \(0{,}5000\) m and the largest \(1{,}5000\) m (NumPy).

What we have. An open planar chain of \(n\) rigid links with \(n\) revolute joints has \(n\) degrees of freedom, and its joint variables \(q_1, \dots, q_{\mathrm{n}}\) are generalized coordinates of chapter 8 (lemma 27.4). For prismatic joints and chains in space we quoted this from SPONG without proof. For the planar RR arm we computed the position of the end, checked it with the double pendulum and determined the workspace. We used three things: the position of a rigid body in the plane (lemma 8.41), the independence of constraints by pivots (definition 8.21) and the addition formulas. In space the position of a link is not written with one angle. The next section therefore writes the rotation of a link with a matrix, called the orientation matrix, and then the position of a link together with a point, since we build the position of the end of the arm from the positions of the links. The idealizations of joints and links that we named at the start of the section hold for all sections of this chapter until we say otherwise.

Notation. \(n\) is the number of joints and the number of degrees of freedom (as in chapter 8), \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) the joint variables and generalized coordinates, \(\vek q\) their column. The letter \(\theta\) is the angle of a revolute joint, \(d\) the displacement of a prismatic one, \(l_{\mathrm{i}}\) the distance between the axes of joints \(i\) and \(i + 1\). The letters \(\mat R\), \(\mat T\), \(\mat J\), \(\mat C\), \(g\) and \(\tau\) have in this chapter a different meaning from earlier in the book, and we shall say it for each in the section where it first appears: in this section \(\mat R(\varphi)\) is still the matrix of the planar rotation of lemma 8.41.

27.2 Orientation of links (orientacija členov)

The bottom line is the base, the fixed support of the robot. A robot arm is a chain of links, and at the end sits a link with a tool, for example a welding torch or a screwdriver. The chosen point of this link we called the gripper (prijemalo, definition 27.1). The torch must stand at a right angle to the seam, the screwdriver must point straight into the screw. So for every link we ask where it is and which way it faces. In this section we treat the second, the facing, which is called the orientation (orientacija): the word says which way a body is turned, not where it is. The position we add in the next section.

The model is the one the chapter on the rigid body sets up: the links are rigid (definition 1.11), so the points of a link keep their mutual distances. Because of the rigidity it is enough to follow one coordinate system, which we fix to the link and which moves with it. We call it the frame of a link (okvir člena), because in it, as in the frame of a picture, we measure all the points of the link, and the frame moves with the link like a frame with its picture. In this chapter frames are right-handed orthogonal Cartesian coordinate systems (definition 2.32) with the same unit of length. Frame 0 is fixed to the base of the robot and stands still, frame 1 is fixed to the link we watch.

Rigidity is an assumption, so let us say what it costs. It is right as long as a link bends under its load by less than the accuracy we ask of the robot. It fails for long slender arms and heavy loads, where the end of a link visibly sags. Its effect on the result is a turn of the frame that the model does not see: if the end of a link tilts by \(0{,}001\) rad because of bending, the tip of a tool \(0{,}1\) m further on moves by the arc \(0{,}1 \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}0001\) m, a tenth of a millimetre (an arc is the radius times the angle in radians). As long as this is below the required accuracy, a link has one orientation and one frame is enough.

We begin with a rotation in the plane, where we know what a rotation is (lemma 8.41). Figure 27.14 looks along the axis \(z\), which points toward us.

First we draw the axes \(x_0\) and \(y_0\) of frame 0, which is the base of the robot. The link has the axes \(x_1\) and \(y_1\) of frame 1, turned from the axis \(y_0\) by the angle \(\theta\). Where the axis \(x_1\) points relative to frame 0 is told by two numbers, how far it points in the direction \(x_0\) and how far in the direction \(y_0\). So we drop the perpendiculars from the tip of the axis \(x_1\) onto the axes of frame 0 and read off \(\cos 30^\circ = 0{,}866\) and \(\sin 30^\circ = 0{,}5\). These are the components of the unit vector of the axis \(x_1\) in frame 0 (the scalar product with the unit vectors of the axes, definition 2.8). In the same way the perpendiculars from the axis \(y_1\) give the components \(-0{,}5\) and \(0{,}866\). We complete both triples with the axis \(z\) and put them into a matrix, one column for each axis of the link.

Definition 27.8 Orientation matrix (matrika orientacije)

Let \(i\) and \(j\) be frames with the same unit of length and \(\vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{z}}\) the unit vectors of the axes of frame \(j\). The orientation matrix of frame \(j\) relative to frame \(i\) is the \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat R^{\ix{i}}_{\mathrm{j}}\) whose columns hold the components of these three vectors in frame \(i\):

\[\mat R^{\ix{i}}_{\mathrm{j}} = \begin{bmatrix} \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{x}} & \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{y}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{x}} & \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{z}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{x}} \\ \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{y}} & \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{y}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{y}} & \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{z}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{y}} \\ \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{z}} & \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{y}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{z}} & \vek e^{j}_{\mathrm{z}}\cdot\vek e^{i}_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} . \tag{27.4}\]

The upper index tells the frame in which the components are written, the lower index the frame whose axes stand in the columns. The matrix is an object of size \(3 \times 3\) that describes the orientation, not the position.

Source: SPONG (2.1), (2.2) (PDF p. 61-63), where the matrix for the plane and for space is written with \(\mat R^0_1\) and columns with the components of the axes of frame 1 in frame 0.

This matrix is the transpose of the rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) of definition 2.44, which has the new axes in its rows (lemma 27.9 proves it). From now on in this chapter we write \(\mat R\) for the orientation matrix, always with both indices. The letter \(\mat R\) is used in the book also for the rotation in the decomposition of the deformation gradient (section 2.13.4) and as \(\mat R(\varphi)\) for the planar \(2 \times 2\) rotation in equation (8.28). We shall not meet them here, and the matrix \(\mat Q(t)\) of definition 8.39 is the same matrix as \(\mat R^0_1(t)\) of a link that lay on frame 0 at time \(0\) and turns about its origin (see the end of the proof of lemma 27.9).

What does the matrix say about the vectors of a link, for example about the vector from one point of the link to another? Let such a vector have the components \(\vek p^{1}\) in frame 1, a column of three numbers, and the components \(\vek p^{0}\) in frame 0. The orientation matrix converts the first into the second. This and the properties of the matrix are stated by the next lemma.

Lemma 27.9 Orientation matrix and turning the axes (matrika orientacije in zasuk osi)

Let 0 and 1 be frames as above and \(\mat Q\) the rotation matrix from frame 0 to frame 1 (definition 2.44). Then:

  1. \(\mat R^0_1 = \mat Q^\T\) (the columns are the axes of frame 1).
  2. \(\mat R^0_1\) is an orthogonal matrix with determinant \(1\) (the axes of both frames are unit, orthogonal and right-handed).
  3. Let a vector have the components \(\vek p^{1}\) in frame 1 and \(\vek p^{0}\) in frame 0. Then \(\vek p^{0} = \mat R^0_1\,\vek p^{1}\) and \(\vek p^{1} = (\mat R^0_1)^\T\,\vek p^{0}\).
  4. \(\mat R^1_0 = (\mat R^0_1)^\T = (\mat R^0_1)^{-1}\) (frame 0 is turned relative to frame 1 by the same angle in the other direction).
Proof

We must show four points. The first is a comparison of columns with rows, the second a restatement of the properties of \(\mat Q\), the third the rule for components in turned axes, the fourth an exchange of frames.

  1. The element in row \(k\) and column \(l\) of \(\mat R^0_1\) is by definition 27.8 the scalar product \(\vek e^{1}_{\mathrm{l}}\cdot\vek e^{0}_{\mathrm{k}}\). The element in row \(l\) and column \(k\) of \(\mat Q\) is by definition 2.44 \(Q_{\mathrm{lk}} = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the old frame 0 and the new frame 1, so the same number. The elements \((k, l)\) of \(\mat R^0_1\) and \((l, k)\) of \(\mat Q\) are equal, hence \(\mat R^0_1 = \mat Q^\T\) (definition 1.101).
  2. The matrix \(\mat Q\) is orthogonal (lemma 2.47), so \(\mat Q\mat Q^\T = \mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\). For \(\mat R = \mat Q^\T\) we have \(\mat R^\T = \mat Q\), so \(\mat R^\T\mat R = \mat Q\mat Q^\T = \mat I\) and \(\mat R\mat R^\T = \mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\). This is orthogonality (definition 2.46).
  3. Determinant: \(\det\mat R = \det\mat Q^\T = \det\mat Q\) (lemma 2.73, point 6). By section 2.10.3, the paragraph after theorem 2.74, \(\det\mat Q = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\times\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}})\), which is \(\pm 1\), and \(1\) when the new frame is right-handed. Frame 1 is right-handed by convention, so \(\det\mat R^0_1 = 1\).
  4. By lemma 2.45, point 2, for the old component \(\vek a = \vek p^{0}\) and the new \(\bar{\vek a} = \vek p^{1}\) we have \(\vek p^{0} = \mat Q^\T\vek p^{1} = \mat R^0_1\vek p^{1}\). Point 1 of the same lemma gives \(\vek p^{1} = \mat Q\,\vek p^{0} = (\mat R^0_1)^\T\vek p^{0}\).
  5. We exchange the frames. Since \(\vek p^{1} = \mat R^1_0\,\vek p^{0}\) for every vector by step 4 applied with the roles exchanged, and also \(\vek p^{1} = (\mat R^0_1)^\T\vek p^{0}\), the matrices \(\mat R^1_0\) and \((\mat R^0_1)^\T\) are equal on the columns \(\vek p^{0} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), hence equal. Since \(\mat R^0_1\) is orthogonal, \((\mat R^0_1)^\T\) is its inverse matrix (step 2 of this proof and definition 1.110).
  6. Let the link lie on frame 0 at time \(0\) and turn about the origin of frame 0, so that the two frames always have a common origin. The vector from this origin to a point of the link has the components \(\vek p^{1} = \vek X\) in frame 1, which are constant because frame 1 moves with the link. The position of the point at time \(t\) is \(\vek p^{0}(t) = \mat R^0_1(t)\,\vek X\). This is the rigid motion \(\vek x(t) = \vek c(t) + \mat Q(t)\vek X\) of definition 8.39 with \(\vek c = \vek 0\), so in this case \(\mat Q(t) = \mat R^0_1(t)\).

Source: SPONG (2.9) (PDF p. 67) for the components, orthogonality and determinant 1 after SPONG p. 62-63. The proof from the rotation matrix of the book is not from the source.

In the figure above \(\mat R^0_1\) is the matrix

\[\mat R^0_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}866 & -0{,}5 & 0 \\ 0{,}5 & 0{,}866 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

the first column holds the components of the axis \(x_1\), the second of the axis \(y_1\). The frames of the figure have a common origin, so the vector from it to a point of the link is a vector of point 3 of the lemma. If it has the components \(\vek p^{1} = (0{,}4;\ 0{,}3;\ 0{,}2)\) m in frame 1, it has by point 3 in frame 0 the components \(\vek p^{0} = \mat R^0_1\vek p^{1} = (0{,}1964;\ 0{,}4598;\ 0{,}2000)\) m. The vector is equally long in both frames, \(|\vek p^{1}| = |\vek p^{0}| = 0{,}5385\) m, as it must be for a rigid link: \(|\mat R\vek p|^2 = \vek p\cdot(\mat R^\T\mat R\,\vek p) = |\vek p|^2\) by equation (2.137) and orthogonality.

Why multiplying by the matrix gives the right components is shown in figure 27.15. It draws again frame 0 and frame 1, turned by \(30^\circ\). The vector \(\vek p\) is an arrow drawn on the link. In frame 1 we reach its tip by going \(0{,}4\) m along the axis \(x_1\) and then \(0{,}3\) m along the axis \(y_1\), the third \(0{,}2\) m goes along the axis \(z\) towards us. So the vector is the sum of \(0{,}4\) of the axis \(x_1\), \(0{,}3\) of the axis \(y_1\) and \(0{,}2\) of the axis \(z_1\). The axes of frame 1 are in frame 0 the columns of the matrix \(\mat R^0_1\), so \(\vek p^{0} = 0{,}4\,(0{,}866;\ 0{,}5;\ 0) + 0{,}3\,(-0{,}5;\ 0{,}866;\ 0) + 0{,}2\,(0;\ 0;\ 1)\) m. The product \(\mat R^0_1\vek p^{1}\) computes exactly this sum of the columns multiplied by the components. The perpendiculars from the tip onto the axes of frame 0 read it off: \(0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}866 - 0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}5 = 0{,}196\) m and \(0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}5 + 0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}866 = 0{,}460\) m. The arrow did not move in this, we only changed the frame in which we measure it.

A robot is built from links, so we shall compose rotations many times, and each is a rotation about one axis. We give these rotations names.

Definition 27.10 Basic rotations (osnovni zasuki)

For an angle \(\theta\) in radians the basic rotations about the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are the matrices

\[\mat R_{\mathrm{x},\theta} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} , \quad \mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} , \quad \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} . \tag{27.5}\]

The matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\) is the orientation matrix of the frame that we get from frame 0 by turning by the angle \(\theta\) about its axis \(a\) in the direction of a right-handed screw: seen from the tip of the axis \(a\) toward the origin, the rotation at \(\theta > 0\) is counterclockwise. At \(\theta = 90^\circ\) the axis that follows \(a\) in the order \(x \to y \to z \to x\) goes to the place of the axis after it (at \(a = z\), \(x\) goes to \(y\)).

Source: SPONG (2.3) (PDF p. 64) for \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\) and p. 65 for \(\mat R_{\mathrm{x},\theta}\) and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta}\). The matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\) is the same rotation as in lemma 8.41.

The columns are read off figure 27.14: for \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\) they are precisely the components of the axes \(x_1\) and \(y_1\), \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) and \((-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\), and the axis \(z\) stays. In a rotation about \(x\) the axis \(x\) stays and the axis \(y\) goes toward the axis \(z\), in a rotation about \(y\) the axis \(y\) stays and the axis \(z\) goes toward the axis \(x\). This is the same picture with cyclically renamed axes, so the columns are the same with the places exchanged accordingly. The sign of the direction of rotation, into which axis the first axis in the order goes, is a convention, and the right-handed screw is the same convention as for the right-handed system (definition 2.32).

Lemma 27.11 Properties of the basic rotations (lastnosti osnovnih zasukov)

For every axis \(a \in \{x, y, z\}\) and all angles \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\):

  1. \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\varphi} = \mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta+\varphi}\) (two rotations about the same axis add up).
  2. \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},0} = \mat I\) and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},-\theta} = \mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}^\T = \mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}^{-1}\) (a rotation by \(-\theta\) returns the axes).
  3. \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\) is orthogonal and has determinant \(1\) (the axes stay unit, orthogonal and right-handed).
Proof

We must show three points. One computation for \(z\) is enough, since \(x\) and \(y\) have the same form with cyclically exchanged indices.

  1. By definition 1.99 the upper left \(2 \times 2\) block of the product \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\) is
    \[\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta\cos\varphi - \sin\theta\sin\varphi & -\cos\theta\sin\varphi - \sin\theta\cos\varphi \\ \sin\theta\cos\varphi + \cos\theta\sin\varphi & -\sin\theta\sin\varphi + \cos\theta\cos\varphi \end{bmatrix} ,\]
    and the third row and third column are \((0, 0, 1)\). By the addition theorem (corollary 8.16) the elements are \(\cos(\theta + \varphi)\), \(-\sin(\theta + \varphi)\), \(\sin(\theta + \varphi)\) and \(\cos(\theta + \varphi)\), so the product is \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta+\varphi}\).
  2. At \(\theta = 0\) we have \(\cos 0 = 1\) and \(\sin 0 = 0\) (lemma 8.11, point 2), so \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},0} = \mat I\). By point 1, \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\theta} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},0} = \mat I\), and the same in the opposite order, so \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\theta}\) is the inverse matrix. Since \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\) and \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\) (lemma 8.11, point 4), \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\theta}\) is element by element the transpose \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}^\T\).
  3. From point 2, \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}^\T\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}^\T = \mat I\), which is orthogonality. By definition 2.72, \(\det\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta} = \cos\theta\cdot\cos\theta\cdot 1 - (-\sin\theta)\sin\theta\cdot 1 = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\), since the other four terms are zero (lemma 8.11, point 1).

Source: The proof is not from the source. SPONG (2.4)-(2.6) (PDF p. 64) states the properties for \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\).

An arm has several links, and each turns relative to the previous one. Frame 2 we fix to the next link, for example to the gripper. What is its orientation relative to the base if we know the orientation of frame 1 relative to frame 0 and of frame 2 relative to frame 1? And what if we turn about an axis of frame 0 instead of an axis of the link that has already turned? Let us first look at both possibilities in pictures, then compute them.

In the upper row the initial frame first turns about its axis \(z\) by \(90^\circ\). The axis \(x\) of the gripper now lies along the axis \(y_0\), the axis \(y\) along \(-x_0\), the axis \(z\) stays. Then we turn it about its own axis \(x\), which now lies along \(y_0\). After this rotation the final frame is: the axis \(x\) of the gripper is still along \(y_0\), the axis \(y\) has gone along \(z_0\), the axis \(z\) along \(x_0\). In the lower row we take the same start and the rotations in the other order. First about its own axis \(x\): the axis \(x\) stays, the axis \(y\) goes along \(z_0\) and the axis \(z\) along \(-y_0\). Then about its own axis \(z\), which now points along \(-y_0\). The final frame below has the axis \(x\) along \(z_0\), the axis \(y\) along \(-x_0\) and the axis \(z\) along \(-y_0\). The point on the axis \(x\) ends in two different places: the rotations cannot be exchanged without consequences. The computation confirms this and tells how we compose rotations.

Lemma 27.12 Composition of orientations (sestavljanje orientacij)

Let 0, 1 and 2 be frames as above. Then:

  1. \(\mat R^0_2 = \mat R^0_1\,\mat R^1_2\) and \(\vek p^{0} = \mat R^0_1\mat R^1_2\,\vek p^{2}\) (the matrix from frame 0 to 1, then from 1 to 2).
  2. If frame 2 is obtained from frame 1 by a basic rotation about its own axis \(a\) by the angle \(\theta\), then \(\mat R^0_2 = \mat R^0_1\,\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\) (a rotation about a current axis multiplies from the right).
  3. If frame 2 is obtained by turning the link with frame 1 about the axis \(a\) of frame 0 by the angle \(\theta\), then \(\mat R^0_2 = \mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\,\mat R^0_1\) (a rotation about a fixed axis multiplies from the left).
Proof

We must show three points. The first two are rules for components, the third uses that in a rotation of a rigid link all the vectors of the link are mapped by the same matrix.

  1. By point 3 of lemma 27.9, \(\vek p^{0} = \mat R^0_1\vek p^{1}\), \(\vek p^{1} = \mat R^1_2\vek p^{2}\) and \(\vek p^{0} = \mat R^0_2\vek p^{2}\) for every vector. Substituting, \(\vek p^{0} = \mat R^0_1(\mat R^1_2\vek p^{2})\) and by the associativity of the matrix product \(= (\mat R^0_1\mat R^1_2)\vek p^{2}\). This and \(\mat R^0_2\vek p^{2}\) are equal for every \(\vek p^{2}\), so also for \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), which select the columns. The matrices are equal.
  2. The axes of frame 2 have in frame 1 the components of the columns of the matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\) by definition 27.10, applied with frame 1 instead of 0, so \(\mat R^1_2 = \mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\). Point 1 gives \(\mat R^0_2 = \mat R^0_1\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\).
  3. A rotation of the link about the axis \(a\) of frame 0 is a rigid motion of definition 8.39 with \(\vek c = \vek 0\) and \(\mat Q = \mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\), since for a frame 0 that lay on the link the columns of the basic rotation are the new positions of the axes by definition 27.10, (27.5) (step 6 of the proof of lemma 27.9). So every vector of the link with components \(\vek a\) in frame 0 goes into the vector with components \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\vek a\), because the motion maps the difference of two points of a rigid body with the same matrix \(\mat Q\) (the difference of the points \(\vek x_1 - \vek x_2 = \mat Q(\vek X_1 - \vek X_2)\)).
  4. The axes of frame 1 are before the rotation vectors of the link with components in the columns of the matrix \(\mat R^0_1\). After the rotation these are the columns \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}\), where \(\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}\) is column \(k\) of \(\mat R^0_1\). These are the columns of the product \(\mat R_{\mathrm{a},\theta}\mat R^0_1\), and these are the axes of frame 2 by definition 27.8.

Source: SPONG (2.17) (PDF p. 71) for point 1 and point 2, (2.20), (2.22), (2.23) (PDF p. 73-74) for point 3. The proof of point 3 is not from the source. SPONG derives it with the similarity transformation (2.12), (2.20).

Why does a rotation about a current axis multiply from the right and a rotation about a fixed axis from the left? In point 2 the new rotation says where the axes of frame 2 are in frame 1. So the column \(\vek p^{2}\) must first go into frame 1 and only then into frame 0, and the new matrix stands on the right, next to the column. In point 3 the new rotation takes hold of a link that is already described in frame 0: the matrix \(\mat R^0_1\) first carries the column into frame 0, the basic rotation then turns it there, and the new matrix stands on the left. The matrix nearer to the column acts first. Now we can compute figure 27.16. This is also an example in which the rule for the order fails if we forget it.

Example 27.13 Order of rotations (vrstni red zasukov)

A gripper has the frame 0 at the start. We turn it first about its own axis \(z\) by \(90^\circ\) and then about its own axis \(x\) by \(90^\circ\) (upper row of figure 27.16). Then the same in the reverse order (lower row).

  1. By point 2 of lemma 27.12, above \(\mat R^0_2 = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},90^\circ}\mat R_{\mathrm{x},90^\circ}\). From equation (27.5) at \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\) and \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\) we have \(\mat R_{\mathrm{x},90^\circ} = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},90^\circ} = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\), so
    \[\mat R_{\mathrm{z},90^\circ}\mat R_{\mathrm{x},90^\circ} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]
    The columns are \((0, 1, 0)\), \((0, 0, 1)\) and \((1, 0, 0)\): the axis \(x\) of the gripper is along \(y_0\), the axis \(y\) along \(z_0\), the axis \(z\) along \(x_0\), as in the upper figure.
  2. Below, \(\mat R^0_2 = \mat R_{\mathrm{x},90^\circ}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},90^\circ}\),
    \[\mat R_{\mathrm{x},90^\circ}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},90^\circ} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} ,\]
    with the columns \((0, 0, 1)\), \((-1, 0, 0)\) and \((0, -1, 0)\), as in the lower figure. The matrices are different.
  3. A point on the axis \(x\) of the gripper at the distance \(0{,}1\) m has in the frame of the gripper the components \(\vek p^{2} = (0{,}1;\ 0;\ 0)\) m, a tenth of the first column. Above, \(\vek p^{0} = \mat R^0_2\vek p^{2} = (0;\ 0{,}1;\ 0)\) m, below \((0;\ 0;\ 0{,}1)\) m. The distance between the ends is \(\sqrt{0{,}1^2 + 0{,}1^2} = 0{,}1414\) m, more than the \(0{,}1\) m the point has from the origin. The two positions differ in gripping, and a matrix with the factors exchanged would turn the gripper the wrong way.
  4. The same two rotations made about the axes of frame 0, in the same order (first \(z_0\), then \(x_0\)), give by point 3 of lemma 27.12 \(\mat R^0_2 = \mat R_{\mathrm{x},90^\circ}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},90^\circ}\), which is the matrix of step 2. In the figure the frame after the first rotation is the one in the middle of the upper row, with the axis \(x\) of the gripper on \(y_0\). The second rotation now goes about \(x_0\) and not about the axis \(x\) of the gripper, so it lifts this axis from \(y_0\) to \(z_0\), and the final frame is the one of the lower row. So the same rotations in the same order give a different orientation depending on whether the axes are current or fixed.

Source: The numbers are from NumPy (outlines/ch-roboti/num-02.py, N4). SPONG examples 2.5 to 2.7 (PDF p. 71-73) show the same difference for \(\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\varphi}\) and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\).

A rotation matrix has nine numbers, and the orientation of a body in the plane is fixed by one angle. How many numbers do we need in space? The orthogonality \(\mat R^\T\mat R = \mat I\) gives six equations: three for the lengths of the columns and three for the perpendicularity of pairs of columns. So the nine numbers are not free, and SPONG (PDF p. 75) counts three. The next theorem confirms this by another way: three numbers really suffice, and it tells how to choose them. We take three successive rotations as with the gripper.

We start with frame 0. We turn the frame by the angle \(\varphi\) about the axis \(z\) and get frame \(a\), which has the same axis \(z\). We turn frame \(a\) by the angle \(\theta\) about its axis \(y\) and get frame \(b\), then frame \(b\) by the angle \(\psi\) about its axis \(z\) and get frame 1. All three rotations are about current axes, so by point 2 of lemma 27.12 the matrix product is in the same order: \(\mat R^0_{\mathrm{a}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\), \(\mat R^a_{\mathrm{b}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta}\), \(\mat R^b_1 = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi}\) and \(\mat R^0_1 = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi}\). The three numbers are called the Euler angles of the frame (Eulerjevi koti) after the sequence of axes \(z\), \(y\), \(z\) (ZYZ).

Theorem 27.14 ZYZ Euler angles (Eulerjevi koti ZYZ)

Let \(\mat R\) be an orthogonal \(3 \times 3\) matrix with determinant \(1\) and elements \(R_{\mathrm{kl}}\).

  1. There exist numbers \(\varphi\), \(\psi\) and \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) such that \(\mat R = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi}\). The product has the elements
    \[\begin{bmatrix} \cos\varphi\cos\theta\cos\psi - \sin\varphi\sin\psi & -\cos\varphi\cos\theta\sin\psi - \sin\varphi\cos\psi & \cos\varphi\sin\theta \\ \sin\varphi\cos\theta\cos\psi + \cos\varphi\sin\psi & -\sin\varphi\cos\theta\sin\psi + \cos\varphi\cos\psi & \sin\varphi\sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta\cos\psi & \sin\theta\sin\psi & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} . \tag{27.6}\]
  2. If \(R_{33} \ne \pm 1\), then \(\theta \in (0, \pi)\) is uniquely determined by the condition \(\cos\theta = R_{33}\), and the numbers \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) up to multiples of \(2\pi\) by the conditions \((\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) = (R_{13}, R_{23})/\sin\theta\) and \((\cos\psi, \sin\psi) = (-R_{31}, R_{32})/\sin\theta\).
  3. If \(R_{33} = 1\), then \(\theta = 0\) and \(\mat R = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi+\psi}\), so every pair \(\varphi\), \(\psi\) with the same sum gives the same matrix. If \(R_{33} = -1\), then \(\theta = \pi\) and \(\mat R = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi-\psi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}\), so every pair with the same difference gives the same matrix.
Proof

First we compute the product, then for \(R_{33} \ne \pm 1\) we find the angles from the matrix and check them, finally we treat the cases \(R_{33} = \pm 1\).

  1. From definition 27.10,
    \[\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta\cos\psi & -\cos\theta\sin\psi & \sin\theta \\ \sin\psi & \cos\psi & 0 \\ -\sin\theta\cos\psi & \sin\theta\sin\psi & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} .\]
    We multiply rows 1 and 2 by \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\) from the left: the new row 1 is \(\cos\varphi\cdot(\text{row 1}) - \sin\varphi\cdot(\text{row 2})\), the new row 2 is \(\sin\varphi\cdot(\text{row 1}) + \cos\varphi\cdot(\text{row 2})\), row 3 does not change. This is equation (27.6).
  2. Let \(R_{33} \ne \pm 1\). The third column is a unit vector (orthogonality, (2.52)), so \(R_{13}^2 + R_{23}^2 + R_{33}^2 = 1\) and \(|R_{33}| < 1\). The cosine is strictly decreasing on \([0, \pi]\) with \(\cos 0 = 1\) and \(\cos\pi = -1\) (lemma 8.11, points 2 and 3), so there is exactly one \(\theta \in (0, \pi)\) with \(\cos\theta = R_{33}\), and \(\sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - R_{33}^2} > 0\).
  3. From step 2, \(R_{13}^2 + R_{23}^2 = \sin^2\theta\), so the vector \((R_{13}, R_{23})/\sin\theta\) has length \(1\). For every unit vector \((u_1, u_2)\) there is an angle with \((\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) = (u_1, u_2)\), as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 8.41. So we get \(\varphi\), up to multiples of \(2\pi\). Since the third row is a unit vector, \(R_{31}^2 + R_{32}^2 = \sin^2\theta\), and in the same way we get \(\psi\) from \((-R_{31}, R_{32})/\sin\theta\).
  4. Let \(\mat S = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\varphi}\,\mat R\,\mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\psi}\). The matrices \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\pm\varphi}\) and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\pm\psi}\) are orthogonal with determinant \(1\) (lemma 27.11, point 3). A product of orthogonal matrices is orthogonal, \((\mat A\mat B)^\T(\mat A\mat B) = \mat B^\T\mat A^\T\mat A\mat B = \mat I\) (lemma 1.102), and determinants multiply (theorem 2.74), so \(\mat S\) is orthogonal with determinant \(1\).
  5. The third column of \(\mat S\): \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\psi}\) keeps \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), so \(\mat S\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\varphi}\,(R_{13}, R_{23}, R_{33})^\T\). By step 3 this is \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\varphi}(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta)^\T = (\sin\theta(\cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi),\ \sin\theta(-\sin\varphi\cos\varphi + \cos\varphi\sin\varphi),\ \cos\theta)^\T = (\sin\theta,\ 0,\ \cos\theta)^\T\).
  6. The third row of \(\mat S\): \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\varphi}\) keeps the third row, so it equals \((R_{31}, R_{32}, R_{33})\,\mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\psi}\), and by step 3 this is \((-\sin\theta\cos\psi\cdot\cos\psi + \sin\theta\sin\psi\cdot(-\sin\psi),\ -\sin\theta\cos\psi\sin\psi + \sin\theta\sin\psi\cos\psi,\ \cos\theta) = (-\sin\theta,\ 0,\ \cos\theta)\).
  7. So the matrix \(\mat S\) has the form \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} a & b & \sin\theta \\ d & e & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{smallmatrix}\right]\). From orthogonality: columns 2 and 3 are perpendicular, \(b\sin\theta = 0\), so \(b = 0\) (since \(\sin\theta > 0\)). Rows 2 and 3 are perpendicular, \(-d\sin\theta = 0\), so \(d = 0\). Rows 1 and 3 are perpendicular, \(-a\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta = 0\), so \(a = \cos\theta\). Column 2 is a unit vector, so \(e = \pm 1\).
  8. By definition 2.72, \(\det\mat S = a\,e\cos\theta + e\sin^2\theta = e(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = e\), since the other terms are zero. Since \(\det\mat S = 1\), \(e = 1\), and \(\mat S = \mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta}\).
  9. From the definition of \(\mat S\) and lemma 27.11, points 1 and 2, \(\mat R = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\mat S\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi}\). This is point 1 at \(R_{33} \ne \pm 1\).
  10. Uniqueness (point 2). Let \(\mat R = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi'}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta'}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi'}\) with \(\theta' \in (0, \pi)\). By equation (27.6), \(R_{33} = \cos\theta'\), so \(\theta' = \theta\), because the cosine is strictly decreasing on \([0, \pi]\). Then \((R_{13}, R_{23}) = \sin\theta\,(\cos\varphi', \sin\varphi')\) and \(\sin\theta \ne 0\), so \((\cos\varphi', \sin\varphi') = (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)\) and \(\varphi'\) differs from \(\varphi\) by a multiple of \(2\pi\). The same for \(\psi\) from \((R_{31}, R_{32}) = \sin\theta\,(-\cos\psi', \sin\psi')\).
  11. Let \(R_{33} = 1\). By unit length (\(R_{13}^2 + R_{23}^2 = 0\) and \(R_{31}^2 + R_{32}^2 = 0\)) the third column and third row have the elements \((0, 0, 1)\). The remaining \(2 \times 2\) block is orthogonal with determinant \(1\). As in steps 2 to 4 of the proof of lemma 8.41, which need only orthogonality, determinant \(1\) and \(\mat R\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\mat R = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\alpha}\) for some \(\alpha\). By lemma 27.11, \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},0}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi+\psi}\), so \(\varphi\), \(\psi\) with \(\varphi + \psi = \alpha\) are a solution.
  12. Let \(R_{33} = -1\). The matrix \(\mat R\,\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}\) is orthogonal with determinant \(1\) and the \((3, 3)\) element equal to \(R_{33}\cos\pi = 1\), since \(\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi} = \mathrm{diag}(-1, 1, -1)\). By step 11 it equals \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\alpha}\), so \(\mat R = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\alpha}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}^{-1} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\alpha}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}\), since \(\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}\) is its own inverse matrix (lemma 27.11, point 2). Since \(\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},-\psi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}\) (both products are \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} -\cos\psi & \sin\psi & 0 \\ \sin\psi & \cos\psi & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\)), \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi-\psi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\pi}\), which is point 3.

Source: SPONG (2.27)-(2.38) (PDF p. 75-77), where the derivation goes from the element equations with two solutions \(\theta\) and two cases \(\theta = 0\) and \(\theta = \pi\). The proof with the auxiliary matrix \(\mat S\) and point 3 are not from the source.

An example with definite angles. For \(\varphi = 40^\circ\), \(\theta = 50^\circ\) and \(\psi = 30^\circ\) equation (27.6) gives the matrix

\[\mat R = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}1050 & -0{,}8029 & 0{,}5868 \\ 0{,}7408 & 0{,}4568 & 0{,}4924 \\ -0{,}6634 & 0{,}3830 & 0{,}6428 \end{bmatrix} .\]

We get the angles from it by steps 2 and 3 of the proof of the theorem: \(\cos\theta = R_{33} = 0{,}6428\) gives \(\theta = 50^\circ\) and \(\sin\theta = 0{,}7660\). Then \((R_{13}, R_{23})/\sin\theta = (0{,}7660;\ 0{,}6428) = (\cos 40^\circ, \sin 40^\circ)\) and \((-R_{31}, R_{32})/\sin\theta = (0{,}8660;\ 0{,}5000) = (\cos 30^\circ, \sin 30^\circ)\). We get the right angles. Without the condition \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) another triple would give the same matrix: the matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\pi}\mat R_{\mathrm{y},-\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\pi}\) is \(\mat R_{\mathrm{y},\theta}\) (a rotation by \(\pi\) about \(z\) reverses the sign of the \(x\) and \(y\) elements that the matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{y},-\theta}\) mixes with \(z\)), so the triple \((\varphi + \pi, -\theta, \psi + \pi)\) gives the same matrix. It has \(\theta < 0\) and is excluded by the condition \(\theta \in (0, \pi)\). SPONG counts it as the second solution. For the gripper of example 27.13 we have \(R_{33} = 0\), so \(\theta = 90^\circ\), and \((R_{13}, R_{23}) = (1, 0)\), \((-R_{31}, R_{32}) = (0, 1)\) give \(\varphi = 0^\circ\), \(\psi = 90^\circ\).

Point 3 of the theorem is close to something that demands attention in a robot. What if \(\theta = 0\)? Then the axes \(z_0\), \(z_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(z_1\) coincide, and the angles \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) turn about the same axis.

Example 27.15 Euler angles at \(\theta = 0\) are not unique (Eulerjevi koti pri \(\theta = 0\) niso enolični)

Take \(\theta = 0\) and two pairs of angles, \((\varphi, \psi) = (10^\circ, 50^\circ)\) and \((45^\circ, 15^\circ)\) (figure 27.18).

  1. By lemma 27.11, \(\mat R_{\mathrm{y},0} = \mat I\), so \(\mat R = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\psi} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\varphi+\psi}\).
  2. Both pairs have the sum \(60^\circ\), so they give the same matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},60^\circ} = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0{,}5 & -0{,}866 & 0 \\ 0{,}866 & 0{,}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\).
  3. In the left figure the axis \(x\) goes first by \(10^\circ\) and then by \(50^\circ\), in the right one first by \(45^\circ\) and then by \(15^\circ\). Both times the final position of the axis \(x_1\) is at \(60^\circ\) and of \(y_1\) at \(150^\circ\) from the axis \(x_0\). From the matrix \(\mat R\) the angles \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) cannot be separated, only their sum is determined (point 3 of theorem 27.14).

Source: The numbers are from NumPy (outlines/ch-roboti/num-02.py, N8). SPONG (2.36) (PDF p. 77).

At \(\theta = \pi\) only the difference \(\varphi - \psi\) remains, which is the mirror picture. In robotics \(\theta = 0\) or \(\pi\) means a wrist position where two axes lie on each other. The unique computation of angles described above does not exist there, and later we shall see that in this position the arm loses a direction in which the gripper can move. For now we shall use the matrix for orientation and not the angles.

Euler angles use three rotations about three axes. Would one rotation about one axis suffice? Figure 27.19 shows the answer on the example of the gripper that we have already turned.

The axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) carry the labels of both frames, because after two quarter circles they exchange cyclically: \(x_1\) is on \(y_0\), \(y_1\) on \(z_0\) and \(z_1\) on \(x_0\). The blue arrows show where the tip of each axis goes. By its shape this is a rotation that carries the triple of axes into itself so that each goes to the next. One vector does not move in it: the cube diagonal, which is equally far from all three axes. The rotation goes about it.

The same rotation becomes simple when we look at it from another side, from the tip of the diagonal towards the origin (figure 27.20). The diagonal \(\vek v\) is now a dot that points towards us. The axes \(x_0\), \(y_0\) and \(z_0\) lean towards us equally steeply, so we see them as three equally long spokes, \(120^\circ\) apart. The blue arcs are the arrows of the previous figure: each spoke goes to the next, and this is an ordinary plane rotation by a third of a circle, \(360^\circ/3 = 120^\circ\). A vector that lies in the plane of the page is perpendicular to the axis and we see it in its true length. Such is the vector \(\vek w\) of length \(1\), which the rotation carries along the circle of radius \(1\) into the vector \(\mat R\vek w\), through the same angle \(120^\circ\). What this view adds to the previous figure is that we read the angle of the rotation with our eyes: a rotation in space is a plane rotation when we look along its axis. The next theorem shows that every rotation has such an axis.

Theorem 27.16 Axis of a rotation (os zasuka)

Let \(\mat R\) be an orthogonal \(3 \times 3\) matrix with determinant \(1\).
