Arm \(A\) of figure 27.33 has \(z_0\) and \(z_1\) parallel (revolute joints, axes out of the page), so case (ii), and \(\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = 0\). The origin \(o_1\) is at the end of the first link, \(a_1 = l_1\), \(d_1 = 0\) (the perpendicular passes through \(o_0\)), similarly \(a_2 = l_2\), \(d_2 = 0\). The table:

link \(i\) \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(\alpha_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\)
1 \(l_1\) \(0\) \(0\) \(q_1\)
2 \(l_2\) \(0\) \(0\) \(q_2\)

The matrix \(\mat T^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{1}}\) for frames \(0\) and \(1\) equals (27.13), which by lemma 27.28 is indeed \(\mat T_{\mathrm{DH}}(q_1, 0, l_1, 0)\). The product is by equation (27.16)

  1. \(\mat T^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{2}} = \mat T^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{1}}\mat T^{\ix{1}}_{\ix{2}}\), with \(c_{12} = \cos(q_1 + q_2)\) and \(s_{12} = \sin(q_1 + q_2)\).
  2. The rotation: the columns are \((c_1, s_1, 0)\) and \((-s_1, c_1, 0)\) times the columns of the matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{q}_2}\), so the first column is \((c_1c_2 - s_1s_2,\ s_1c_2 + c_1s_2,\ 0)\), which by the addition theorem (corollary 8.16) is \((c_{12}, s_{12}, 0)\). The arm is planar, so \(\mat R^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{2}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{q}_1+\mathrm{q}_2}\): frame \(2\) is frame \(0\) turned by \(q_1 + q_2\).
  3. The origin of the tip: \(\vek o^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{2}} = \vek o^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{1}} + \mat R^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{1}}\vek o^{\ix{1}}_{\ix{2}} = (l_1c_1 + l_2c_{12},\ l_1s_1 + l_2s_{12},\ 0)\), again by the addition theorem.

At \(q = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)\) we have \(\vek o_1 = (0{,}8660,\ 0{,}5000,\ 0)\) m, the tip \(\vek o_2 = (0{,}8660,\ 1{,}0000,\ 0)\) m, and \(\mat R^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{2}}\) is a turn by \(90^\circ\), first column \((0, 1, 0)\): the second link points vertically up (NumPy, num-04.py), which the figure (left) also shows: the triangle of \(\vek o_1\) has the sides \(0{,}8660\) and \(0{,}5000\) m, and the height of the tip is \(1\) m.

A check with example 8.50. There the axis \(x_0\) is down, the axis \(y_0\) to the right, the angle \(\theta_1 = 30^\circ\) from the axis \(x_0\) to the first bar and \(\theta_2 = 60^\circ\) to the second, measured from the vertical down, so from the axis \(x_0\). The relative angle is \(q_2 = \theta_2 - \theta_1 = 30^\circ\), which in the table is \(\theta_2\) (figure 27.33, right). The computation gives in the axes \(x_0\), \(y_0\) the position of joint \(2\) and of the tip, \(\vek o_1 = (0{,}8660,\ 0{,}5000)\) m and \(\vek o_2 = (1{,}1160,\ 0{,}9330)\) m (the sides of the triangles on the right). For a reader who looks vertically up and to the right this is \((0{,}5000,\ -0{,}8660)\) m and \((0{,}9330,\ -1{,}1160)\) m, exactly the numbers of example 8.50. So the DH table gives the same position as the coordinates of chapter 8.

How is it for a spatial arm, where the axes are turned? Arm \(B\) has three revolute joints. Joint \(1\) turns about a vertical axis, joints \(2\) and \(3\) about horizontal axes, parallel to each other and perpendicular to the plane of the arm (figure 27.40).

Example 27.33 Arm B: table and tip position (roka B)

We draw the links: a vertical first link of height \(d_1\) from \(o_0\) to \(o_1\), then links \(a_2\) and \(a_3\). At every joint we place a frame by the procedure. The axis \(z_0\) is the axis of joint \(1\), vertical. The axis \(z_1\) is the axis of joint \(2\): it meets the axis \(z_0\) (case (iii)), so \(o_1\) is the intersection at the height \(d_1\), \(a_1 = 0\), the axis \(x_1\) is perpendicular to the plane of the axes \(z_0\) and \(z_1\), and \(\alpha_1 = 90^\circ\), because \(z_1\) is horizontal. The axes \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are parallel (case (ii)): \(o_2\) is at the end of the second link, \(a_2 = 0{,}5\) m, \(d_2 = 0\), \(\alpha_2 = 0\). Similarly for the tool: \(z_3 \parallel z_2\), \(a_3 = 0{,}4\) m, \(d_3 = 0\), \(\alpha_3 = 0\). The table:

link \(i\) \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(\alpha_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\)
1 \(0\) \(90^\circ\) \(0{,}4\) m \(q_1\)
2 \(0{,}5\) m \(0\) \(0\) \(q_2\)
3 \(0{,}4\) m \(0\) \(0\) \(q_3\)

At the joint angles \(q = (30^\circ, 45^\circ, -60^\circ)\) by equation (27.15) we get

  1. \(\mat T^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{1}} = \mat T_{\mathrm{DH}}(q_1, 0{,}4, 0, 90^\circ)\) has origin \((0, 0, 0{,}4)\) m, \(x_1 = (0{,}8660,\ 0{,}5000,\ 0)\) and \(z_1 = (0{,}5000,\ -0{,}8660,\ 0)\) (point 3 of theorem 27.30: \(z_1 = (s_\theta s_\alpha, -c_\theta s_\alpha, c_\alpha)\) at \(\alpha = 90^\circ\)).
  2. The origins \(o_2 = (0{,}3062,\ 0{,}1768,\ 0{,}7536)\) m, and \(o_3 = (0{,}6408,\ 0{,}3700,\ 0{,}6500)\) m (NumPy, num-04.py).
  3. A check with geometry: the reach in the horizontal plane is \(a_2\cos q_2 + a_3\cos(q_2 + q_3) = 0{,}5\cdot 0{,}7071 + 0{,}4\cdot 0{,}9659 = 0{,}7399\) m, the height \(d_1 + a_2\sin q_2 + a_3\sin(q_2 + q_3) = 0{,}4 + 0{,}3536 - 0{,}1035 = 0{,}6500\) m, and the plane of the arm is turned by \(q_1\), so the coordinates of the tip are \(x = 0{,}7399\cos 30^\circ = 0{,}6408\) m, \(y = 0{,}7399\sin 30^\circ = 0{,}3700\) m. We get the same from the product of matrices.
  4. The rotation of the tool \(\mat R^{\ix{0}}_{\ix{3}}\) has first column \((0{,}8365,\ 0{,}4830,\ -0{,}2588)\), third column \((0{,}5000,\ -0{,}8660,\ 0)\): the direction of the axis \(z_3\) equals that of the axis \(z_1\), since the axes \(z_1\), \(z_2\) and \(z_3\) are parallel (\(\alpha_2 = \alpha_3 = 0\)).

Arm \(B\) at \(q_1 = 30^\circ\) is in a plane that is turned about the vertical by this angle, and in the computation of the geometry we do see this. Without the DH table we would compute the origins with three special geometric considerations, with it we only multiply matrices.

What remains is the announced path. The notation of this section also has other meanings in the book. \(\mat T^{\ix{i-1}}_{\ix{i}}\) is a \(4 \times 4\) matrix, while the letter \(T\) also denotes the kinetic energy and, in chapter 7, the transformation matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\) of an element. The angle \(\alpha_{\mathrm{i}}\) of this section must not be confused with \(\alpha\) in thermal expansion in chapter 3 and in damping in chapter 10. The letter \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\) is only an offset and has nothing to do with a differential, \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\) are neither vectors nor derivatives. We use the parameters further: the position of the tip from equation (27.16) we will invert in the following sections (inverse kinematics) and differentiate with respect to time (velocities and the Jacobian matrix).

27.5 Inverse kinematics

So far we chose the joint angles and computed where the end effector is (definition 27.31). A robot, however, gets its task the other way round: "grasp the object at the point \(P\)", and it has to find the joint angles itself, because motors set them. Since we have turned the direction of the map around, this task is called inverse kinematics (inverzna kinematika, from Latin inversus, turned around, and Greek kinema, motion, kinematics describing position and motion without forces). We ask three questions. Can the angles for a given point be found at all? How many sets of angles reach it? And do the angles change smoothly when the point moves? On the two-link arm of example A we settle all three by calculation, and for more general arms we say what is known and cite the source.

The model is the one of section 27.1: a planar arm with two rigid links of lengths \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m, with ideal joints without friction or backlash (definition 27.2). The angle \(q_1\) is the angle of link 1 with the axis \(x_0\), and \(q_2\) the angle between the extension of link 1 and link 2, both in radians. The tip (konica) of the arm is the point at the end of link 2 where the end effector sits (definition 27.1). We want only the position of the tip and not the orientation of the end effector. A point of the plane has two numbers and the arm has two joint variables, so we may hope for finitely many solutions. The tip is at the point

\[\Phi(q_1, q_2) = \big(l_1\cos q_1 + l_2\cos(q_1 + q_2),\ \ l_1\sin q_1 + l_2\sin(q_1 + q_2)\big) . \tag{27.17}\]

Link 1 makes the angle \(q_1\) with the axis \(x_0\) and link 2 the angle \(q_1 + q_2\), because the angles of rotations add (lemma 27.12 for two rotations about the same axis, written with matrices as \(\mat R(q_1)\,\mat R(q_2) = \mat R(q_1 + q_2)\) by the addition formulas (8.11)). The tip lies at the vector of link 1 plus the vector of link 2, which is (27.17). The function \(\Phi\) takes two numbers in and gives a point of the plane out, so it is a map in the sense of definition 4.42. At \(\vek q = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)\) (example A1) we get \(\Phi = (0{,}8660,\ 1{,}0000)\) m, and this is the point we choose for \(P\).

We build the figure as one would draw it on a board. The axes \(x_0\) and \(y_0\) belong to the fixed frame, joint 1 sits at the origin \(O\) and the tip has to be at the point \(P\). First we draw the posture we already know, the blue arm: link 1 of length \(l_1\) at the angle \(q_1 = 30^\circ\) up to the elbow \(o_1\), and link 2 of length \(l_2\) from there to \(P\), straight up. The elbow is joint 2, because the arm bends there like a human arm. The angle \(q_2 = 60^\circ\) is measured from the dashed extension of link 1 to link 2. Then we ask whether another posture exists. The two links and the segment from \(O\) to \(P\) form a triangle with sides \(l_1 = 1\) m, \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m and \(r = \sqrt{0{,}866^2 + 1^2} = 1{,}3229\) m. A triangle with three given sides is fixed up to reflection (the SSS congruence theorem), so the second posture arises by reflecting the elbow in the segment \(OP\): the orange arm has its elbow \(o_1'\) at \((0{,}3712,\ 0{,}9286)\) m, the mirror image of \(o_1 = (0{,}8660,\ 0{,}5000)\) m (computation num-05.out, C9). Its angles are \(q_1' = 68{,}213^\circ\) and \(q_2' = -60^\circ\). We tell the two elbows apart by their position relative to the line \(OP\), looking with the axis \(y_0\) upward: in the blue arm the elbow is below it (elbow down, \(q_2 > 0\)), in the orange arm above it (elbow up, \(q_2 < 0\)).

Both idealizations of the model enter right here. Rigid links mean that the sides \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) of the triangle have the same length in every posture, otherwise we could not compute with three sides. A joint without clearance means that the angle at the joint is exactly the one the motor sets. How much this matters is told by the distance \(r\): if joint 1 has a clearance of \(0{,}1^\circ = 0{,}00175\) rad, the tip moves along an arc by \(r\cdot 0{,}00175 = 1{,}3229\cdot 0{,}00175\) m \(= 2{,}3\) mm. The model is therefore good as long as the accuracy demanded of the tip position is coarse compared with such a shift, and it fails for tasks where tenths of a millimetre count.

Reflection is the idea, and the theorem turns it into a calculation valid for every point and every pair of link lengths. The matrix \(\mat R(q_1)\) appears in it, the matrix of a planar rotation from lemma 8.41. Its columns are the axes of the frame of link 1 in the base frame, so it is the orientation matrix \(\mat R^0_1\) of section 27.2 in the planar case. It is the transpose of the rotation matrix of definition 2.44, as stated after lemma 8.41.

The proof will run on figure 27.42, so we build it first. The axes \(x_0\), \(y_0\) and joint 1 at \(O\) are the same as before. We first lay the arm so that link 1 lies on the axis \(x_0\), that is \(q_1 = 0\), and leave the elbow bent by \(q_2 = 60^\circ\): this is the grey dashed arm. We call its tip \(\vek w\). Its components can be read straight off the figure: along the axis \(x_0\) the whole of link 1 and the projection of link 2, \(w_1 = l_1 + l_2\cos q_2 = 1 + 0{,}5\cdot 0{,}5 = 1{,}25\) m, and vertically only the height of link 2, \(w_2 = l_2\sin q_2 = 0{,}5\cdot 0{,}866 = 0{,}433\) m. The segment from \(O\) to \(\vek w\) has the length \(r\) and makes the angle \(\beta = 19{,}107^\circ\) with the axis \(x_0\). Now we turn the whole grey arm as one rigid piece about \(O\) by \(q_1 = 30^\circ\): the tip travels along the blue arc of the circle of radius \(r\) and lands at the point \(P\), and the arm becomes the orange one. A turn about \(O\) changes no distance from \(O\), so the segment \(OP\) is as long as the segment from \(O\) to \(\vek w\), and its angle with the axis is \(\varphi = \beta + q_1 = 19{,}107^\circ + 30^\circ = 49{,}107^\circ\) (NumPy). These two observations are the whole proof: the length \(r\) knows nothing about \(q_1\), so it fixes \(q_2\), and the angle \(\varphi\) then fixes \(q_1 = \varphi - \beta\). At the elbow of the grey arm the two angles are marked that we shall need for the law of cosines: \(q_2\) is measured from the extension of link 1, and the angle of the triangle between the links is \(\pi - q_2\).

Theorem 27.34 Inverse kinematics of the two-link planar arm (inverzna kinematika dvočlenske ravninske roke)

Let \(l_1 > 0\) and \(l_2 > 0\) be the link lengths and \(\Phi\) the map (27.17). Let \((x, y)\) be a point of the plane other than the origin, \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) and

\[c = \frac{r^2 - l_1^2 - l_2^2}{2\,l_1 l_2} . \tag{27.18}\]

Let \(\varphi\) be an angle with \((\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) = (x, y)/r\). Then:

  1. A pair of angles \((q_1, q_2)\) with \(\Phi(q_1, q_2) = (x, y)\) exists if and only if \(|c| \le 1\), that is \(|l_1 - l_2| \le r \le l_1 + l_2\).
  2. For every such pair \(\cos q_2 = c\), and \(q_1 = \varphi - \beta\) up to multiples of \(2\pi\), where \(\beta\) is an angle with \(r\,(\cos\beta, \sin\beta) = (l_1 + l_2\cos q_2,\ l_2\sin q_2)\).
  3. For \(|c| < 1\) there are exactly two solutions up to multiples of \(2\pi\), with \(q_2 = \theta\) and \(q_2 = -\theta\), where \(\theta \in (0, \pi)\) and \(\cos\theta = c\). For \(c = 1\) there is one solution, with \(q_2 = 0\), for \(c = -1\) one, with \(q_2 = \pi\).
Proof

We have to show that the tip \(\Phi\) arises from a vector \(\vek w\) by a rotation through \(q_1\), that a rotation preserves length and so determines \(\cos q_2\), and that the angle \(q_1\) can then be chosen.

  1. Let \(\vek w = (w_1, w_2)\) with \(w_1 = l_1 + l_2\cos q_2\) and \(w_2 = l_2\sin q_2\). By the addition formulas (8.11), \(l_2\cos(q_1 + q_2) = l_2\cos q_1\cos q_2 - l_2\sin q_1\sin q_2\) and \(l_2\sin(q_1 + q_2) = l_2\sin q_1\cos q_2 + l_2\cos q_1\sin q_2\). From (27.17) we therefore get \(\Phi = (w_1\cos q_1 - w_2\sin q_1,\ w_1\sin q_1 + w_2\cos q_1) = \mat R(q_1)\,\vek w\) with the matrix \(\mat R\) of lemma 8.41. In figure 27.42, \(\vek w\) is the tip of the grey arm with the components \(w_1\) and \(w_2\), and multiplying by \(\mat R(q_1)\) is the blue turn that carries it into the orange arm.
  2. A rotation preserves length, the segments from \(O\) to \(\vek w\) and from \(O\) to \(P\) both have the length \(r\): \(|\mat R(q_1)\vek w|^2 = (w_1\cos q_1 - w_2\sin q_1)^2 + (w_1\sin q_1 + w_2\cos q_1)^2 = (w_1^2 + w_2^2)(\cos^2 q_1 + \sin^2 q_1) = w_1^2 + w_2^2\), because the mixed terms cancel and \(\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1\) by lemma 8.11, item 1. From \(\Phi = (x, y)\) we therefore get \(r^2 = |\vek w|^2 = l_1^2 + 2l_1l_2\cos q_2 + l_2^2\,(\cos^2 q_2 + \sin^2 q_2) = l_1^2 + l_2^2 + 2l_1l_2\cos q_2\). This is \(\cos q_2 = c\), the first part of item 2.
  3. By lemma 8.11, item 1, \(|\cos q_2| \le 1\), so \(|c| \le 1\) must hold. The condition \(c \le 1\) is \(r^2 \le (l_1 + l_2)^2\), the condition \(c \ge -1\) is \(r^2 \ge (l_1 - l_2)^2 = |l_1 - l_2|^2\). The numbers \(r\), \(l_1 + l_2\) and \(|l_1 - l_2|\) are nonnegative, so lemma 1.29 turns the squares into \(|l_1 - l_2| \le r \le l_1 + l_2\). This proves necessity in item 1.
  4. Conversely let \(|c| \le 1\). By item 1 of definition 8.10 there is \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) with \(\cos\theta = c\). For \(q_2 = \theta\), step 2 read backwards gives \(|\vek w| = r > 0\), so \(\vek w/r\) is a point of the unit circle. By the construction in step 2 of the proof of lemma 8.41 there is an angle \(\beta\) with \(\vek w = r\,(\cos\beta, \sin\beta)\), and an angle \(\varphi\) with \((x, y) = r\,(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)\). For \(q_1 = \varphi - \beta\) step 1 and the addition formulas give \(\Phi = \mat R(q_1)\,\vek w = r\,(\cos(q_1 + \beta),\ \sin(q_1 + \beta)) = r\,(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) = (x, y)\). This is existence in item 1.
  5. Two angles \(a\) and \(b\) with the same \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) differ by a multiple of \(2\pi\). By the addition formula, \(\cos(a - b) = \cos a\cos b + \sin a\sin b = \cos^2 a + \sin^2 a = 1\), and by definition 8.10 the cosine equals \(1\) only at multiples of \(2\pi\) (on \([0, \pi]\) it is strictly decreasing by lemma 8.11, item 3, and \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\)). For a given \(q_2\), from \(\mat R(q_1)\vek w = (x, y)\), step 4 and the addition formulas, \((\cos(q_1 + \beta), \sin(q_1 + \beta)) = (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)\), so \(q_1 = \varphi - \beta\) up to a multiple of \(2\pi\). This is the second part of item 2.
  6. The number of solutions. By step 2, \(\cos q_2 = c\). On \([0, \pi]\) the cosine, being strictly decreasing, takes the value \(c\) at exactly one \(\theta\), and on \([-\pi, 0)\) we have \(\cos q_2 = \cos(-q_2)\), hence \(q_2 = -\theta\). Up to multiples of \(2\pi\) only \(q_2 = \theta\) and \(q_2 = -\theta\) are therefore possible (lemma](27.42:pred) 8.11, item 4). For \(|c| < 1\) we have \(0 < \theta < \pi\), so \(\sin\theta > 0\), and \(\theta\) and \(-\theta\) also differ by something other than a multiple of \(2\pi\), because otherwise \(\sin\theta = \sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\) and \(\sin\theta = 0\). For each of them step 5 gives one \(q_1\), two solutions in all. For \(c = 1\) we have \(\theta = 0\) and for \(c = -1\) we have \(\theta = \pi\) (item 2 of lemma 8.11), \(\theta\) and \(-\theta\) agree up to \(2\pi\), one solution. In figure 27.42, \(q_2 = \theta\) is the grey arm above the axis \(x_0\) and \(q_2 = -\theta\) its mirror image below the axis, and [a turn by its own \(q_1\) carries each to the same point \(P\).

Source: SPONG (5.24) and (5.25), PDF p. 173, state the same conclusion for an elbow arm by the law of cosines, \(\cos\theta_3 = D\) and \(\theta_3 = \operatorname{Atan2}(D, \pm\sqrt{1 - D^2})\), and point to equations (1.10) and (1.11) for the two-link arm. The proof by rotation and addition formulas is not from the sources.

The theorem says that \(\cos q_2\) is determined by the distance \(r\), which is the same in both postures, so the postures are mirror images of each other. Equation (27.18) is the law of cosines for the triangle with sides \(l_1\), \(l_2\) and \(r\), which we see in figure 27.41. The sign in front of \(2l_1l_2\cos q_2\) is plus and not minus, because the angle of the triangle at the elbow is \(\pi - q_2\) (\(q_2\) is measured from the extension of link 1) and \(\cos(\pi - q_2) = -\cos q_2\). For example A at the point \(P\) we have \(c = (1{,}75 - 1 - 0{,}25)/1 = 0{,}5\), so \(\theta = 60^\circ\), and the two solutions are \((30^\circ, 60^\circ)\) and \((68{,}213^\circ, -60^\circ)\) (example A4, num-05.out, C2). We read the angles \(q_1\) off figure 27.42: the segment \(OP\) has the angle \(\varphi = 49{,}107^\circ\), for elbow down \(\beta = 19{,}107^\circ\) and \(q_1 = \varphi - \beta = 30^\circ\). For elbow up the grey arm is mirrored below the axis \(x_0\), so \(\beta = -19{,}107^\circ\) and \(q_1' = \varphi + 19{,}107^\circ = 68{,}213^\circ\) (NumPy, from unrounded values). Both solutions were checked with \(\Phi\) and give \(P\). The theorem does not treat the point \((0, 0)\). Only an arm with \(l_1 = l_2\) and \(q_2 = \pi\) reaches it, and then \(q_1\) is arbitrary, as at a configuration that we shall call singular in section 27.7.

The condition \(|c| \le 1\) is the workspace of lemma 27.7, and the theorem now also tells us which sets of angles we get. We test it on points near the edge.

The workspace is an annulus (kolobar), a plane figure between two circles, like a wheel with a hole, centred at joint 1 \(O\) between the circles of radii \(l_1 - l_2 = 0{,}5\) m and \(l_1 + l_2 = 1{,}5\) m, marked with their radii. On the axis \(x_0\) we first take the point \(E = (1{,}5,\ 0)\) m on the outer circle. There \(c = (2{,}25 - 1{,}25)/1 = 1\) and \(\theta = 0\), so the only solution is \(q = (0, 0)\), the arm stretched out as the blackwhite segment in the figure. Why only one? The triangle with sides \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m and the third side \(r = 1{,}5\) m is flattened into a segment, and the mirror image of a segment in itself is the same segment. Next we look at the point \(Q = (1{,}6,\ 0)\) m just beyond the edge. There \(c = (2{,}56 - 1{,}25)/1 = 1{,}31 > 1\) and no number \(q_2\) has cosine \(1{,}31\) (lemma 8.11, item 1). The arm reaches \(l_1 + l_2 = 1{,}5\) m and \(Q\) is \(0{,}1\) m farther. On the inner side the story is the same. The point \(H = (0{,}5,\ 0)\) m has \(c = (0{,}25 - 1{,}25)/1 = -1\) and \(q_2 = \pi\), the arm folded back, while the point \(W = (0{,}4,\ 0)\) m in the hole has \(c = -1{,}09\) and no solution. Inside the annulus, for instance at the point \(P\) of figure 27.41, there are two solutions. The last values were checked in num-05.out, C3.

At the edge, then, two solutions merge into one. This raises the third question: what happens to a solution when the point moves? At the point \(P\) the sets of angles are \((30^\circ, 60^\circ)\) and \((68{,}213^\circ, -60^\circ)\), and we expect both to change continuously if \(P\) is moved a little. This holds at every configuration where the matrix of partial derivatives of the map \(\Phi\) is invertible, and that we must prove. We compute it from (27.17) with the theorem on the derivatives of sine and cosine (theorem 8.13) and the rules of differentiation:

\[\mat F_\Phi(q_1, q_2) = \begin{pmatrix} -l_1\sin q_1 - l_2\sin(q_1 + q_2) & -l_2\sin(q_1 + q_2) \\ l_1\cos q_1 + l_2\cos(q_1 + q_2) & l_2\cos(q_1 + q_2) \end{pmatrix} . \tag{27.19}\]

The entries are continuous, so \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42). In section 27.6 we shall meet this matrix as the Jacobian matrix of the robot, here it is only the matrix of partial derivatives of a map.

Corollary 27.35 Local inverse of the two-link arm (lokalna inverzna preslikava dvočlenske roke)

Let \(\Phi\) be the map (27.17) and \(\vek q_* = (q_{1*}, q_{2*})\) a set of angles with \(\sin q_{2*} \neq 0\). Then \(\det\mat F_\Phi(\vek q) = l_1l_2\sin q_2\), and there is a ball \(B\) centred at \(\vek q_*\) such that \(\Phi\) is injective on \(B\), \(V = \Phi(B)\) is open, and the inverse map \(\Psi\) of \(\Phi\) on \(B\) is continuously differentiable on \(V\) with

\[\mat F_\Psi(\Phi(\vek q)) = \mat F_\Phi(\vek q)^{-1} \quad\text{for every } \vek q \text{ in } B . \tag{27.20}\]
Proof

We have to show that the matrix of partial derivatives at \(\vek q_*\) has two pivots, so that theorem 8.34 can be used.

  1. By theorem 8.13 and the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82), \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable on the plane of all pairs \((q_1, q_2)\), with the matrix of partial derivatives (27.19).
  2. By definition (2.72) the determinant is \((-l_1\sin q_1 - l_2\sin(q_1 + q_2))\,l_2\cos(q_1 + q_2) + l_2\sin(q_1 + q_2)\,(l_1\cos q_1 + l_2\cos(q_1 + q_2))\). The terms with \(l_2^2\) cancel, leaving \(l_1l_2\,(\sin(q_1 + q_2)\cos q_1 - \sin q_1\cos(q_1 + q_2)) = l_1l_2\sin q_2\) by the addition formula (8.11) with \(\alpha = q_1 + q_2\) and \(\beta \to -q_1\) (evenness and oddness, lemma 8.11, item 4).
  3. For \(\sin q_{2*} \neq 0\) we have \(\det\mat F_\Phi(\vek q_*) \neq 0\). By lemma 4.49 the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(\vek q_*)\) has an inverse, so \(\mat F_\Phi(\vek q_*)\vek w = \vek 0\) implies \(\vek w = \mat F_\Phi(\vek q_*)^{-1}\vek 0 = \vek 0\), and by lemma 8.22 the matrix has two pivots.
  4. Theorem 8.34 with \(n = 2\), \(D\) the plane of all pairs and \(\vek x_0 = \vek q_*\) gives the ball \(B\), the openness of \(V\), the injectivity and continuous differentiability of \(\Psi\), and (27.20).

Source: SPONG PDF p. 163, in the introduction to chapter 5, mentions that the Jacobian inverse method is similar to a Newton-Raphson search, but does not state the corollary. The proof is not from the sources.

The corollary says that near every configuration with \(\sin q_2 \neq 0\) a smooth inverse exists. For example A this does not cover every configuration: \(\sin q_2 = 0\) means \(q_2 = 0\) or \(q_2 = \pi\), a stretched or completely folded arm, and these are exactly the two edges of the annulus in figure 27.43. The determinant also has a picture. In figure 27.42 the triangle made of the two links and the segment \(r\) lies on the axis \(x_0\): its base is link 1 of length \(l_1\), its height above the base is \(w_2 = l_2\sin q_2\). The area of the triangle is half the base times the height, \(\frac12\,l_1l_2\sin q_2\), and the turn does not change it. The determinant \(l_1l_2\sin q_2\) is therefore twice the area of the triangle of the arm, for example A \(1\cdot 0{,}433 = 0{,}433\) m\(^2\), with the sign plus for elbow down and minus for elbow up. To the calculation in steps 2 and 3 of the proof this adds a view by eye: the determinant is zero exactly when the triangle flattens into a segment, and exactly then the two mirror postures merge into one. The condition of the corollary and the number of solutions in theorem 27.34 are the same picture.

A calculation on example A. At \(\vek q_* = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)\) we have \(\mat F_\Phi = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -0{,}5 \\ 0{,}866 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) m, \(\det = 0{,}4330\) m\(^2\) \(= l_1l_2\sin 60^\circ\) and

\[\mat F_\Phi^{-1} = \frac{1}{0{,}4330}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0{,}5 \\ -0{,}866 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1{,}1547 \\ -2{,}0 & -2{,}3094 \end{pmatrix} \ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

By (27.20) these are the partial derivatives of the local inverse map: \(\partial q_1/\partial x = 0\), \(\partial q_1/\partial y = 1{,}1547\) rad/m, \(\partial q_2/\partial x = -2{,}0\) rad/m and \(\partial q_2/\partial y = -2{,}3094\) rad/m. We check by computer: difference quotients with steps \(h = 10^{-6}\) m around \(P\), computed from the formulas of theorem 27.34 on the elbow-down branch, give the columns \((0,\ -2{,}0)\) and \((1{,}1547,\ -2{,}3094)\) (num-05.out, C4 and C5). On the elbow-up branch \(\sin q_2 = \sin(-60^\circ) < 0\), the determinant is \(-0{,}4330\) m\(^2\) and the inverse is \(\begin{pmatrix} -1{,}1429 & -0{,}1650 \\ 2{,}0 & 2{,}3094 \end{pmatrix}\) m\(^{-1}\). The point \(P\) therefore has two local inverse maps, each around its own set of angles. The corollary guarantees each separately, and theorem 27.34 says there are no others.

What these numbers mean we show on the first column, \(\partial q_1/\partial x = 0\) and \(\partial q_2/\partial x = -2{,}0\) rad/m. The axes and joint 1 at \(O\) are as before, the grey dashed arm is the posture \((30^\circ, 60^\circ)\) with link 2 straight above the elbow \(o_1\). If we turn joint 2 alone, the tip travels along the circle of radius \(l_2\) round the elbow. At the point \(P\) this circle runs horizontally, because the tangent of a circle is perpendicular to the radius, and the radius here is the vertical link 2. A small horizontal shift of the tip is therefore done by joint 2 alone and \(q_1\) stays at rest. Hence the zero in the matrix. By how much must joint 2 turn? The length of an arc is the radius times the angle in radians, so a shift \(\Delta x\) needs the angle \(\Delta x/l_2\), and with the lever \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m this is \(1/0{,}5 = 2\) rad per metre. The sign is minus, because the tip goes to the right when link 2 turns clockwise, that is, when \(q_2\) decreases.

A derivative is a statement about small shifts, so we test it on a large one. We move the tip by \(0{,}1\) m to the point \(P' = (0{,}966,\ 1{,}0)\) m. The derivatives predict \(\Delta q_1 = 0\) and \(\Delta q_2 = -2{,}0\cdot 0{,}1 = -0{,}2\) rad \(= -11{,}46^\circ\). Theorem 27.34 gives for \(P'\) exactly the orange arm with \(q = (30{,}766^\circ,\ 46{,}905^\circ)\): the elbow angle decreases by \(13{,}09^\circ\), and link 1 rises by \(0{,}77^\circ\) (NumPy). The prediction for \(q_2\) is off by \(1{,}63^\circ\), because the circle is not straight: after a turn by \(0{,}2\) rad the tip on the arc is already \(l_2\,(1 - \cos 0{,}2) = 0{,}01\) m below the height of the point \(P\), and both joints have to correct this. For a shift ten times smaller, \(0{,}01\) m, the elbow angle decreases by \(1{,}159^\circ\) against the predicted \(1{,}146^\circ\), so the error \(0{,}013^\circ\) is about a hundred times smaller. The linear prediction with derivatives holds for small shifts, and its error falls roughly with the square of the shift.

What happens when the condition \(\sin q_2 \neq 0\) is dropped? It turns out that the conclusion of the corollary fails.

Take the configuration \(\vek q_* = (0, 0)\), where the arm is stretched and \(\sin q_2 = 0\). The blue arm has its elbow \(o_1\) on the axis \(x_0\) and a small angle \(q_2 = 0{,}6\) rad at the elbow. Its tip is at the point \(P = (1{,}4127,\ 0{,}2823)\) m, a little inside the outer edge. By theorem 27.34 there is another solution there (\(c = 0{,}8253\)), the orange arm with \(q_1' = 0{,}3945\) rad and \(q_2' = -0{,}6\) rad. Each posture is near \(\vek q_*\), since \(|q_2| \le 0{,}6\) rad and \(q_1 \in \{0,\ 0{,}3945\}\). With a smaller \(q_2\) the postures come closer still: at \(q_2 = 0{,}1\) rad the posture \((0, 0{,}1)\) has the same tip \((1{,}4975,\ 0{,}0499)\) m as the posture \((0{,}0666, -0{,}1)\), and at \(q_2 = 0{,}01\) rad the posture \((0, 0{,}01)\) has the same tip as \((0{,}0067, -0{,}01)\) (num-05.out, C7).

That this holds for every small angle and not only for three numbers follows from step 1 of the proof of theorem 27.34. For \(0 < t < \pi\) we have \(\Phi(0, t) = \vek w(t) = (l_1 + l_2\cos t,\ l_2\sin t)\). Let \(\beta\) be the angle of item 2 of the theorem, \(\vek w(t) = |\vek w(t)|\,(\cos\beta, \sin\beta)\). Both components are positive, \(l_1 + l_2\cos t \ge l_1 - l_2 = 0{,}5\) m and \(l_2\sin t > 0\) (lemma 8.11, item 3), so we choose \(\beta\) between \(0\) and \(\pi/2\). The cosine is even and the sine odd (the same lemma, item 4), so \(\vek w(-t) = |\vek w(t)|\,(\cos\beta, -\sin\beta)\), the mirror image of \(\vek w(t)\) in the axis \(x_0\). By step 1 and the addition formulas, \(\Phi(2\beta, -t) = \mat R(2\beta)\,\vek w(-t) = |\vek w(t)|\,(\cos\beta, \sin\beta) = \vek w(t)\). The set \((0, t)\) and the set \((2\beta, -t)\) are therefore different and have the same tip. At \(t = 0{,}1\) rad we get \(2\beta = 0{,}0666\) rad, exactly the \(q_1'\) above (NumPy). It remains to estimate that both are close to \((0, 0)\). From \(|\vek w(t)|^2 = l_1^2 + l_2^2 + 2l_1l_2\cos t \ge (l_1 - l_2)^2\) (step 2 of the proof and \(\cos t \ge -1\)) we get \(|\vek w(t)| \ge l_1 - l_2\) (lemma 1.29). With \(\sin t \le t\) (lemma 8.20, step 2 of the proof) this gives \(\sin\beta = l_2\sin t/|\vek w(t)| \le l_2\,t/(l_1 - l_2) = t\). By the same lemma \(\beta - \sin\beta \le \beta^3/6 \le \beta\,\pi^2/24\), because \(\beta < \pi/2\), so \(\beta \le \sin\beta/(1 - \pi^2/24) < 1{,}7\,t\). Both sets are thus closer to \((0, 0)\) than \(2\cdot 1{,}7\,t + t = 4{,}4\,t\), which for small enough \(t\) is less than the radius of any ball around \((0, 0)\). In every ball around \((0, 0)\) there are therefore two different sets of angles with the same tip, and \(\Phi\) is not injective on any ball. A local inverse map does not exist, although \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable everywhere. The condition of the corollary is missing: \(\det\mat F_\Phi = l_1l_2\sin q_2\) is only \(0{,}0499\) m\(^2\) at \(q_2 = 0{,}1\) rad, \(0{,}005\) m\(^2\) at \(0{,}01\) rad and zero at \(0\).

We see the same if we follow how fast the angle \(q_2\) changes with the distance of the point from the edge. On the axis \(x_0\) we have \(r = x\). From (27.18), \(1 - c = ((l_1 + l_2)^2 - r^2)/(2l_1l_2) = (1{,}5 - r)(1{,}5 + r)\) (for example A, \(2l_1l_2 = 1\) m\(^2\)) and \(1 - c = 2\sin^2(q_2/2)\), because \(\cos q_2 = 1 - 2\sin^2(q_2/2)\) by the addition formula, For small angles \(\sin(q_2/2)\) is about \(q_2/2\) (lemma 8.20), so \(2\sin^2(q_2/2)\) is about \(q_2^2/2\), and near the edge \(1{,}5 + r\) is about \(3\) m. Hence \(q_2^2 \approx 6\,(1{,}5 - r)\) with the distance in metres and the angle in radians: \(|q_2|\) grows like the square root of the distance to the edge. At \(0{,}1\) m from the edge this is \(\sqrt{0{,}6} = 0{,}775\) rad \(= 44{,}4^\circ\), at \(0{,}01\) m it is \(\sqrt{0{,}06} = 0{,}245\) rad \(= 14{,}0^\circ\). Our own arm feels this: a stretched arm has to bend by as much as \(14^\circ\) at the elbow before the reach shortens by a single centimetre, because a link that starts to bend at first hardly shortens along the arm. The derivative of a square root, however, is unbounded at zero. Computed at points on the axis \(x_0\) (num-05.out, C6):

\(r\) in m \(\lvert q_2\rvert\) in degrees \(\partial q_2/\partial r\) in rad/m
1,4 44,77 \(-3{,}98\)
1,49 14,05 \(-12{,}28\)
1,499 4,44 \(-38{,}74\)
1,4999 1,40 \(-122{,}48\)
1,5 0 not defined

Figure 27.46 draws the columns of the table. Horizontally the distance \(r\) of the tip from joint 1, vertically the angle \(|q_2|\), the dashed vertical is the edge \(r = l_1 + l_2 = 1{,}5\) m. The blue curve is \(|q_2|\) from (27.18): towards the edge it falls ever more steeply and meets the axis at the edge vertically. At \(r = 1{,}4\) m, that is \(0{,}1\) m from the edge, the angle is \(44{,}77^\circ\) and the orange tangent has slope \(-3{,}98\) rad/m. At \(r = 1{,}49\) m, \(0{,}01\) m from the edge, the angle is still \(14{,}05^\circ\), while the tangent with slope \(-12{,}28\) rad/m is already three times steeper.

When the distance to the edge is ten times smaller, the derivative is about \(\sqrt{10} = 3{,}16\) times larger. The conclusion of the corollary (the derivative of the inverse is continuous in a neighbourhood of the point \(\Phi(\vek q_*)\), hence bounded there) therefore fails when the condition fails. For a robot this means: near the edge of the workspace a small motion of the tip demands a much faster rotation of the elbow. In section 27.7 we shall call the same configuration singular and see what it means for velocities and forces.

Corollary 27.35 says only that a local inverse exists, not how to find it. For the two-link arm we have theorem 27.34, which gives it in closed form. For a general arm with \(n\) joints the task is given by \(\mat T^0_{\mathrm{n}}(\vek q) = \mat H\) (the product of 27.31 and a given homogeneous transformation \(\mat H\), definition 27.20), which is twelve nonlinear equations for \(n\) unknowns, SPONG (5.2) and (5.4), PDF p. 163-164. It does not always have a solution, the solution is not always unique, and we cannot always write it in closed form (SPONG PDF p. 165). For robots with six joints whose wrist has three axes through one point, SPONG splits it into two tasks, for position and for orientation: the position of the wrist centre \(\vek o_{\mathrm{c}}\) depends by (5.10), PDF p. 166, only on the first three angles, and the orientation of the wrist by (5.13), PDF p. 167, on the last three. We do not prove this here, because it lies beyond the subject of the chapter.

We build the figure on the board. The first three links stand on the base and carry the wrist. The end of the third link is the wrist centre \(o_{\mathrm{c}}\), where the three wrist axes meet. On the wrist is the gripper. The first three angles move \(o_{\mathrm{c}}\), while the last three only turn the gripper about \(o_{\mathrm{c}}\) and do not move \(o_{\mathrm{c}}\), so the task splits into position and orientation.

For the first three angles of such a robot the calculation we have made suffices, because links 2 and 3 move in a plane (SPONG, PDF p. 172-173). We look at it on arm B of section 27.4, an elbow arm with a turning base and two links turning about horizontal axes: \(d_1 = 0{,}4\) m, \(a_2 = 0{,}5\) m, \(a_3 = 0{,}4\) m (our values, the layout is from SPONG, example 4.9, PDF p. 147-150).

Example 27.36 Inverse kinematics of the elbow arm B (inverzna kinematika komolčne roke B)

Let \(\vek q = (30^\circ, 45^\circ, -60^\circ)\), which by example B1 gives the tip \(T = (0{,}6408,\ 0{,}3700,\ 0{,}6500)\) m. We find all sets of angles that give this point.

  1. Links 2 and 3 lie in the vertical plane that \(q_1\) turns away from the axis \(x_0\). The tip is therefore \(T = (\rho\cos q_1,\ \rho\sin q_1,\ d_1 + a_2\sin q_2 + a_3\sin(q_2 + q_3))\) with \(\rho = a_2\cos q_2 + a_3\cos(q_2 + q_3)\) (checked with the product of DH matrices, num-05.out, D1). In this plane \(\rho\) is the abscissa of the tip and \(s = z - d_1\) the ordinate, and links 2 and 3 are the planar two-link arm of theorem 27.34 with \(l_1 = a_2\), \(l_2 = a_3\) and the angles \(q_2\) and \(q_3\).
  2. Let \(T = (0{,}6408,\ 0{,}3700,\ 0{,}6500)\) m. The horizontal distance from the axis \(z_0\) is \(r = \sqrt{0{,}6408^2 + 0{,}3700^2} = 0{,}7399\) m, the height above the shoulder is \(s = 0{,}65 - 0{,}4 = 0{,}25\) m, and \(r^2 + s^2 = 0{,}61\) m\(^2\). By (27.18), \(\cos q_3 = (0{,}61 - 0{,}25 - 0{,}16)/(2\cdot 0{,}5\cdot 0{,}4) = 0{,}5\), so \(q_3 = \pm 60^\circ\).
  3. The first two components of the tip give \((\rho\cos q_1, \rho\sin q_1) = (x, y)\), so \(\rho^2 = \rho^2(\cos^2 q_1 + \sin^2 q_1) = x^2 + y^2 = r^2\) (lemma 8.11, item 1) and \(\rho = r\) or \(\rho = -r\). For \(\rho = r\) we get \((\cos q_1, \sin q_1) = (x, y)/r = (\cos 30^\circ, \sin 30^\circ)\), so \(q_1 = 30^\circ\). For \(\rho = -r\) we get \((\cos q_1, \sin q_1) = -(\cos 30^\circ, \sin 30^\circ) = (\cos 210^\circ, \sin 210^\circ)\), so \(q_1 = 210^\circ\). The cosine and the sine fix an angle up to a multiple of \(2\pi\) (step 5 of the proof of theorem 27.34), so there are no other angles \(q_1\). For each \(\rho\), theorem 27.34 for the point \((\rho, s)\) gives two values \(q_3 = \pm 60^\circ\) and one \(q_2\) for each. In all there are four sets (num-05.out, D3): \((30^\circ, -7{,}659^\circ, 60^\circ)\), \((30^\circ, 45^\circ, -60^\circ)\), \((210^\circ, 135^\circ, 60^\circ)\) and \((210^\circ, -172{,}341^\circ, -60^\circ)\). Each gives the tip \(T\) by equation (27.16).

We build the figure on the board. The axis \(z_0\) is the vertical line through the base. Link 1 of length \(d_1\) is vertical up to the shoulder \(S\). From the shoulder we draw the blue links 2 and 3 with the elbow \(45^\circ\) above the horizontal and a bend downward by \(60^\circ\) towards the tip \(T\), and the orange ones with the elbow below the horizontal. Both end at the same point \(T\), at the distance \(r\) and height \(s\). Comparing solutions 2 and 3 we see that they have the same elbow and tip: the links lie on the same segments, but the sets of angles differ, because at \(q_1 = 210^\circ\) the arm is turned by half a turn about the axis \(z_0\) and \(q_2\) is raised past the vertical. The four sets of angles therefore give only two positions of the segments, which for ideal links without extent cannot be seen (the idealization of section 27.1).

We see the same from above. The axes \(x_0\) and \(y_0\) are the axes of the base, the axis \(z_0\) points at the reader. The point \(T\) is the projection of the tip, and the distance \(r\) from the axis \(z_0\) to it is the same in both solutions. For \(\rho = r\), links 2 and 3 lie in the direction \(q_1 = 30^\circ\) and reach \(T\). For \(\rho = -r\) the abscissa of the tip in the plane of the links is negative, so the base is turned half a turn to \(q_1 = 210^\circ\) and the links reach backwards over the axis to the same point \(T\).

The example does not behave like this everywhere. If the tip is on the axis \(z_0\), \(x = y = 0\), step 3 of the example does not determine the angle \(q_1\): from \((\rho\cos q_1, \rho\sin q_1) = (0, 0)\) we only get \(\rho = 0\), and \(q_1\) can be any angle.

The left side of the figure shows the posture in which links 2 and 3 have equal and opposite horizontal projections: \(\rho = a_2\cos 45^\circ + a_3\cos(45^\circ + 107{,}1144^\circ) = 0{,}3536 - 0{,}3536 = 0\) (num-05.out, D4). The tip is on the axis at \(z = 0{,}9406\) m and rotating the base does not move it. Every angle \(q_1\) gives the same point, as the view from above shows with the elbow going round a circle for different \(q_1\). There are infinitely many solutions, and this is the shoulder singularity that SPONG mentions at (5.18) and (5.19), PDF p. 170, and in figure 5.5, PDF p. 171. What fails is step 3 of the example, not theorem 27.34. The theorem holds for the point \((\rho, s) = (0,\ 0{,}5406)\) m in the plane of links 2 and 3, which is not the origin of that plane, and gives two pairs \((q_2, q_3)\), \((45^\circ,\ 107{,}1144^\circ)\) and \((135^\circ,\ -107{,}1144^\circ)\) with \(\cos q_3 = -0{,}2943\) (NumPy). For every \(q_1\) there are therefore two solutions. They are infinitely many because \(r = 0\), and step 3 cannot divide by \(r\) to get \((\cos q_1, \sin q_1)\) from \((x, y)\).

27.6 The Jacobian matrix of a robot (Jacobijeva matrika robota)

We draw the robot as a chain. The base is fixed to the floor, link 1 turns about joint 1, link 2 about joint 2. Each motor has its own rate, \(\dot q_1\) and \(\dot q_2\), drawn as an arc about the joint. At the end of the chain is the end effector. Its velocity shows where it moves, its rotation how fast it turns. We look for the relation between the two arcs on one side and the velocity and rotation of the end effector on the other.

So far we have given the robot a position: the joint variables (spremenljivke zglobov) \(\vek q = (q_1, \dots, q_{\mathrm{n}})\) (section 27.1) give, by direct kinematics (definition 27.31), the origin \(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}(\vek q)\) and the orientation matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{n}}(\vek q)\) of the end effector (končni efektor, definition 27.8). Motors, however, do not turn by a fixed angle. Each has its own rate \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\). The question is how fast the end effector moves and how fast it turns. We need the answer three times: to find the positions where the robot can no longer move in every direction (section 27.7), for the joint forces that balance a load on the end effector (section 27.7), and for the kinetic energy of the links (section 27.8).

The model is the one used before (section 27.1): rigid links (definition 1.11), ideal joints with one degree of freedom held by motors, and an open chain. Friction and motor inertia do not appear. The variables \(q_{\mathrm{i}}(t)\) are twice continuously differentiable functions of time, like the entries of the matrix \(\mat Q(t)\) in definition 8.39. Notation: the orientation matrix of link \(n\) relative to frame \(0\) is written in short \(\mat R_{\mathrm{n}} = \mat R^0{}_{\mathrm{n}}\). Its columns are the axes of frame \(n\) in frame \(0\) (definition 27.8), so it is the transpose of the rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) of definition 2.44, where the axes are in the rows. It is not the polar factor of chapter 2 and not \(\mat R(\varphi)\) of chapter 8. The origin of frame \(i\) in frame \(0\) is \(\vek o_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek o^0{}_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the unit vector of the \(z\) axis of frame \(i\) in frame \(0\) is \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek k\) with \(\vek k = (0, 0, 1)\). The matrix we shall build is written \(\mat J(\vek q)\). The inertia tensor of chapter 8, written \(\mat J_{\mathrm{k}}\) there, is written \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\) in this chapter, so that the two symbols never meet.

27.6.1 Angular velocity of a link (kotna hitrost člena)

We draw a single link. Frame 0 is at rest, the link is a rigid body with its own axes at the point \(\vek o\). We pick a point of the link \(\vek x\) and the vector \(\vek x - \vek o\) from the origin to it. The origin moves with velocity \(\dot{\vek o}\), and the link turns about an axis through the origin with angular velocity \(\vek\omega\). Because of the turning the point runs along a circle and has velocity \(\vek\omega\times(\vek x - \vek o)\), tangent to the circle. The sum of both velocities is the velocity of the point \(\dot{\vek x}\).

First we need the velocities of the points of one link. For the motion \(\vek x = \vek c + \mat Q\,\vek X\), chapter 8 showed that all points of a rigid body have the velocity \(\dot{\vek c} + \vek\omega\times(\vek x - \vek c)\) (lemma 8.87) with one single angular velocity \(\vek\omega\) (definition 8.86). Link \(n\) is such a body. A point with constant coordinates \(\vek p^n\) in the frame of the link has the position \(\vek x = \vek o_{\mathrm{n}} + \mat R_{\mathrm{n}}\,\vek p^n\) in frame \(0\) by lemma 27.9, which is the form \(\vek c + \mat Q\,\vek X\) with \(\mat R_{\mathrm{n}}\) in place of \(\mat Q\). The matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{n}}\) need not equal the unit matrix at time \(0\), so we repeat the proof of lemma 8.85 for \(\mat R_{\mathrm{n}}\).

Why \(\mat\Omega\) must be antisymmetric is seen on two arrows fixed to the link. At time \(t\), the arrow \(\vek u\) and the arrow \(\vek v\) equal the axes \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\) of frame \(0\), they have unit length and are perpendicular. The link turns with the angular velocity \(\omega\) about an axis perpendicular to the page. At time \(t + \Delta t\) both have turned by the same angle \(\omega\,\Delta t\), and their tips stay on the unit circle. An arrow \(\vek y = \mat R\,\vek p\) fixed to the link has, by step 4 of the proof below, the velocity \(\dot{\vek y} = \dot{\mat R}\,\vek p = \mat\Omega\,\vek y\). So \(\Omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\mat\Omega\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the component along \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) of the velocity of the arrow that equals \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) at time \(t\). The velocity \(\dot{\vek u}\) is tangent to the circle and perpendicular to \(\vek u\), so \(\Omega_{11} = 0\). The arrow \(\vek u\) tilts towards \(\vek v\), so \(\Omega_{21} = \omega\). The arrow \(\vek v\) tilts away from \(\vek u\) by the same angle, its velocity \(\dot{\vek v}\) points along \(-\vek e_1\) and \(\Omega_{12} = -\omega\). If \(\Omega_{11}\) were not \(0\), \(\vek u\) would grow longer or shorter. If \(\Omega_{12}\) were not \(-\Omega_{21}\), the right angle would open or close. The proof says the same with matrices: the orthogonality of the matrix \(\mat R\) means exactly that lengths and angles are kept.

Lemma 27.37 Derivative of the orientation matrix and angular velocity of a link (odvod matrike orientacije in kotna hitrost člena)

Let \(\mat R(t)\) be the orientation matrix of a link relative to frame \(0\), with twice continuously differentiable entries, and \(\mat\Omega = \dot{\mat R}\,\mat R^\T\). Then \(\mat\Omega\) is antisymmetric, for \(\vek\omega = (\Omega_{32},\ \Omega_{13},\ \Omega_{21})\) we have \(\mat\Omega\,\vek y = \vek\omega\times\vek y\) for every vector \(\vek y\), and \(\dot{\mat R} = \mat\Omega\,\mat R\). A point with constant coordinates \(\vek p\) in the frame of the link, which has the position \(\vek x = \vek o + \mat R\,\vek p\) in frame \(0\), has the velocity

\[\dot{\vek x} = \dot{\vek o} + \vek\omega\times(\vek x - \vek o) . \tag{27.21}\]
Proof

We must show that \(\mat\Omega\) is antisymmetric and then use that \(\vek p\) is constant.

  1. The matrix \(\mat R\) is orthogonal (lemma 27.9), so \(\mat R\,\mat R^\T = \mat I\) at every time. By the product rule (lemma 1.82), applied to every entry, \(\dot{\mat R}\,\mat R^\T + \mat R\,\dot{\mat R}^\T = \mat 0\).
  2. By lemma 1.102, \(\mat\Omega^\T = \mat R\,\dot{\mat R}^\T\), which by step 1 equals \(-\mat\Omega\). The matrix \(\mat\Omega\) is antisymmetric.
  3. Steps 3 and 4 of the proof of lemma 8.85 use only \(\mat\Omega^\T = -\mat\Omega\) and (2.39), so they give \(\mat\Omega\,\vek y = \vek\omega\times\vek y\).
  4. From \(\mat R^\T\mat R = \mat I\) (lemma 27.9), \(\dot{\mat R} = \dot{\mat R}\,\mat R^\T\mat R = \mat\Omega\,\mat R\).
  5. Since \(\vek p\) is constant, \(\dot{\vek x} = \dot{\vek o} + \dot{\mat R}\,\vek p\). By step 4 and step 3 with \(\vek y = \mat R\,\vek p = \vek x - \vek o\), \(\dot{\mat R}\,\vek p = \mat\Omega\,\mat R\,\vek p = \vek\omega\times(\vek x - \vek o)\).

Source: SPONG (4.18) (PDF p. 129) for \(\dot{\mat R} = \mat S(\vek\omega)\,\mat R\), (4.32) and (4.35) (PDF p. 132) for the velocity of a point. The step-by-step proof for \(\mat R\) is a copy of the proof of lemma 8.85 and is not from the source.

For the motion treated in lemma 8.87, \(\mat Q(t) = \mat R(t)\,\mat R(0)^\T\), because it has the value \(\mat I\) at time \(0\) and turns the point \(\vek X\) of the frame as \(\mat R(t)\,\vek p\) does. Hence \(\dot{\mat Q}\,\mat Q^\T = \dot{\mat R}\,\mat R(0)^\T\mat R(0)\,\mat R^\T = \dot{\mat R}\,\mat R^\T\), and the angular velocity of lemma 27.37 is exactly the angular velocity of definition 8.86. The motion of the points of a link is thus described by two vectors, \(\dot{\vek o}\) and \(\vek\omega\), that is, by six numbers. The connection between them and the joint rates \(\dot{\vek q}\) is sought in the next subsection.

We draw three links. Frame 0 is at rest, frame 1 is attached to link 1, which turns with angular velocity \(\vek\omega_1\) relative to frame 0. Link 2 turns relative to link 1 with rate \(\vek\omega^1{}_{1,2}\), which is measured in frame 1, so we draw it converted to frame 0. Relative to frame 0 its angular velocity \(\vek\omega_2\) is the sum of the first vector and the second. We repeat this for link 3: its relative rate is added and gives the total rate \(\vek\omega_3\).

A robot has several links that turn relative to each other, so angular velocities have to be added. We know the angular velocity of link \(1\) relative to frame \(0\) and that of link \(2\) relative to link \(1\). What is the angular velocity of link \(2\) relative to frame \(0\)? Vectors written in different frames must not be added, so we first need an identity that tells how the vector product behaves under a rotation.

The left part shows a rotation. We take vector \(\vek a\), vector \(\vek b\) and their vector product \(\vek a\times\vek b\), perpendicular to the plane of both. The rotation \(\mat R\) turns all three together as a rigid triple: \(\mat R\,\vek a\), \(\mat R\,\vek b\) and \(\mat R\,(\vek a\times\vek b)\) result. For the proof we take an arbitrary vector \(\vek c\) and its preimage \(\vek u = \mat R^\T\vek c\) before the rotation. The box on \(\vek u\), \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and the box on \(\vek c\), \(\mat R\,\vek a\), \(\mat R\,\vek b\) have the same volume, since a rotation keeps volume. The right part shows why we need \(\det\mat R = 1\): for the reflection \(\mat R = -\mat I\) we have the vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and their product \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), the reversed vectors and their product, again \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), but the reversed original product points to \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Lemma 27.38 The vector product and a rotation (vektorski produkt in zasuk)

Let \(\mat R\) be an orthogonal \(3 \times 3\) matrix with \(\det\mat R = 1\). Then for all vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\)

\[(\mat R\,\vek a)\times(\mat R\,\vek b) = \mat R\,(\vek a\times\vek b) . \tag{27.22}\]

If an antisymmetric matrix \(\mat\Omega\) satisfies \(\mat\Omega\,\vek y = \vek a\times\vek y\) for every \(\vek y\), then \(\mat R\,\mat\Omega\,\mat R^\T\vek y = (\mat R\,\vek a)\times\vek y\) for every \(\vek y\).

Proof

We must show that the two vectors in (27.22) have the same scalar product with every vector, and then use this.

  1. Let \(\vek c\) be any vector and \(\vek u = \mat R^\T\vek c\), so \(\vek c = \mat R\,\vek u\) (lemma 27.9).
  2. The scalar triple product is the determinant of the matrix with the vectors in its columns ((2.71)), so \(\vek c\cdot\big((\mat R\,\vek a)\times(\mat R\,\vek b)\big) = \det(\mat R\,\vek u,\ \mat R\,\vek a,\ \mat R\,\vek b)\).
  3. The columns of \(\mat R\,\mat M\) are \(\mat R\) times the columns of \(\mat M\) ((1.39)). So the determinant of step 2 is \(\det\big(\mat R\,(\vek u, \vek a, \vek b)\big) = \det\mat R\cdot\det(\vek u, \vek a, \vek b)\) by theorem 2.74, that is, \(\vek u\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b)\).
  4. By lemma 1.102, \(\vek u\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = (\mat R^\T\vek c)\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = \vek c\cdot\mat R\,(\vek a\times\vek b)\).
  5. The difference \(\vek d = (\mat R\,\vek a)\times(\mat R\,\vek b) - \mat R\,(\vek a\times\vek b)\) therefore satisfies \(\vek c\cdot\vek d = 0\) for every \(\vek c\). For \(\vek c = \vek d\) we get \(|\vek d|^2 = 0\) and \(\vek d = \vek 0\). This is (27.22).
  6. Second part: \(\mat R\,\mat\Omega\,\mat R^\T\vek y = \mat R\,(\vek a\times\mat R^\T\vek y)\) by assumption, which by (27.22) equals \((\mat R\,\vek a)\times(\mat R\,\mat R^\T\vek y) = (\mat R\,\vek a)\times\vek y\).

Source: SPONG (4.9) and (4.8) (PDF p. 127): both identities are stated in the source with "verified by direct calculation". The proof is ours.

The condition \(\det\mat R = 1\) is needed. The reflection \(\mat R = -\mat I\) has \(\det\mat R = -1\) and is orthogonal, but for \(\vek a = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek b = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) we get \((\mat R\,\vek a)\times(\mat R\,\vek b) = (-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\times(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), whereas \(\mat R\,(\vek a\times\vek b) = -\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) (num-06.out N4). Step 3 of the proof is where the factor \(\det\mat R = -1\) would show. Rotations preserve right-handedness (lemma 27.9), reflections do not.

Lemma 27.39 Addition of angular velocities (seštevanje kotnih hitrosti)

Let \(\mat R_2 = \mat R_1\,\mat R^1{}_2\) by lemma 27.12, all three matrices with twice continuously differentiable entries. Let \(\vek\omega_1\) be the angular velocity of \(\mat R_1\) and \(\vek\omega^1{}_{1,2}\) that of \(\mat R^1{}_2\) by lemma 27.37 (the components of the first in frame \(0\), of the second in frame \(1\), because \(\mat R^1{}_2\) is measured in it). Then the angular velocity of \(\mat R_2\) is

\[\vek\omega_2 = \vek\omega_1 + \mat R_1\,\vek\omega^1{}_{1,2} . \tag{27.23}\]

For a chain of \(n\) links, \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^n \mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\,\vek\omega^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}-1,\mathrm{i}}\) with \(\mat R_0 = \mat I\).

Proof

We must show that \(\dot{\mat R}_2\,\mat R_2^\T\) is the sum of two antisymmetric matrices that we know, and then read off the vector.

  1. By the product rule (lemma 1.82), \(\dot{\mat R}_2 = \dot{\mat R}_1\,\mat R^1{}_2 + \mat R_1\,\dot{\mat R}^1{}_2\).
  2. By lemma 1.102, \(\mat R_2^\T = (\mat R^1{}_2)^\T\mat R_1^\T\). Multiplying and using \(\mat R^1{}_2(\mat R^1{}_2)^\T = \mat I\) gives \(\dot{\mat R}_2\,\mat R_2^\T = \dot{\mat R}_1\,\mat R_1^\T + \mat R_1\,\big(\dot{\mat R}^1{}_2(\mat R^1{}_2)^\T\big)\,\mat R_1^\T\).
  3. The first term is \(\mat\Omega_1\), with angular velocity \(\vek\omega_1\). In the second, the bracket is by lemma 27.37 the matrix with \(\vek y \mapsto \vek\omega^1{}_{1,2}\times\vek y\). By the second part of lemma 27.38, the second term is the map \(\vek y \mapsto (\mat R_1\,\vek\omega^1{}_{1,2})\times\vek y\).
  4. So the matrix \(\mat\Omega_2\) acts as \(\vek y \mapsto (\vek\omega_1 + \mat R_1\,\vek\omega^1{}_{1,2})\times\vek y\). If a matrix acts as \(\vek y \mapsto \vek a\times\vek y\), then \(\Omega_{32} = (\vek a\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})_{\mathrm{z}} = a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Omega_{13} = (\vek a\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}})_{\mathrm{x}} = a_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Omega_{21} = (\vek a\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{y}} = a_{\mathrm{z}}\), so its vector by definition 8.86 is exactly \(\vek a\). This is (27.23).
  5. For a chain we use (27.23) with induction on \(n\): \(\mat R_{\mathrm{n}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{n}-1}\,\mat R^{n-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}}\) (lemma 27.12) gives \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek\omega_{\mathrm{n}-1} + \mat R_{\mathrm{n}-1}\,\vek\omega^{n-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}-1,\mathrm{n}}\), and \(\vek\omega_1 = \mat R_0\,\vek\omega^0{}_{0,1}\) is the start.

Source: SPONG (4.20)-(4.26) (PDF p. 130-131) and (4.28)-(4.30) (PDF p. 131). The step-by-step proof is ours, the source uses (4.8) and \(\mat S(\vek a) + \mat S(\vek b) = \mat S(\vek a + \vek b)\).

The sum (27.23) is an addition of vectors, correct only when all components are written in the same frame: \(\mat R_1\,\vek\omega^1{}_{1,2}\) is the angular velocity of link \(2\) relative to link \(1\), converted into frame \(0\) (lemma 27.9). That is why the last step of the proof has the matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) in front of every term.

On the left is a revolute joint. The axis \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) runs through the joint, link \(i-1\) is at rest relative to it, link \(i\) turns about it along the arc \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\). The angular velocity vector lies along the axis and has length \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\). In the middle is a prismatic joint: the slider moves along the axis with the sliding rate, there is no turning, so the angular velocity is zero. On the right we look at the turning from above: the axes before the turn and the axes after a small turn \(\Delta\theta\), the vector \(\vek y\) and the vector \(\vek k\times\vek y\), which is turned by \(90^\circ\) in the direction of the rotation.

What is the angular velocity of one joint? By section 27.4, \(\mat R^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta_\mathrm{i}}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{x},\alpha_\mathrm{i}}\) (lemma 27.28, definition 27.10). At a revolute joint \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the variable \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) (or \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) plus a constant) and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant, at a prismatic joint \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant.

Lemma 27.40 Angular velocity of a joint (kotna hitrost zgloba)

Let \(\mat K = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\). Then \(\mat K\,\vek y = \vek k\times\vek y\) for every \(\vek y\) and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta} = \mat K\,\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\). At a revolute joint \(i\), \(\vek\omega^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}-1,\mathrm{i}} = \dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek k\), at a prismatic joint \(\vek\omega^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}-1,\mathrm{i}} = \vek 0\).

Proof

We must show both derivatives and then compute \(\dot{\mat R}\,\mat R^\T\).

  1. By (2.39), \(\vek k\times\vek y = (0\cdot y_3 - 1\cdot y_2,\ 1\cdot y_1 - 0\cdot y_3,\ 0) = (-y_2,\ y_1,\ 0) = \mat K\,\vek y\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\) has the entries \(\cos\theta\), \(-\sin\theta\), \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) and \(1\). The derivatives are \(\sin' = \cos\) and \(\cos' = -\sin\) (theorem 8.13), so the derivative of the matrix with respect to \(\theta\) is \(\begin{pmatrix} -\sin\theta & -\cos\theta & 0 \\ \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), which is \(\mat K\,\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\) by the definition of the matrix product (definition 1.99).
  3. At a revolute joint, \(\dot{\mat R}^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}} = \dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mat K\,\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta_\mathrm{i}}\mat R_{\mathrm{x},\alpha_\mathrm{i}}\) by the chain rule and step 2. By lemma 1.102, \((\mat R^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}})^\T = \mat R_{\mathrm{x},\alpha_\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta_\mathrm{i}}^\T\), hence \(\dot{\mat R}^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}}(\mat R^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}})^\T = \dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mat K\), since both rotations are orthogonal (lemma 27.9). By step 1 it acts as \(\vek y \mapsto \dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek k\times\vek y\), and the vector of definition 8.86 is \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek k\) (step 4 of the proof of lemma 27.39).
  4. At a prismatic joint \(\mat R^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant, its derivative is \(\mat 0\), and so \(\vek\omega^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}-1,\mathrm{i}} = \vek 0\).

Source: SPONG (4.43) and (4.44) (PDF p. 134). The step-by-step proof is ours.

Each revolute joint thus turns the next link about its axis \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) at the rate \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\), and a prismatic joint does not turn it. The next subsection builds the angular part of the Jacobian matrix from this.

27.6.2 The matrix that maps joint rates to the velocity of the end effector (matrika, ki preslika hitrosti zglobov v hitrost efektorja)

Let us see how the velocity of the end effector is assembled from the motor rates on robot A, the planar arm with two links, \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m, met in section 27.1 (the link masses are our choice, we do not need them here). Draw the arm at \(\vek q = (30^\circ;\ 60^\circ)\) (figure 27.57). The base is at the origin. Link 1 goes from the base to the second joint at the angle \(30^\circ\), link 2 continues at the angle \(q_1 + q_2 = 90^\circ\), vertically upward, to the tip of the end effector. The axes of both joints, \(\vek z_0\) and \(\vek z_1\), point perpendicular to the page toward us, because the arm turns in the plane of the page.

Now let only motor 1 turn, at the rate \(\dot q_1\) (left part of the figure). Motor 2 is at rest, so both links behave as one rigid body that turns about the axis \(\vek z_0\) with the angular velocity \(\dot q_1\,\vek z_0\) (lemma 27.40). The tip, on the lever arm \(\vek r_1 = \vek o_2 - \vek o_0\) from the axis to the tip, has by lemma 27.37 (with the fixed origin \(\vek o_0\)) the velocity \(\dot q_1\,\vek z_0\times\vek r_1\). The vector product is perpendicular to the lever arm (lemma 2.34, item 4), which also has a reason in the picture: a point of a turning body moves on a circle about the axis, so its velocity lies along the tangent of that circle, and the tangent is perpendicular to the radius, which here is the lever arm. The length of the product is \(|\vek r_1| = \sqrt{0{,}866^2 + 1^2} = 1{,}3229\) m times \(\dot q_1\). For \(\dot q_1 = 1\) rad/s this is the velocity \(\vek J_1\), drawn from the tip. In plain words: at the same angular velocity a point on a long lever arm moves faster than a point on a short one, and the direction of motion is perpendicular to the lever arm. In the second part (middle of the figure) only motor 2 turns, at the rate \(\dot q_2\). Link 1 is at rest, link 2 turns about the axis \(\vek z_1\) through the second joint, the lever arm \(\vek r_2\) is only the length of link 2, \(|\vek o_2 - \vek o_1| = 0{,}5\) m, and the tip moves with the velocity \(\vek J_2\) \(= \vek z_1\times\vek r_2\) at \(\dot q_2 = 1\) rad/s. In the right part both motors turn at once, each with its own rate. The velocity of the tip is the time derivative of its position, and this position is a function of both angles, so by the chain rule (lemma 8.30) the velocity is the sum of the two contributions, each multiplied by its motor rate, \(\vek v = \vek J_1\,\dot q_1 + \vek J_2\,\dot q_2\). The numbers \(\dot q_1\) and \(\dot q_2\) thus determine the tip velocity through a matrix that has \(\vek J_1\) and \(\vek J_2\) as columns.

The name Jacobian matrix is already borne by the matrix of derivatives of a map from chapter 4 (definition 4.42). This matrix is also a matrix of derivatives: column \(i\) is the derivative of the tip position with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) (step 3 of theorem 27.42), which is why it is so called. For the angular velocity there are no such derivatives (lemma 27.44), so we define the matrix for both parts together by its task.

Definition 27.41 Jacobian matrix of a robot (Jacobijeva matrika robota)

Let a robot have \(n\) joints, joint variables \(\vek q\) and the end-effector orientation matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{n}}(\vek q)\). Let \(\vek v = \dot{\vek o}_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the velocity of the end-effector origin, \(\vek\omega = \vek\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) the angular velocity of \(\mat R_{\mathrm{n}}\) by lemma 27.37 (both in frame \(0\)) and \(\vek\xi = (\vek v;\ \vek\omega)\) the column of six numbers. The Jacobian matrix of the robot is the \(6 \times n\) matrix \(\mat J(\vek q)\) that is a function of the variables \(\vek q\) only and satisfies, for every motion \(\vek q(t)\),

\[\vek\xi = \mat J(\vek q)\,\dot{\vek q} . \tag{27.24}\]

We call the upper \(3\) rows \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\) and the lower \(3\) rows \(\mat J_\omega\), so \(\vek v = \mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\,\dot{\vek q}\) and \(\vek\omega = \mat J_\omega\,\dot{\vek q}\). Column \(i\) is called \(\mat J_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Source: SPONG (4.37)-(4.42) (PDF p. 133), where \(\vek\xi\) is called a "body velocity" and the matrix is written as \(6 \times n\). Here the matrix is defined by property (27.24), existence and uniqueness are in theorem 27.42.

Units: \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\) is in rad/s for a revolute and in m/s for a prismatic joint, so the matrix \(\mat J\) has columns with different units (the column of a revolute joint has m above and 1 below, that of a prismatic joint 1 above and 0 below). The definition does not say whether such a matrix exists and what it is. The figure shows that column \(i\) is the velocity obtained when only joint \(i\) turns. The theorem proves it.

We draw a general chain, the links from the base with its origin \(\vek o_0\). The vector \(\vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) points to joint \(i\), through which the axis \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) runs. The lever \(\vek r\) leads from the joint axis to the end effector \(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}\). If only joint \(i\) turns with rate \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\), the angular velocity has the direction of the axis and the end effector has velocity perpendicular to the lever and to the axis. Below is a prismatic joint: its axis points in the sliding direction, and the velocity of the end effector is just the axis vector, with no turning.

Theorem 27.42 Columns of the Jacobian matrix (stolpci Jacobijeve matrike)

Let \(\vek q(t)\) be a twice continuously differentiable motion of a robot with \(n\) joints and DH frames \(0, \dots, n\) (section 27.4). Let \(\rho_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) for a revolute and \(\rho_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for a prismatic joint \(i\). Then the Jacobian matrix of the robot exists, is unique, and has the columns

\[\mat J_{\mathrm{i}} = \begin{pmatrix} \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1}) \\ \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1} \end{pmatrix} \text{ (revolute joint)} , \qquad \mat J_{\mathrm{i}} = \begin{pmatrix} \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1} \\ \vek 0 \end{pmatrix} \text{ (prismatic joint)} . \tag{27.25}\]
Proof

We must show first that \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \rho_{\mathrm{i}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\), then that \(\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\) equals the upper part of column \(i\), and finally use the chain rule.

  1. By lemma 27.40, \(\vek\omega^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}-1,\mathrm{i}} = \rho_{\mathrm{i}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek k\). By lemma 27.39, \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \rho_{\mathrm{i}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\,\vek k = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \rho_{\mathrm{i}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\). This is \(\mat J_\omega\,\dot{\vek q}\) with the column \(\rho_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\), which is the lower part of (27.25).
  2. The positions are composed by lemma 27.22 from \(\mat T^0{}_{\mathrm{n}} = \mat T^0{}_{\mathrm{i}-1}\,\mat T^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mat T^i{}_{\mathrm{n}}\). Hence \(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1} + \mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\,\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}} = \mat R^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek o^i{}_{\mathrm{n}} + \vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}}\). By lemma 27.28 every \(\mat T^{j-1}{}_{\mathrm{j}}\) contains only the variable \(q_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(\vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) do not contain \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\), and neither does \(\vek o^i{}_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  3. By the chain rule (lemma 8.30, item 1), \(\dot{\vek o}_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \dfrac{\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\). The vector \(\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\) is thus column \(i\) of \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\) and is the end-effector velocity when \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) and all other \(\dot q_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\).
  4. Prismatic joint: \(q_{\mathrm{i}} = d_{\mathrm{i}}\) and by lemma 27.28 \(\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta_\mathrm{i}}\,(a_{\mathrm{i}},\ 0,\ d_{\mathrm{i}})\), while \(\mat R^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}}\) does not depend on \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\). Hence \(\partial\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial d_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta_\mathrm{i}}\,\vek k = \vek k\) and by step 2 \(\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial d_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\,\vek k = \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\).
  5. Revolute joint: \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}} = q_{\mathrm{i}}\) or \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) plus a constant, which does not change the derivative. By lemma 27.28, \(\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta_\mathrm{i}}\,\vek w\) with \(\vek w = (a_{\mathrm{i}},\ 0,\ d_{\mathrm{i}}) + \mat R_{\mathrm{x},\alpha_\mathrm{i}}\,\vek o^i{}_{\mathrm{n}}\), which does not depend on \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\) (step 2). By lemma 27.40, \(\partial\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}/\partial\theta = \mat K\,\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta}\) and \(\mat K\,\vek y = \vek k\times\vek y\). Hence \(\partial\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial\theta_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek k\times\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  6. By step 2 and by (27.22), \(\dfrac{\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\,(\vek k\times\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}}) = (\mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\,\vek k)\times(\mat R_{\mathrm{i}-1}\,\vek o^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{n}}) = \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1})\).
  7. Steps 1 and 3 together with 4 and 6 give \(\vek\xi = \mat J\,\dot{\vek q}\) with (27.25). Uniqueness: if \(\mat J'\) also satisfies (27.24), we take the motion \(\vek q + t\,\vek u\) with a vector \(\vek u\) and get \(\mat J'\,\vek u = \mat J\,\vek u\) for every \(\vek u\). For \(\vek u = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) the columns \(i\) are equal.

Source: SPONG (4.43)-(4.47) (PDF p. 134) for the angular part, (4.48)-(4.54) (PDF p. 135-137) for the velocity part and (4.55)-(4.58) (PDF p. 137) for the columns. The source uses figures 4.1 and 4.2 (PDF p. 135-136) instead of a computation with partial derivatives. The step-by-step proof is ours, the source has the same idea of one joint at a time.

The column of a revolute joint is thus what the figure drew: the angular velocity \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and the tip velocity \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times\vek r\) with the lever arm \(\vek r = \vek o_{\mathrm{n}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) from the joint axis to the tip. The column of a prismatic joint is the velocity \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) along the axis and no angular velocity. We look at three examples.

A frequent mistake is the lever arm from the base instead of from the joint axis. For robot A it would mean \(\mat J_2 = \vek k\times(\vek o_2 - \vek o_0)\), which is \((-1;\ 0{,}866)\) m instead of \((-0{,}5;\ 0)\) m (left and middle part of figure 27.57). At \(\dot{\vek q} = (1;\ 0{,}5)\) rad/s the tip would get the velocity \((-1{,}5;\ 1{,}299)\) m/s instead of \((-1{,}25;\ 0{,}866)\) m/s, which is \((-0{,}25;\ 0{,}433)\) m/s too much (num-06.out N3). Joint \(2\) turns only link \(2\) about its own axis, so the lever arm is the distance to that axis, as the theorem says.

Example A, the planar arm. At \(\vek q = (30^\circ;\ 60^\circ)\) (figure 27.57) the origins are \(\vek o_0 = (0, 0, 0)\), \(\vek o_1 = (0{,}866;\ 0{,}5;\ 0)\) m, \(\vek o_2 = (0{,}866;\ 1;\ 0)\) m and the axes \(\vek z_0 = \vek z_1 = \vek k\) (the plane \(xy\), turning about the axis \(z\)). By (27.25), \(\mat J_1 = \vek k\times(\vek o_2 - \vek o_0) = \vek k\times(0{,}866;\ 1;\ 0) = (-1;\ 0{,}866;\ 0)\) m, because \(\vek k\times\vek y = (-y_2,\ y_1,\ 0)\), and \(\mat J_2 = \vek k\times(0;\ 0{,}5;\ 0) = (-0{,}5;\ 0;\ 0)\) m above, and \(\vek k\) below in both columns. The matrix is

\[\mat J = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -0{,}5 \\ 0{,}866 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} .\]

The first column is exactly \(\vek J_1\) from the left and the second \(\vek J_2\) from the middle of the figure. At \(\dot{\vek q} = (1;\ 0{,}5)\) rad/s, \(\vek\xi = \mat J\,\dot{\vek q} = (-1{,}25;\ 0{,}866;\ 0;\ 0;\ 0;\ 1{,}5)\), the tip velocity is \((-1{,}25;\ 0{,}866)\) m/s (right part of the figure) and the angular velocity of the end effector is \((\dot q_1 + \dot q_2)\,\vek k = 1{,}5\,\vek k\) rad/s. We checked the computation with central differences of the tip position and of the matrix \(\mat R_2\) at the step \(10^{-6}\) s: the tip velocity agrees to \(10^{-10}\) m/s, and \(\dot{\mat R}_2\,\mat R_2^\T\) gives \(\Omega_{21} = 1{,}5\) rad/s (num-06.out A4, A5). The upper \(2 \times 2\) matrix is the matrix of partial derivatives \(\partial\vek o_2/\partial\vek q\) (definition 4.42), and its determinant is \(0{,}433 = l_1\,l_2\sin q_2\) m\(^2\). The bottom row of ones says that the end effector turns with the sum of the two motor rates, which equals the sum of the angles \(q_1 + q_2 = 90^\circ\) of the position.

Example C, a prismatic joint. The arm with one revolute and one prismatic joint (figure 27.59) has its base at the origin, and the axis \(\vek z_0\) points out of the page. The sleeve turns about the base through the angle \(q_1\), the rod slides in it and is at the distance \(d\) from the base, drawn as a distance with end bars. The revolute joint has the rate \(\dot q_1\), shown by an arc, the prismatic joint the rate \(\dot d\) along the rod. We choose \(q_1 = 30^\circ\) and \(d = 1{,}2\) m. The axis of the prismatic joint is the direction of the rod, so \(\vek z_1 = (\cos q_1,\ \sin q_1,\ 0) = (0{,}866;\ 0{,}5;\ 0)\), which we get from a DH table with the row \((a, \alpha, d, \theta) = (0, 90^\circ, 0, q_1 + 90^\circ)\) (\(\mat R_1 = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{q}_1 + 90^\circ}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{x},90^\circ}\) has the third column \((\cos q_1,\ \sin q_1,\ 0)\), and the constant \(90^\circ\) does not change the derivative). The tip is at \(\vek o_2 = d\,\vek z_1 = (1{,}039;\ 0{,}6;\ 0)\) m, the origins \(\vek o_0 = \vek o_1\) are at the base. By (27.25), \(\mat J_1 = (\vek k\times\vek o_2;\ \vek k) = (-0{,}6;\ 1{,}039;\ 0;\ 0;\ 0;\ 1)\) and \(\mat J_2 = (\vek z_1;\ \vek 0) = (0{,}866;\ 0{,}5;\ 0;\ 0;\ 0;\ 0)\). At \(\dot q_1 = 0{,}5\) rad/s and \(\dot d = 0{,}2\) m/s, \(\vek v = (-0{,}127;\ 0{,}620;\ 0)\) m/s, the contribution of turning \((-0{,}3;\ 0{,}520)\) m/s and the contribution of sliding \((0{,}173;\ 0{,}1)\) m/s lie along the tangent and along the rod, and their sum is the tip velocity. The direct derivative \(\dot d\,\vek z_1 + d\,\dot q_1\,(-\sin q_1,\ \cos q_1,\ 0)\) gives the same (num-06.out C2, C3). The prismatic column has no lever-arm term, because a motion along the axis involves no turning.

We draw a spatial arm with three revolute joints. The base carries the vertical axis \(\vek z_0\) of the first joint. Link 1 is vertical up to the origin \(\vek o_1\). The axes \(\vek z_1\) and \(\vek z_2\) of the second and third joint are parallel, link 2 and link 3 lie in a plane perpendicular to them. The tip \(\vek o_3\) is the end of link 3. The lever from the axis of the second joint to the tip is \(\vek o_3 - \vek o_1\), the velocity of the tip when joint 2 alone turns is perpendicular to it and to the axis, and the angular velocity has the direction of the axis \(\vek z_1\).

Example B, the spatial arm. The three-dimensional arm with three revolute joints (DH table \((a, \alpha, d, \theta)\): \((0, 90^\circ, 0{,}4, q_1)\), \((0{,}5, 0, 0, q_2)\), \((0{,}4, 0, 0, q_3)\) m, from section 27.4, our dimensions) has at \(\vek q = (30^\circ;\ 45^\circ;\ -60^\circ)\) the origins \(\vek o_0 = \vek 0\), \(\vek o_1 = (0;\ 0;\ 0{,}4)\), \(\vek o_3 = (0{,}6408;\ 0{,}37;\ 0{,}65)\) m and the axes \(\vek z_0 = (0;\ 0;\ 1)\), \(\vek z_1 = \vek z_2 = (0{,}5;\ -0{,}866;\ 0)\) (num-06.out B1). Column \(2\) by (27.25) with \(\vek o_3 - \vek o_1 = (0{,}6408;\ 0{,}37;\ 0{,}25)\) m is

\[\vek z_1\times(\vek o_3 - \vek o_1) = \begin{pmatrix} (-0{,}866)(0{,}25) - 0\cdot 0{,}37 \\ 0\cdot 0{,}6408 - 0{,}5\cdot 0{,}25 \\ 0{,}5\cdot 0{,}37 - (-0{,}866)(0{,}6408) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}2165 \\ -0{,}125 \\ 0{,}7399 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m} ,\]

by (2.39), and below it is \(\vek z_1\). The other columns are computed the same way, and

\[\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}37 & -0{,}2165 & 0{,}0897 \\ 0{,}6408 & -0{,}125 & 0{,}0518 \\ 0 & 0{,}7399 & 0{,}3864 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m} , \qquad \mat J_\omega = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0{,}5 & 0{,}5 \\ 0 & -0{,}866 & -0{,}866 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} .\]

At \(\dot{\vek q} = (0{,}3;\ -0{,}2;\ 0{,}5)\) rad/s, \(\vek\xi = (-0{,}0229;\ 0{,}2431;\ 0{,}0452;\ 0{,}15;\ -0{,}2598;\ 0{,}3)\). A comparison with central differences of the tip position and of the matrix \(\mat R_3\) (step \(10^{-6}\) s) agrees to better than \(10^{-8}\) (num-06.out B4). Columns \(2\) and \(3\) of \(\mat J_\omega\) are equal, because the axes of the second and third joint are parallel (\(\vek z_1 = \vek z_2\)): the turns about them add up about the same axis.

We draw the chain up to link \(k\). The links up to link \(k\) turn about the axes \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\). On link \(k\) there are the origin \(\vek o_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the point \(\vek c\), at the vector \(\vek p\) from the origin. The lever \(\vek r = \vek o_{\mathrm{c}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) points from the axis to the point, the velocity of the point when joint \(i\) turns is perpendicular to it. The links after link \(k\) are drawn faded, because the joints after link \(k\) do not move the point \(\vek c\).

The Jacobian matrix does not hold only for the end effector. The velocity of any point rigidly attached to link \(k\) is the derivative of its position by the chain rule, and the steps of theorem 27.42 can be repeated.

Corollary 27.43 Jacobian matrix of a point of a link (Jacobijeva matrika točke člena)

Let \(\vek o_{\mathrm{c}} = \vek o_{\mathrm{k}} + \mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek p\) be the position of a point with constant coordinates \(\vek p\) in the frame of link \(k\). Then \(\dot{\vek o}_{\mathrm{c}} = \mat J_{\mathrm{v}}^{(c)}\,\dot{\vek q}\) and \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat J_\omega^{(k)}\,\dot{\vek q}\), where the \(3 \times n\) matrices have, for \(i \le k\), the columns \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times(\vek o_{\mathrm{c}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1})\) and \(\rho_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) at a revolute joint and \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(\vek 0\) at a prismatic one, and zero columns for \(i > k\). For the centre of mass \(\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}\) of link \(k\) these are the matrices \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the proof of theorem 8.97.

Proof

We must show that steps 1 to 7 of theorem 27.42 hold if \(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}\) is replaced by \(\vek o_{\mathrm{c}}\) and the chain is shortened to \(k\) links.

  1. The point \(\vek c\) has in frame \(i \le k\) the position \(\vek o^i{}_{\mathrm{c}} = \mat R^i{}_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek p + \vek o^i{}_{\mathrm{k}}\), which contains only \(q_{\mathrm{i}+1}, \dots, q_{\mathrm{k}}\) (step 2 of theorem 27.42). So steps 2 and 4 to 6 of the theorem can be repeated with \(\vek o^i{}_{\mathrm{c}}\) in place of \(\vek o^i{}_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  2. For \(i > k\) the position \(\vek o_{\mathrm{c}} = \vek o_{\mathrm{k}} + \mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek p\) contains only \(q_1, \dots, q_{\mathrm{k}}\), so \(\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{c}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek 0\). The same holds for \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i} \le \mathrm{k}}\rho_{\mathrm{i}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) by step 1 of theorem 27.42 with the shortened chain.
  3. In the proof of theorem 8.97 (step 1) the velocity of the centre of mass is \(\vek v_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}} = \mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot{\vek q}\) and the angular velocity \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot{\vek q}\) for scleronomic constraints, such as the joints of a robot.
