A \(3 \times n\) matrix with this property is unique (the same argument as in step 7), so \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat J_{\mathrm{v}}^{(c)}\) for the \(\vek p\) of the centre of mass and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat J_\omega^{(k)}\).

Source: SPONG example 4.6 (PDF p. 138-139): "the usual Jacobian with \(\vek o_{\mathrm{c}}\) in place of \(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}\)". The connection with \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\) is ours.

We apply the corollary to the centres of mass of the links of robot A. They are \(\vek c_1 = (0{,}433;\ 0{,}25;\ 0)\) m (the middle of link 1) and \(\vek c_2 = (0{,}866;\ 0{,}75;\ 0)\) m (the middle of link 2, which points vertically upward). By corollary 27.43, \(\mat A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}25 & 0 \\ 0{,}433 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) (link 1 does not depend on \(q_2\)) and \(\mat A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}75 & -0{,}25 \\ 0{,}866 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) (upper two rows). The matrices \(\mat W_1\) and \(\mat W_2\) have zero first two rows, and their third rows are \((1,\ 0)\) and \((1,\ 1)\). At \(\dot{\vek q} = (1;\ 0{,}5)\) rad/s the velocities of the centres are \((-0{,}25;\ 0{,}433)\) and \((-0{,}875;\ 0{,}866)\) m/s, equal to central differences of the position (num-06.out A7, A8). These are the matrices that section 27.8 will insert into the mass matrix.

27.6.3 The angular velocity is not the derivative of any three angles (kotna hitrost ni odvod nobenih treh kotov)

The upper rows of the matrix \(\mat J\) are the matrix of partial derivatives (definition 4.42) of the map \(\vek q \mapsto \vek o_{\mathrm{n}}\), the derivative of something we measure. Is the lower part \(\vek\omega = \mat J_\omega\,\dot{\vek q}\) also the derivative of some three numbers that describe the orientation, for example three angles, just as \(\dot{\vek o}_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the derivative of the three coordinates of the tip? If it were, we could take \(\mat J_\omega\) as a matrix of partial derivatives and save the separate treatment. The answer is no, and it holds however the angles are chosen.

Imagine a single rigid frame that we turn four times about the axes of the base frame, each time by \(90^\circ\) between time \(0\) and \(1\) s at a constant angular velocity: about the axis \(x\) by \(+90^\circ\), about \(z\) by \(+90^\circ\), about \(x\) by \(-90^\circ\), about \(z\) by \(-90^\circ\). In each turn about an axis of the base frame the orientation matrix is multiplied from the left (lemma 27.12). Figure 27.62 shows the states \(t_0\) to \(t_4\) of the frame, that is, the columns of the matrix \(\mat R\) in frame \(0\), and the four turns between them. We view the frame obliquely: in state \(t_0\) the axis \(x\) points toward us (drawn slanting down to the left), the axis \(y\) to the right and the axis \(z\) up. The first turn, about the axis \(x\) by \(90^\circ\), raises the axis \(y\) up and turns the axis \(z\) to the left, which is state \(t_1\). The second, about the axis \(z\) by \(90^\circ\), turns the axis \(x\) to the right and the axis \(z\) toward us, which is state \(t_2\). The third, about the axis \(x\) by \(-90^\circ\), turns the axis \(x\) down and the axis \(y\) to the right, which is state \(t_3\). The fourth, about the axis \(z\) by \(-90^\circ\), gives the last state. The end is not the start: the last frame has its axis \(x\) down, its axis \(y\) toward us and its axis \(z\) to the left, while the initial one, drawn dashed, has \(x\) toward us, \(y\) to the right and \(z\) up.

The figure shows what the proof below says. On the left is the plane of the components \(x\) and \(z\) of the sum \(\int_0^t\vek\omega\,\mathrm{d}\tau\), whose component \(y\) stays \(0\). The first turn moves the sum by \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) along the axis \(x\), the second by \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) along the axis \(z\), the third and the fourth by the same amounts back. After the four turns the sum is back at the origin. If \(\vek\omega\) were the derivative of three numbers \(\vek\varphi(\mat R)\), then by the fundamental theorem the difference \(\vek\varphi(\mat R(t)) - \vek\varphi(\mat I)\) would walk exactly this path and return to \(\vek 0\). On the right is the frame itself: the last one does not coincide with the first one, and the tip of its axis \(x\) has moved by \(0{,}1414\) m. A closed path on the left and an open one on the right cannot both hold, and this is the contradiction of the proof.

Lemma 27.44 The angular velocity is not the derivative of an orientation (kotna hitrost ni odvod orientacije)

There is no function \(\vek\varphi(\mat R)\) that assigns three numbers to every orientation matrix so that \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\vek\varphi(\mat R(t)) = \vek\omega(t)\) for every motion and that two different matrices have different triples.

Proof

We must show that such a function would imply that the four turns of figure 27.62 return the frame to the start, which does not hold.

  1. In the first part, let the turn about the axis \(x\) move as \(\mat R(t) = \mat R_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{t})}\,\mat R_0\) with \(\mat R_0\) at the start of the part and \(s(t) = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,t\). Then \(\dot{\mat R}\,\mat R^\T = \dot{\mat R}_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{s}}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{s}}^\T\) (as in lemma 27.40 for the axis \(z\)), which is \(\dot s\) times the matrix that acts as \(\vek y \mapsto \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek y\). So \(\vek\omega = \dot s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) by lemma 27.37. The same holds for the axis \(z\) with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  2. On each of the four parts \(\vek\omega\) is constant, so the integrals of \(\vek\omega\) over the time of the parts are, in order, \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Their sum is \(\vek 0\).
  3. If \(\vek\omega = \dot{\vek\varphi}\), then by the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.55), applied to each part separately, the change of \(\vek\varphi\) on each part would equal the integral of \(\vek\omega\) over that part. By step 2 the changes over the four parts add up to \(\vek 0\), so \(\vek\varphi(\mat R_{\text{end}}) = \vek\varphi(\mat I)\). By the assumption of different triples, \(\mat R_{\text{end}} = \mat I\).
  4. The end is \(\mat R_{\text{end}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{z},-90^\circ}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{x},-90^\circ}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{z},90^\circ}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{x},90^\circ} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \neq \mat I\). The point \((0{,}1;\ 0;\ 0)\) m of the end effector goes to \((0;\ 0;\ -0{,}1)\) m, \(0{,}1414\) m from the start. This is a contradiction.

Source: SPONG (PDF p. 133 and 162): "this velocity vector is not the derivative of a position variable, since the angular velocity vector is not the derivative of any particular time-varying quantity" (stated without proof). The proof and the computation are ours, the numbers are from num-06.out N2.

What the lemma says matters for the following sections: the relation \(\vek\xi = \mat J\,\dot{\vek q}\) cannot be integrated into \(\vek\xi = \tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\ldots)\), and the orientation cannot be read off from the integral of the angular velocity. For the orientation we would need three numbers, for example the Euler angles of section 27.2, and their derivatives are connected to \(\vek\omega\) by a matrix that is not the unit matrix and has no inverse at \(\sin\theta = 0\) (SPONG, PDF p. 144). At \(\theta = 0\) the same orientation matrix belongs to all pairs \(\varphi\), \(\psi\) with the same sum (section 27.2). The matrix of derivatives of such angles is called by the source the analytical Jacobian matrix (SPONG section 4.8, PDF p. 143), which we neither prove nor use here. We stay with the geometric matrix \(\mat J\) and with \(\vek\omega\) as the angular velocity of a body by definition 8.86.

We began this section with the question of how fast the end effector moves. The answer is equation (27.24) with a matrix whose column \(i\) is the velocity when joint \(i\) alone turns (theorem 27.42). The same matrix forms the basis of what follows: section 27.7 will look in it for the positions where the robot loses a direction of motion and use it for the joint forces, and section 27.8 will use the matrices \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\) of corollary 27.43 for the kinetic energy.

27.7 Singular configurations and joint forces

The Jacobian matrix \(\mat J(\vek q)\) of section 27.6 connects the velocity of the arm's tip (figure 27.64) with the velocities of the joints, \(\vek\xi = \mat J\dot{\vek q}\) (definition 27.41). Now we use it for two questions that everyone who steers an arm asks. First: the tip is to move with a given velocity, how fast must the joints turn? Second: a load acts on the tip, what torques must the motors supply so that the arm stays at rest? Both questions end at the same matrix. In the first we must invert it, in the second transpose it (swap its rows and columns). We shall see that both have trouble in the same configurations of the arm.

Anyone who has carried a heavy bucket knows the answer to the second question from their muscles. With the arm stretched downward the bucket hardly tires us, with the arm stretched out horizontally it does quickly. The weight is the same, what changes is the distance between the line of the weight and the shoulder (figure 27.66). In the subsection 27.7.3 we shall write this simple fact down for every joint of the arm.

The model of the arm of figure 27.64 is the same as in the previous sections (section 27.1): rigid links (definition 1.11), ideal joints with one degree of freedom, an open chain, motors that put torques and forces \(\boldsymbol\tau\) into the joints, no friction and no inertia of motors and gears. A real joint has friction, which helps at rest, and a real motor has a gearbox with its own inertia. We model neither here. For the velocities and forces of the tip it is enough that the joints are ideal.

27.7.1 When the tip cannot be moved in every direction

Take arm A of section 27.1, the planar arm with lengths \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m, and put it in the configuration \(\vek q = (30°, 60°)\). Figure 27.64 (left) draws it step by step. First the axis \(x_0\), from which we measure the angle \(q_1\). Then the two links: the first goes from the base \(O\), the origin \(o_0\) of frame 0, to the first joint \(o_1\), the second from \(o_1\) to the tip \(o_2\). The angle \(q_1 = 30°\) lies between the axis and the first link, the angle \(q_2 = 60°\) between the extension of the first link (dashed) and the second link. The tip lies at \((0{,}866;\ 1{,}000)\) m. Now we ask where the tip moves if we turn a single joint. The two columns of the matrix \(\mat J\) are exactly that: \(\vek j_1\) is the velocity of the tip at \(\dot{\vek q} = (1, 0)\) rad/s, \(\vek j_2\) at \(\dot{\vek q} = (0, 1)\) rad/s. By theorem 27.42 column \(i\) of \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\) for a revolute joint is \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times(\vek o_2 - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1})\), for arm A with \(\vek z = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and positions \(\vek o_0 = \vek 0\), \(\vek o_1 = l_1(\cos q_1, \sin q_1)\) therefore

\[\mat J = \begin{pmatrix} -l_1\sin q_1 - l_2\sin(q_1+q_2) & -l_2\sin(q_1+q_2) \\ l_1\cos q_1 + l_2\cos(q_1+q_2) & l_2\cos(q_1+q_2) \end{pmatrix} . \tag{27.26}\]

For arm A we are interested only in the components of the tip velocity in the plane, so from the matrix \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\) (three rows, the third is zero) we take the upper two rows and in this section write them just as \(\mat J\). At \(\vek q = (30°, 60°)\) we have \(\sin(q_1+q_2) = \sin 90° = 1\) and \(\cos(q_1+q_2) = \cos 90° = 0\), so

\[\vek j_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0{,}866 \end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{m} , \qquad \vek j_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{m} .\]

By the definition of the product of a matrix and a vector (definition 1.97) the tip velocity is the sum \(\mat J\dot{\vek q} = \dot q_1\,\vek j_1 + \dot q_2\,\vek j_2\). The two columns point in two different directions of the plane, so we can build every planar velocity from them. Let the tip move at \(0{,}1\) m/s in the direction \(x_0\), \(\vek v = (0{,}1;\ 0)\) m/s. The second row \(0{,}866\,\dot q_1 = 0\) gives \(\dot q_1 = 0\), the first \(-0{,}5\,\dot q_2 = 0{,}1\) gives \(\dot q_2 = -0{,}2\) rad/s. Indeed: only the second joint turns, and the end of the second link, which is \(0{,}5\) m long and points vertically, then moves horizontally at \(0{,}5 \cdot 0{,}2 = 0{,}1\) m/s, by the law for the velocity of a point of a rigid body (lemma 8.87).

Now stretch the arm and keep the first angle, \(\vek q = (30°, 0)\) (figure 27.64, right). Both links lie on the same line through \(O\). The columns are now \(\vek j_1 = (-0{,}75;\ 1{,}299)\) m and \(\vek j_2 = (-0{,}25;\ 0{,}433)\) m, and \(\vek j_1 = 3\,\vek j_2\). They are drawn side by side so that they do not overlap, and they point in the same direction, perpendicular to the arm. The reason is the law for the velocity of a point of a rigid body (lemma 8.87). The first link turns about \(O\) with angular velocity \(\dot q_1\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), so its contribution to the tip velocity is \(\dot q_1\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times(\vek o_2 - \vek o_0)\), and a cross product is perpendicular to both factors (lemma 2.34). The second link turns relative to the first about \(o_1\) and contributes \(\dot q_2\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times(\vek o_2 - \vek o_1)\), perpendicular to \(\vek o_2 - \vek o_1\). Since \(\vek o_2 - \vek o_0\) and \(\vek o_2 - \vek o_1\) lie on the same line, both contributions are perpendicular to the same line. Every tip velocity that we get from joint velocities therefore has component zero along the arm. The radial direction (dashed, crossed) cannot be reached, however fast we turn the joints.

We name the configuration in which this happens (right in figure 27.64). The word comes from the Latin singularis, single, exceptional: such configurations are exceptions among all configurations of the arm. In matrices the same word names those that have no inverse. The Jacobian matrix in such configurations is not invertible, so we call the configuration singular. Which rows of the matrix we count is decided by the task. For arm A we care about the planar position of the tip, so two rows. For arm B of this section, a three-joint arm in space, we care about the position of the tip, so the matrix \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\) with three rows. We count the independent rows with the pivots of the section on elimination (definition 8.21).

Definition 27.45 Singular configuration (singularna lega)

Let \(\mat J_*(\vek q)\) be a matrix of size \(m \times n\) with \(m \le n\) whose rows are the components of the tip velocity that the task requires (for arm A the two planar components, for arm B the three components of \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\), for a six-joint arm all six rows of \(\mat J\)) and whose columns are one per joint. The configuration \(\vek q\) is singular if \(\mat J_*(\vek q)\) does not have a pivot in every row (definition 8.21), like the parallel columns of the stretched arm A. Otherwise the configuration is regular (regularna). For a square matrix \(m = n\) this means that it does not have \(n\) pivots.

Source: SPONG §4.9 (PDF pp. 144-145) defines singular configurations by the number of independent rows being smaller than its maximum. We use pivots instead of this number, because the book introduces them in the section on elimination.

The word configuration (lega) is the one of definition 8.42: the set of all joint variables. Singularity is a property of the configuration, not of the arm: the same arm is regular in most configurations (left in figure 27.64).

For square matrices of order 2 and 3 we have a simple test, the determinant. Determinants in the book are defined for order 3 (definition 2.72), for order 2 we write \(\det\mat A = A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21}\).

Lemma 27.46 Determinant and pivots (determinanta in pivoti)

A square matrix \(\mat A\) of order 2 or 3 has a full set of pivots if and only if \(\det\mat A \neq 0\).

Proof

We must show that \(\det\mat A = 0\) implies missing pivots and the converse. Order 3 is a direct consequence of two known lemmas, order 2 we show separately.

  1. Order 3. By lemma 8.22 \(\mat A\) has three pivots if and only if \(\mat A\vek w = \vek 0\) implies \(\vek w = \vek 0\). By lemma 2.75 \(\det\mat A = 0\) if and only if there is \(\vek w \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat A\vek w = \vek 0\). The two statements are opposite, so \(\det\mat A \neq 0\) if and only if the pivots are full.
  2. Order 2, \(\det\mat A \neq 0\). The matrix \(\mat B = \begin{pmatrix} A_{22} & -A_{12} \\ -A_{21} & A_{11} \end{pmatrix}\) gives by multiplication \(\mat A\mat B = (\det\mat A)\,\mat I\). If \(\mat A\vek w = \vek 0\), then \((\det\mat A)\,\vek w = \mat B\mat A\vek w = \vek 0\) (also \(\mat B\mat A = (\det\mat A)\,\mat I\)), so \(\vek w = \vek 0\). By lemma 8.22 \(\mat A\) has two pivots.
  3. Order 2, \(\det\mat A = 0\). The column \(\vek w = (A_{22}, -A_{12})\) gives \(\mat A\vek w = (\det\mat A,\ 0) = \vek 0\). If \(\vek w \neq \vek 0\), by lemma 8.22 \(\mat A\) does not have two pivots. If \(\vek w = \vek 0\), the second column of the matrix is zero, so \(\mat A(0,1) = \vek 0\) with a nonzero vector, and \(\mat A\) again does not have two pivots.

Source: The proof is not from the sources.

Now we show what a singular configuration means for velocities and for forces. Both statements follow from the same deficiency of the matrix, so we write them together.

Theorem 27.47 Velocities at a singular configuration (hitrosti pri singularni legi)

Let \(\mat J_*\) be a square matrix of order \(n\) and \(\vek\xi = \mat J_*\dot{\vek q}\) the relation between the joint velocities and the tip velocity.

  1. If the configuration is regular, \(\mat J_*\dot{\vek q} = \vek\xi\) has for every \(\vek\xi\) exactly one solution \(\dot{\vek q} = \mat J_*^{-1}\vek\xi\).
  2. If the configuration is singular, there is \(\vek w \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat J_*\vek w = \vek 0\) (the joints turn, the tip is at rest) and there is \(\vek u \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat J_*^\T\vek u = \vek 0\). Every velocity \(\vek\xi = \mat J_*\dot{\vek q}\) satisfies \(\vek u\cdot\vek\xi = 0\), and the velocity \(\vek\xi = \vek u\) belongs to no \(\dot{\vek q}\).
Proof

We must show both points. The first is the lemma on pivots, the second applies the same lemma to \(\mat J_*\) and to its transpose.

  1. A regular configuration means \(n\) pivots (definition 27.45). By lemma 8.22 the system \(\mat J_*\dot{\vek q} = \vek\xi\) has exactly one solution for every right-hand side and \(\mat J_*\) has an inverse matrix.
  2. A singular configuration means fewer than \(n\) pivots. By lemma 8.22 (\(n\) pivots if and only if \(\mat A\vek w = \vek 0\) implies \(\vek w = \vek 0\)) there is \(\vek w \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat J_*\vek w = \vek 0\).
  3. We apply the same lemma to \(\mat J_*^\T\). If \(\mat J_*^\T\) had \(n\) pivots, then by this lemma so would \((\mat J_*^\T)^\T = \mat J_*\). It does not, so there is \(\vek u \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat J_*^\T\vek u = \vek 0\).
  4. For every \(\dot{\vek q}\) we have \(\vek u\cdot(\mat J_*\dot{\vek q}) = (\mat J_*^\T\vek u)\cdot\dot{\vek q} = 0\) (lemma 1.102). If \(\mat J_*\dot{\vek q} = \vek u\) held, we would have \(\vek u\cdot\vek u = 0\), which is false for \(\vek u \neq \vek 0\).
Explanation

The vector \(\vek u\) is the dashed unreachable direction in the figures of this section, the vector \(\vek w\) the motion of the joints that does not move the tip.

Source: SPONG §4.9 (PDF pp. 144-145) says the same with the number of independent rows, the proof is not from the source.

The right part of figure 27.64 shows point 2 on an example: at \(\vek q = (30°, 0)\) we have \(\vek u = (\cos 30°, \sin 30°) = (0{,}866;\ 0{,}5)\), the unit vector along the arm, and \(\vek u\cdot\vek j_1 = \vek u\cdot\vek j_2 = 0\). The vector \(\vek w\) is here \((1, -3)\), since \(\vek j_1 - 3\vek j_2 = \vek 0\). A singular configuration is not just a point where something does not work: already near it the joint velocities grow beyond every bound when the tip velocity has a component in the direction \(\vek u\). How fast, the determinant shows.

Lemma 27.48 Singular configurations of arm A (singularne lege roke A)

Arm A has \(\det\mat J = l_1l_2\sin q_2\). The configuration is singular if and only if \(q_2 = 0\) or \(q_2 = \pi\) (up to full turns), that is, when the arm is stretched or folded. The angle \(q_1\) does not matter.

Proof

We must show the expression for the determinant and its zeros. The matrix is (27.26), its determinant is \(J_{11}J_{22} - J_{12}J_{21}\) (notation before lemma 27.46). We write \(s_1 = \sin q_1\), \(c_1 = \cos q_1\), \(s_{12} = \sin(q_1+q_2)\), \(c_{12} = \cos(q_1+q_2)\).

  1. \(\det\mat J = (-l_1s_1 - l_2s_{12})\,l_2c_{12} - (-l_2s_{12})(l_1c_1 + l_2c_{12})\).
  2. The terms \(-l_2^2s_{12}c_{12}\) and \(+l_2^2s_{12}c_{12}\) cancel, what remains is \(\det\mat J = l_1l_2\,(s_{12}c_1 - s_1c_{12})\).
  3. By the addition formula (corollary 8.16) \(s_{12}c_1 - s_1c_{12} = \sin((q_1 + q_2) - q_1) = \sin q_2\). So \(\det\mat J = l_1l_2\sin q_2\).
  4. Since \(l_1l_2 = 0{,}5\) m² \(\neq 0\), \(\det\mat J = 0\) exactly when \(\sin q_2 = 0\), that is \(q_2 = k\pi\). By lemma 27.46 this is exactly the singular configuration. The figure says the same: \(|\det\mat J|\) is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns \(\vek j_1\) and \(\vek j_2\). On the left of figure 27.64 the area is \(0{,}433\) m² (at \(q_2 = 60°\)), on the right, where the columns are parallel, the parallelogram is flat and the area is zero.

Source: SPONG, equation (4.62) and PDF page 151 (the same determinant, zeros at \(\theta_2 = 0, \pi\)). The step-by-step writing and the proof are not from the source.

The stretched arm (\(q_2 = 0\), right in figure 27.64) is on the outer edge of the workspace (lemma 27.7), the folded one (\(q_2 = \pi\)) on its inner edge. For arm A the singular configurations are therefore on the edges. Arm B will show that this is not necessary.

We also look at what "near" means (configurations between the left and the right part of figure 27.64). Let the tip velocity be \(\vek v = (0{,}1;\ 0)\) m/s, \(q_1 = 30°\). The inverse of a matrix of order 2 is \(\mat J^{-1} = \mat B/\det\mat J\) with \(\mat B\) from step 2 of the proof of lemma 27.46, so

\[\dot q_1 = \frac{0{,}1\,\cos(q_1+q_2)}{l_1\sin q_2} \ \text{m/s} . \tag{27.27}\]

The denominator is \(\sin q_2\), from lemma 27.48. The table shows what happens as \(q_2\) falls toward zero.

\(q_2\) \(\dot q_1\) (rad/s) \(\dot q_2\) (rad/s) \(\det\mat J\) (m²)
\(60°\) \(0\) \(-0{,}2\) \(0{,}43301\)
\(10°\) \(0{,}4411\) \(-1{,}4386\) \(0{,}08682\)
\(5°\) \(0{,}9399\) \(-2{,}9272\) \(0{,}04358\)
\(1°\) \(4{,}9115\) \(-14{,}8359\) \(0{,}00873\)
\(0{,}1°\) \(49{,}5696\) \(-148{,}8088\) \(0{,}00087\)

The tip velocity is the same in all rows, \(0{,}1\) m/s (configurations between the left and the right part of figure 27.64). When the angle drops from \(10°\) to \(1°\), \(\sin q_2\) falls by the factor \(\sin 10°/\sin 1° = 9{,}95\), and \(\cos(q_1+q_2)\) rises from \(\cos 40° = 0{,}766\) to \(\cos 31° = 0{,}857\), that is by the factor \(1{,}119\). By (27.27) \(\dot q_1\) grows by \(9{,}95 \cdot 1{,}119 = 11{,}1\), and indeed \(4{,}9115/0{,}4411 = 11{,}1\). A motor does not have unbounded speed, so a real arm cannot keep this tip velocity any more as it approaches the stretched configuration, before it reaches the configuration. At \(q_2 = 0\) there is no solution if the velocity has a component along the arm (theorem 27.47, point 2), and ours has one, \(\vek u\cdot\vek v = 0{,}866 \cdot 0{,}1 = 0{,}0866\) m/s. If the component along the arm is zero, there are infinitely many solutions: by theorem 27.47 we add to every solution a multiple of the vector \(\vek w = (1, -3)\), for which the tip is at rest.

A measure of how far a configuration is from a singular one is the manipulability (manipulability) \(\mu = |\det\mat J|\) for a square matrix. SPONG names it in §4.12 (equations (4.121) and (4.123), PDF p. 156) and extends it to general matrices with the root of \(\det\mat J\mat J^\T\) and the manipulability ellipsoid. We only cite this and do not prove it. For arm A (figure 27.64) we have \(\mu = l_1l_2|\sin q_2|\): \(0{,}5\) m² at \(q_2 = 90°\), \(0{,}433\) m² at \(60°\), \(0{,}087\) m² at \(10°\) and \(0\) at \(0°\).

27.7.2 An arm in space: elbow and shoulder singularities

In arm A all singular configurations are on the edges of the workspace. An arm with three revolute joints in space has one more kind. Take arm B, an elbow arm (komolčna roka), after the layout of the book SPONG (Example 4.9, PDF pp. 147-148, figure 4.5) with our dimensions \(d_1 = 0{,}4\) m, \(a_2 = 0{,}5\) m, \(a_3 = 0{,}4\) m. We repeat its DH table from section 27.4: the rows \((a_{\mathrm{i}}, \alpha_{\mathrm{i}}, d_{\mathrm{i}}, \theta_{\mathrm{i}})\) are \((0,\ 90°,\ d_1,\ q_1)\), \((a_2,\ 0,\ 0,\ q_2)\), \((a_3,\ 0,\ 0,\ q_3)\). The first joint turns the base about the vertical axis \(z_0\), the second and third joints have parallel, horizontal axes and raise the upper arm and the forearm (figure 27.65).

How do we get to the columns of \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\)? By theorem 27.42 they are \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times(\vek o_3 - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1})\). We need the axes and origins of frames 0, 1, 2. By theorem 27.30 \(\vek o_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1} + d_{\mathrm{i}}\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1} + a_{\mathrm{i}}\vek x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and by lemma 27.28 the columns of \(\mat R^{i-1}_{\mathrm{i}}\) are the axes of frame \(i\). From the first row of the table, frame 1 has \(\vek x_1 = (c_1, s_1, 0)\), \(\vek y_1 = (0, 0, 1)\) and \(\vek z_1 = (s_1, -c_1, 0)\) (because of \(\alpha_1 = 90°\) the axis \(z\) is horizontal) and origin \(\vek o_1 = (0, 0, d_1)\). In the second and third rows \(\alpha = 0\), the axes \(z\) do not change, \(\vek z_2 = \vek z_1\), and the frame turns about it: \(\vek x_2 = c_2\vek x_1 + s_2\vek y_1 = (c_1c_2,\ s_1c_2,\ s_2)\) and by the same computation \(\vek x_3 = (c_1c_{23},\ s_1c_{23},\ s_{23})\) with \(c_{23} = \cos(q_2+q_3)\) and \(s_{23} = \sin(q_2+q_3)\). The origins are \(\vek o_2 = \vek o_1 + a_2\vek x_2\) and \(\vek o_3 = \vek o_2 + a_3\vek x_3\). With the notation \(r = a_2c_2 + a_3c_{23}\) and \(w = a_2s_2 + a_3s_{23}\) the tip is

\[\vek o_3 = (c_1 r,\ s_1 r,\ d_1 + w) . \tag{27.28}\]

At \(\vek q = (30°, 45°, -60°)\) we have \(r = 0{,}7399\) m, \(w = 0{,}25\) m and \(\vek o_3 = (0{,}6408;\ 0{,}37;\ 0{,}65)\) m. The rotation axis of the base \(z_0\) is drawn dashed in figure 27.65, the links as thick lines from the joint \(o_1\) to \(o_2\) and from \(o_2\) to \(o_3\), the angle \(q_2\) lies between the horizontal in the direction of the axis \(\vek x_1\) (dashed) and the upper arm.

Lemma 27.49 Singular configurations of arm B (singularne lege roke B)

For arm B

\[\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = \begin{pmatrix} -s_1 r & -c_1 w & -a_3c_1s_{23} \\ c_1 r & -s_1 w & -a_3s_1s_{23} \\ 0 & r & a_3c_{23} \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \det\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = -a_2a_3\sin q_3\ (a_2\cos q_2 + a_3\cos(q_2+q_3)) . \tag{27.29}\]

The configuration is singular if and only if \(\sin q_3 = 0\) (elbow stretched or folded) or \(a_2\cos q_2 + a_3\cos(q_2+q_3) = 0\), that is \(r = 0\) (the tip on the axis \(z_0\)). In the first case \(\vek u = \vek x_2\) is an unreachable direction, in the second the first column is zero, so turning the base does not move the tip.

Proof

We must show the columns, the determinant and the zeros. We compute the columns from theorem 27.42 and the expressions before the lemma, the determinant by expansion along the first column.

  1. Column 1. \(\vek z_0 = (0,0,1)\) and \(\vek o_3 - \vek o_0 = (c_1r,\ s_1r,\ d_1 + w)\). The cross product \((0,0,1)\times(a,b,c) = (-b,\ a,\ 0)\) gives \((-s_1r,\ c_1r,\ 0)\).
  2. Column 2. \(\vek z_1 = (s_1, -c_1, 0)\) and \(\vek o_3 - \vek o_1 = (c_1r,\ s_1r,\ w)\). By the formula for the cross product \((a_1,a_2,a_3)\times(b_1,b_2,b_3) = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1 - a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)\) the components are \((-c_1w,\ -s_1w,\ s_1\cdot s_1r + c_1\cdot c_1r) = (-c_1w,\ -s_1w,\ r)\).
  3. Column 3. \(\vek z_2 = \vek z_1\) and \(\vek o_3 - \vek o_2 = a_3\vek x_3 = a_3(c_1c_{23},\ s_1c_{23},\ s_{23})\). The same product gives \(a_3(-c_1s_{23},\ -s_1s_{23},\ s_1^2c_{23} + c_1^2c_{23}) = a_3(-c_1s_{23},\ -s_1s_{23},\ c_{23})\).
  4. Expansion along the first column: \(\det\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = (-s_1r)\,M_{11} - (c_1r)\,M_{21}\) with the minors \(M_{11} = (-s_1w)(a_3c_{23}) - (-a_3s_1s_{23})\,r = a_3s_1K\) and \(M_{21} = (-c_1w)(a_3c_{23}) - (-a_3c_1s_{23})\,r = a_3c_1K\), where \(K = s_{23}r - c_{23}w\).
  5. The sum: \(\det\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = -a_3rK\,(s_1^2 + c_1^2) = -a_3rK\).
  6. \(K = s_{23}(a_2c_2 + a_3c_{23}) - c_{23}(a_2s_2 + a_3s_{23}) = a_2(s_{23}c_2 - c_{23}s_2) = a_2\sin q_3\) by the addition formula (corollary 8.16). So \(\det\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = -a_2a_3\sin q_3\,r\).
  7. By lemma 27.46 the configuration is singular exactly when \(\det\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\). Since \(a_2a_3 \neq 0\), this means \(\sin q_3 = 0\) or \(r = 0\).
  8. The unreachable direction. If \(\sin q_3 = 0\), then \(\vek x_3 = \pm\vek x_2\), so \(\vek o_3 - \vek o_1\) and \(\vek o_3 - \vek o_2\) are multiples of \(\vek x_2\). Columns 2 and 3 are cross products with \(\vek x_2\) and by lemma 2.34 are perpendicular to it. For column 1 we have \(\vek x_2\cdot(-s_1r,\ c_1r,\ 0) = r\,c_2(-c_1s_1 + s_1c_1) = 0\). So \(\vek x_2\cdot\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = \vek 0\), that is \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\vek x_2 = \vek 0\).
  9. If \(r = 0\), all three components \(-s_1r\), \(c_1r\), \(0\) of column 1 are zero.

Source: SPONG, Example 4.9 (PDF pp. 147-148), equations (4.97) and (4.98). The book states the determinant and leaves the computation to the reader (Problem 4-12), so the proof by steps is ours.

Let us look at both cases in figure 27.65. At \(\vek q = (30°, 45°, 0)\) (left) the elbow is stretched: \(\vek o_1\), \(\vek o_2\), \(\vek o_3\) lie on one line with the unit vector \(\vek x_2 = (0{,}6124;\ 0{,}3536;\ 0{,}7071)\). The column \(\vek j_2\) points perpendicular to this line (column 3 is parallel to it), and the line is unreachable, as in arm A. Column 1 is still nonzero, the base can turn and move the tip horizontally, perpendicular to the plane of the arm. The matrix \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\) therefore still has two pivots: one direction is unreachable, the other two the tip reaches. In arm A at \(q_2 = 0\) there is only one pivot, because the columns are parallel, \(\vek j_1 = 3\,\vek j_2\). At \(q_3 = 180°\) (folded elbow) the same holds with the same direction \(\vek x_2\).

The other case is more interesting. At \(\vek q = (30°, 45°, 107{,}1144°)\) (figure 27.65, right) we have \(r = a_2\cos 45° + a_3\cos(152{,}1144°) = 0\): the tip is on the axis \(z_0\), at the height \(0{,}9406\) m, and \(\det\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\). Why is it singular exactly here? The base turns about \(z_0\) with angular velocity \(\dot q_1\vek z_0\), and the velocity of a point on the axis is by the law for the velocity of a rigid body \(\dot q_1\vek z_0\times(\vek o_3 - \vek o_0)\) (lemma 8.87), and this is \(\vek 0\), since \(\vek o_3 - \vek o_0 = (0, 0, 0{,}9406)\) m is a multiple of \(\vek z_0\) (lemma 2.34, points 1 and 3). Turning the base does not move the tip, as the zero first column shows. The unreachable direction is the horizontal tangent \(\vek u = (-s_1,\ c_1,\ 0) = (-0{,}5;\ 0{,}866;\ 0)\), since \(\vek u^\T\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} = (r,\ 0,\ 0)\) (columns 2 and 3 have in the first two rows the ratio \(c_1 : s_1\), so they are perpendicular to \(\vek u\)). The tip is \(0{,}9406 - 0{,}4 = 0{,}5406\) m from the shoulder \(o_1\), more than \(a_2 - a_3 = 0{,}1\) m and less than \(a_2 + a_3 = 0{,}9\) m, so it lies inside the workspace (lemma 27.7 for the two links in the plane of the arm), not on its edge, and yet in this configuration it cannot move in the direction \(\vek u\). So arm B has two kinds of singular configurations: the elbow ones on the edges of the workspace and the shoulder one in its interior. SPONG (PDF p. 148) says that in an arm with an offset in the elbow or the shoulder the wrist cannot hit the axis \(z_0\) (Figure 4.8, PDF p. 149), and that points reachable in a singular configuration may no longer be reachable after a small change of the dimensions.

As in the stretched elbow of arm B (figure 27.65), singularity also arises when the axes of two revolute joints lie on one line. In a spherical wrist (kroglasto zapestje), which arms with six joints have, this happens when the axes \(\vek z_3\) and \(\vek z_5\) are collinear, that is at \(q_5 = 0\) or \(\pi\) (SPONG §4.9.2, PDF p. 147). We see the reason in the angular velocity. Let the first three joints be at rest. By lemma 27.39 then \(\vek\omega = \vek z_3\dot q_4 + \vek z_4\dot q_5 + \vek z_5\dot q_6\), and at \(\vek z_5 = \vek z_3\) the choice \((\dot q_4, \dot q_5, \dot q_6) = (1, 0, -1)\) rad/s gives angular velocity zero: the joints turn, the wrist is at rest. SPONG separates the singularities of the arm and of the wrist by splitting the matrix \(\mat J\) into blocks (§4.9.1, PDF pp. 145-147). We do not prove this splitting.

27.7.3 Joint forces

Back to the bucket. Let arm A be in the configuration \(\vek q = (0°, 45°)\), the first link horizontal, the second pointing up at \(45°\) to the first (figure 27.66). From the tip hangs a load of \(5\) kg, which pulls with the vertical downward force \(\vek F\) of magnitude \(5 \cdot 9{,}81 = 49{,}05\) N. The force acts along its line, downward through the tip, and it pulls: the arrow starts at the tip. What must the motors do? The magnitude of the moment of a force about a point (definition 2.37) is the force times the lever arm, the perpendicular distance of the point from the line of the force (lemma 2.38). The line of the force is vertical, so the lever arm about the joint \(O\) is the horizontal distance \(1{,}354\) m (the horizontal coordinate of the tip), and about the joint \(o_1\) it is \(0{,}354\) m. The moment of the force about \(O\) is \(1{,}354 \cdot 49{,}05 = 66{,}39\) N m, about \(o_1\) it is \(0{,}354 \cdot 49{,}05 = 17{,}34\) N m. If we do not count the weight of the links for now, then for rest the motor in each joint must supply a torque of equal magnitude and opposite sense. Why this is exactly what the matrix \(\mat J\) says, we show below. First we write down what a load on the tip means.

In general a load on the tip (figure 27.66) is a force \(\vek f\) at the point \(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}\) and a moment \(\vek m\) acting on the last link. We write them as a column \(\vek F = (\vek f,\ \vek m)\) of six numbers, arranged like \(\vek\xi = (\vek v,\ \vek\omega)\) in section 27.6. The load is the force with which the surroundings (the load, the workpiece, the ground) act on the arm, not the other way round. The motor torques \(\boldsymbol\tau\) are by the notation of the chapter (notation in section 27.6) the generalized forces of the drives, as in definition 8.51. The weight of the links we write as a column \(\vek g(\vek q)\) (bold, to tell it from the gravitational acceleration \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s²): the torques that the motors need merely to hold the links. Let link \(k\) have mass \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) and centre of mass \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\) with velocity \(\vek v_{\mathrm{c},\mathrm{k}} = \mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\dot{\vek q}\) (theorem 8.97), and let the unit vector \(\vek e\) point vertically up. Then

\[\vek g(\vek q) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} m_{\mathrm{k}}\,g\,\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\vek e . \tag{27.30}\]

Why this form will be shown by the proof of the theorem. For arm A with the centres at the middle of the links, \(m_1 = 10\) kg and \(m_2 = 5\) kg (both masses are our choice, not a source's), \(g_1 = m_1gl_{\mathrm{c}1}\cos q_1 + m_2g(l_1\cos q_1 + l_{\mathrm{c}2}\cos(q_1+q_2))\) and \(g_2 = m_2gl_{\mathrm{c}2}\cos(q_1+q_2)\) with \(l_{\mathrm{c}1} = 0{,}5\) m and \(l_{\mathrm{c}2} = 0{,}25\) m. At \(\vek q = (0°, 45°)\) we have \(\vek g = (106{,}771;\ 8{,}671)\) N m.

Theorem 27.50 Joint torques of a static load (sile v zglobih)

Let an open chain of \(n\) joints with rigid links and ideal joints (section 27.1), whose joint variables are generalized coordinates (for a planar chain with revolute joints lemma 27.4 says so), have the Jacobian matrix \(\mat J(\vek q) = \begin{pmatrix}\mat J_{\mathrm{v}} \\ \mat J_\omega\end{pmatrix}\) and a load \(\vek F = (\vek f,\ \vek m)\) on the last link. The generalized force of the load is \(\mat J^\T\vek F\), so its \(s\)-th component is \(\vek f\cdot\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek m\cdot\vek w_{\mathrm{s}}\) with the \(s\)-th column \(\vek w_{\mathrm{s}}\) of \(\mat J_\omega\). The arm is at rest in the configuration \(\vek q\) if and only if the motors supply

\[\boldsymbol\tau = \vek g(\vek q) - \mat J(\vek q)^\T\vek F . \tag{27.31}\]

Component \(i\) of \(\mat J^\T\vek F\) is for a revolute joint the moment of the load about the axis of the joint, \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\cdot\big((\vek o_{\mathrm{n}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1})\times\vek f + \vek m\big)\), for a prismatic joint the component of the force along the axis, \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\cdot\vek f\).

Proof

We must show that the load has the generalized force \(\mat J^\T\vek F\) and that equilibrium is the sum of all generalized forces. We use equilibrium in generalized coordinates from chapter 8.

  1. The joint variables are generalized coordinates of the chain (hypothesis of the theorem, for a planar chain with revolute joints lemma 27.4), the joints are ideal constraints (definition 8.3). So theorem 8.53 holds: the configuration \(\vek q\) is an equilibrium if and only if the sum of the generalized forces of all external forces and moments is zero (in figure 27.66 the load and the motor torques).
  2. The generalized force of the load: by definition 8.51 its component \(s\) is \(\vek f\cdot\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek m\cdot\vek w_{\mathrm{s}}\), where \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}}\vek w_{\mathrm{s}}\,\delta q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is the virtual rotation of the last link.
  3. With \(\dot{\vek q} = \vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\) in \(\vek v = \mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\dot{\vek q}\) (theorem 27.42) and \(\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{s}}(\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}})\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) (lemma 8.30) the \(s\)-th column of \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\) equals \(\partial\vek o_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\). The same holds for \(\mat J_\omega\) and \(\vek w_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  4. From steps 2 and 3 the \(s\)-th component of the generalized force is \((\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\vek f + \mat J_\omega^\T\vek m)_{\mathrm{s}} = (\mat J^\T\vek F)_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  5. The generalized force of gravity: the force on the centre \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(-m_{\mathrm{k}}g\,\vek e\), by definition 8.51 its component \(s\) is \(-m_{\mathrm{k}}g\,\vek e\cdot\partial\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\), which is \(-m_{\mathrm{k}}g\,(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\vek e)_{\mathrm{s}}\) by the same argument as in step 3. The sum over the links is \(-\vek g(\vek q)\).
  6. The motors supply the generalized forces \(\boldsymbol\tau\) (notation of the chapter). By step 1 the equilibrium is \(\boldsymbol\tau - \vek g(\vek q) + \mat J^\T\vek F = \vek 0\), so (27.31).
  7. Component \(i\). For a revolute joint column \(i\) of \(\mat J\) is by theorem 27.42 \((\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times(\vek o_{\mathrm{n}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1});\ \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1})\). Its scalar product with \(\vek F\) is \((\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times\vek r)\cdot\vek f + \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\cdot\vek m\) with \(\vek r = \vek o_{\mathrm{n}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1}\). By the cyclic exchange in the mixed product (lemma 2.73, point 1) \((\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times\vek r)\cdot\vek f = \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\cdot(\vek r\times\vek f)\). For a prismatic joint the column is \((\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1};\ \vek 0)\) and the component is \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\cdot\vek f\). In figure 27.66, for arm A, \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\cdot(\vek r\times\vek f)\) is the force times the lever arm: \(49{,}05 \cdot 1{,}354 = 66{,}39\) N m about \(O\) and \(49{,}05 \cdot 0{,}354 = 17{,}34\) N m about \(o_1\).
Explanation

For \(\vek F = \vek 0\) and links without weight the theorem says only \(\boldsymbol\tau = \vek 0\). With a load and without the weight of the links the torques needed are \(-\mat J^\T\vek F\): opposite to the generalized force of the load \(\mat J^\T\vek F\).

Source: SPONG §4.10 (PDF pp. 151-152), equation (4.104) \(\boldsymbol\tau = \mat J^\T\vek F\), with an informal virtual work and "infinitesimal displacements" \(\delta X = J\,\delta q\) (PDF p. 152). We derive it from equilibrium in generalized coordinates and virtual displacements of chapter 8, without infinitesimal numbers. In equation (4.106) SPONG writes the work as \(F^T\delta X - \tau^T\delta q\), so his \(F\) is the force of the tip on the surroundings, with the opposite sign to our load. The proof by steps is ours.

For arm A the components of the theorem are exactly those that we computed in figure 27.66 as moments. At \(\vek q = (0°, 45°)\) we have by theorem 27.42 \(\mat J = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}3536 & -0{,}3536 \\ 1{,}3536 & 0{,}3536\end{pmatrix}\) m and

\[\mat J^\T\vek F = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}3536 & 1{,}3536 \\ -0{,}3536 & 0{,}3536\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ -49{,}05\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-66{,}392 \\ -17{,}342\end{pmatrix}\ \text{N m} . \tag{27.32}\]

These are exactly \(x_{\mathrm{o}_2}F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1{,}3536 \cdot (-49{,}05)\) and \((x_{\mathrm{o}_2} - x_{\mathrm{o}_1})F_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}3536 \cdot (-49{,}05)\), the moments about the joints \(O\) and \(o_1\), as step 7 says. To hold the load alone the motors must supply \(-\mat J^\T\vek F = (66{,}392;\ 17{,}342)\) N m, including the weight of the links by equation (27.31) \(\boldsymbol\tau = \vek g - \mat J^\T\vek F = (106{,}771 + 66{,}392;\ 8{,}671 + 17{,}342) = (173{,}163;\ 26{,}013)\) N m.

At \(\vek q = (30°, 60°)\) and the same load \(\mat J^\T\vek F = (-42{,}479;\ 0)\) N m. The second link points vertically (left in figure 27.64), the line of the force passes through \(o_1\) and the lever arm about \(o_1\) is zero, the first torque is \(0{,}866 \cdot (-49{,}05) = -42{,}479\) N m. A force whose line passes through a joint needs no torque in that joint, since \(\vek r\) and \(\vek f\) of step 7 of theorem 27.50 are parallel and \(\vek r\times\vek f = \vek 0\).

The same matrices also serve the power (figure 27.66): a load \(\vek F\) at the tip, which moves with velocity \(\vek v = \mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\dot{\vek q}\), has power \(\vek F^\T\mat J\dot{\vek q} = (\mat J^\T\vek F)^\T\dot{\vek q}\) (lemma 1.102). At \(\dot{\vek q} = (1, 0)\) rad/s and \(\vek q = (0°, 45°)\) this is \(-66{,}392\) W, the same on both sides. That is why the transposed matrix appears: \(\mat J\) carries joint velocities into tip velocity, and \(\mat J^\T\) carries the force of the tip into joint torques, so that the power stays the same.

27.7.4 Statics at a singular configuration

The inverse of the matrix \(\mat J^\T\) in theorem 27.50 exists in a regular configuration and there the load is determined exactly by the torques: \(\vek F = -\mat J_*^{-\T}\,\boldsymbol\tau\) (theorem 27.47, point 1, for \(\mat J_*^\T\), which by lemma 8.22 also has \(n\) pivots). In a singular configuration it is not so. Why, the stretched arm from the second part of figure 27.64 shows, this time loaded.

Theorem 27.51 Statics at a singular configuration (statika pri singularni legi)

Let \(\mat J_*\) be a square matrix of order \(n\) that belongs to the load \(\vek F_*\) (for arm A a force \(\vek f\) without a moment, for arm B a force without a moment and \(\mat J_{\mathrm{v}}\)). For \(\boldsymbol\tau = -\mat J_*^\T\vek F_*\) (without the weight of the links):

  1. If the configuration is regular, for every \(\boldsymbol\tau\) there is exactly one load \(\vek F_* = -\mat J_*^{-\T}\boldsymbol\tau\).
  2. If the configuration is singular, there is a load \(\vek F_* \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat J_*^\T\vek F_* = \vek 0\), so the torques are zero: the structure holds the arm, not the motors. And there is \(\vek w \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat J_*\vek w = \vek 0\), so \(\vek w\cdot\boldsymbol\tau = 0\) for every balanced load: torques with \(\vek w\cdot\boldsymbol\tau \neq 0\) are balanced by no load and the arm moves.
Proof

We must show both points of theorem 27.47, translated into forces.

  1. Regular configuration: by lemma 8.22 \(\mat J_*^\T\) has \(n\) pivots and an inverse matrix, \(\mat J_*^\T\vek F_* = -\boldsymbol\tau\) has exactly one solution.
  2. Singular configuration: by theorem 27.47, point 2, there is \(\vek u \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat J_*^\T\vek u = \vek 0\). We take \(\vek F_* = \vek u\). For arm A this is the radial force along the stretched arm, which passes through both joints (figure 27.67).
  3. By the same theorem there is \(\vek w \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat J_*\vek w = \vek 0\). For every \(\vek F_*\) we have \(\vek w\cdot\boldsymbol\tau = -\vek w\cdot(\mat J_*^\T\vek F_*) = -(\mat J_*\vek w)\cdot\vek F_* = 0\) (lemma 1.102).

Source: SPONG §4.9 (PDF p. 145) states that at singular configurations "bounded joint torques may correspond to unbounded end-effector forces and torques". The proof and both directions are ours.

Take arm A at \(\vek q = (30°, 0)\) with a force of \(100\) N along the arm (figure 27.67, top, the arm is turned so that it is horizontal). The line of the force passes through both joints, the lever arm about both is zero, so \(\tau_1 = \tau_2 = 0\) by step 7 of theorem 27.50. Directly: \(\mat J^\T\vek F_{\mathrm{r}} = (0;\ 0)\) N m. The structure carries the force along the link (like the stretched arm with a bucket hanging down), the motors have no work. A force of \(100\) N perpendicular to the arm (bottom) has lever arms \(1{,}5\) m about \(O\) and \(0{,}5\) m about \(o_1\) (measured along the arm), so \(\mat J^\T\vek F_{\mathrm{t}} = (150;\ 50)\) N m. The ratio is \(\tau_1 : \tau_2 = 3 : 1\). The vector \(\vek w = (1, -3)\) of theorem 27.47 therefore indeed gives \(\vek w\cdot\boldsymbol\tau = 150 - 150 = 0\). Conversely, torques with \(\tau_1 \neq 3\tau_2\), for example \((150;\ 0)\) N m, are balanced by no load: by theorem 8.53 the arm is not in equilibrium and starts to move.

Why is it different in a regular configuration (figure 27.64, left)? At \(q_1 = 30°\) and \(q_2 = 60°\) the joint torques \(\boldsymbol\tau = (10;\ 0)\) N m are balanced by exactly one force \(\vek F = -\mat J^{-\T}\boldsymbol\tau = (0;\ -11{,}547)\) N, vertically downward. The closer the configuration is to the stretched one, the larger the force that the same torque still balances: at \(q_2 = 10°\) it is \(57{,}588\) N, at \(1°\) it is \(572{,}987\) N and at \(0{,}1°\) it is \(5729{,}581\) N. The reason is the same as for (27.27): \(\mat J^{-\T} = \mat B^\T/\det\mat J\) with \(\mat B\) of step 2 of the proof of lemma 27.46, and the determinant in the denominator goes to zero. Bounded torques therefore correspond to ever larger forces of the tip as the configuration approaches a singular one (SPONG, PDF p. 145).

Back to the two opening questions. We can move the tip in every direction and every set of motor torques is balanced by exactly one load exactly when the configuration is not singular (theorem 27.47 and theorem 27.51), for arm A exactly when \(\sin q_2 \neq 0\) (lemma 27.48), for arm B when \(\sin q_3\,r \neq 0\) (lemma 27.49). Velocities and forces belong to the same matrix \(\mat J\), one to its columns, the other to its rows. We need the weight of the links \(\vek g(\vek q)\) and \(\mat J^\T\) also in section 27.8: there \(\vek g(\vek q) = \partial V/\partial\vek q\) with the gravitational potential energy \(V\), and equation (27.30) is an expression for the same thing link by link.

27.8 Equations of motion of a robot

Until now the arm was at rest or we prescribed its velocities. Section 27.6 connected the joint velocities with the velocity of the tip, and section 27.7 connected the motor torques with the load when the arm is at rest: \(\boldsymbol\tau = \vek g(\vek q) - \mat J^\T\vek F\) (theorem 27.50). In motion something else happens. Arm A of section 27.1 holds the configuration \(\vek q = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)\) without a load with the torques \((84{,}957,\ 0)\) N m. If the first link turns with angular acceleration \(2\) rad/s\(^2\) and angular velocity \(1\) rad/s, and the second with \(0{,}5\) rad/s and acceleration \(-1\) rad/s\(^2\), the motor of the first joint needs \(102{,}562\) N m and the motor of the second \(2{,}749\) N m, which is more than for holding (the sum is computed step by step in example 27.58). What torques do the motors need for a prescribed motion \(\vek q(t)\), and conversely, how does the arm move if we prescribe the torques of the motors? We call this inverse and direct dynamics (obratna in neposredna dinamika). In the inverse problem we compute the torques from the motion, in the direct problem the motion from the torques.

In figure 27.68 each motor gets its own axis and its own scale. For the first motor the grey dashed holding torque is \(84{,}957\) N m, the orange moving torque is \(102{,}562\) N m, and the blue difference of \(17{,}6\) N m is what the motion adds to holding. For the second motor (axis) holding is zero, because the weight does not turn the second joint in this configuration, while moving needs \(2{,}749\) N m, so the whole difference is \(2{,}749\) N m. The arm needs not only the torque to hold itself but also the torque to accelerate.

The idea is not new. The joint variables are generalized coordinates of the chain (lemma 27.4), the links are rigid bodies (definition 1.11) and the joints are ideal constraints (definition 8.3), so the arm is a system of chapter 8. Lagrange's equations hold for it (theorem 8.101), and they need the kinetic energy \(T\) and the potential energy \(V\) as functions of \(\vek q\) and \(\dot{\vek q}\) and the generalized forces of the remaining forces, here of the motors and the load. The work of this section is therefore to write \(T\) and \(V\) with the matrices we already have and to carry the differentiation through to the end.

The model has four idealizations (idealizacije), and a real arm violates each of them.

  1. The links are rigid (definition 1.11). Flexible links belong to chapter 28.
  2. The joints are ideal and each has one degree of freedom, without friction and without play. A real joint has friction, and the equation we shall derive does not contain it. Friction always opposes the motion of the joint, so for the same motion the motor needs more torque than the equation predicts, and at rest it holds within limits the model does not know.
  3. A motor gives between links \(i - 1\) and \(i\) a torque (revolute joint) or a force (prismatic joint) \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}}\). We do not model the inertia of the motor and of the gearbox. For one link with a gearbox of ratio \(r : 1\), \(\theta_{\mathrm{m}} = r\theta_\ell\), the motor adds \(r^2 J_{\mathrm{m}}\) to the inertia of the link, with the moment of inertia of the motor \(J_{\mathrm{m}}\) (SPONG, PDF pp. 189-190), so at \(r = 100\) it is \(10^4\,J_{\mathrm{m}}\) and is not small.
  4. Apart from the load the arm is free: only the weight, which is constant, and the torques of the motors act on the links.

Arm A has the same links as before: lengths \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m, uniform thin rods with masses \(m_1 = 10\) kg and \(m_2 = 5\) kg (the masses are ours, not from the source), centres of mass \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) in the middle of the links, so at distances \(l_{\mathrm{c}1} = 0{,}5\) m and \(l_{\mathrm{c}2} = 0{,}25\) m from the joint, and moments of inertia about the centre of mass \(m_{\mathrm{k}}l_{\mathrm{k}}^2/12\) (equation (8.91)), that is \(0{,}8333\) and \(0{,}1042\) kg m\(^2\).

27.8.1 Kinetic energy of a robot

Theorem 8.92 requires the velocity of the centre of mass and the angular velocity of every link. Take arm A in the configuration \((30^\circ, 60^\circ)\) (figure 27.71) and ask how fast the centre of mass of the second link moves.

We start with frame 0, the axes \(x_0\) and \(y_0\) at the base, which stays at rest. In it we place both links as thick lines: the first goes from the joint at \(O\) to the joint at \(o_1\), the second from \(o_1\) to the tip. The angles are the same as in section 27.1: \(q_1\) from the axis \(x_0\) to the first link and \(q_2\) from the extension of the first link to the second. Every link has a centre of mass, the point in which theorem 8.92 gathers all the mass for the translational motion: \(G_1\) in the middle of the first and \(G_2\) in the middle of the second link. Their positions are \(\vek c_1 = (0{,}433,\ 0{,}25)\) m and \(\vek c_2 = (0{,}866,\ 0{,}75)\) m.

The centre of mass \(G_2\) moves because of both joints. If only the first one turns, with \(\dot q_1 = 1\) rad/s, the whole arm turns like one body about \(O\) and by equation (8.87) of lemma 8.87 (the point \(O\) is at rest, \(\vek\omega = \dot q_1\vek z_0\)) the velocity of the centre of mass is \(\vek z_0\times(\vek c_2 - \vek o_0)\). This is the arrow \(\vek j_1\), perpendicular to the radius \(OG_2\) of length \(|OG_2| = 1{,}1456\) m, so \(\vek j_1 = (-0{,}75,\ 0{,}866)\) m. If only the second joint turns, only the second link turns about \(o_1\), and the velocity of \(G_2\) is \(\vek z_0\times(\vek c_2 - \vek o_1) = (-0{,}25,\ 0)\) m, which is the arrow \(\vek j_2\), perpendicular to the radius \(o_1G_2\), whose length is \(l_{\mathrm{c}2} = 0{,}25\) m. When both turn at once the velocities add, \(\vek v_{\mathrm{G}2} = \dot q_1\vek j_1 + \dot q_2\vek j_2\). This is the product of a matrix and a vector (definition 1.97) with the matrix \(\mat A_2\) made of the columns \(\vek j_1\) and \(\vek j_2\).

The same holds for every arm, as theorem 27.42 says. Its proof speaks about a point of the last link that is fixed in the axis of this link, so it holds also for the centre of mass \(\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}\) of link \(k\) with the chain of the first \(k\) joints. Column \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) of size \(3 \times n\) is for a revolute joint \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times(\vek c_{\mathrm{k}} - \vek o_{\mathrm{i}-1})\), for a prismatic joint \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\), and column \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\) (angular velocity) is \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) or \(\vek 0\) respectively. For \(i > k\) both columns are zero, because link \(k\) does not move if only the joints after it turn. So \(\vek v_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}} = \mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\dot{\vek q}\) and \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\dot{\vek q}\) are exactly the velocities of step 1 of the proof of theorem 8.97. For arm A

\[\mat A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}25 & 0 \\ 0{,}433 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m}, \quad \mat A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}75 & -0{,}25 \\ 0{,}866 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m}, \quad \mat W_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mat W_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{27.33}\]

The second column of the matrix \(\mat A_1\) is zero, because the first link does not move if only the second joint turns.

The inertia tensor of link \(k\) is constant in an axis attached to the link, so in frame \(k\) (lemma 8.90, point 3), and we write it \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\). The letter \(G\) separates it from the matrix \(\mat J\) of section 27.6. From it we get the tensor in frame 0, in which the velocities are written, and this is the last component of the energy.

Theorem 27.52 Mass matrix of a robot (masna matrika robota)

Let the robot be an open chain of \(n\) joints with ideal joints and rigid links \(k = 1, \dots, n\) with masses \(m_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) and inertia tensors \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\) about the centre of mass in the axis of link \(k\) (section 27.1). Let \(\mat R_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat R^0_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q)\) be the orientation matrix of link \(k\) (definition 27.8), \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\) the matrices of size \(3 \times n\) from the description above. The kinetic energy of the robot is

\[T = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M(\vek q)\,\dot{\vek q} , \qquad \mat M = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{n}\Big(m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\Big) , \tag{27.34}\]

where \(\mat M(\vek q)\) is a symmetric positive definite matrix of size \(n \times n\) with continuously differentiable elements that depend only on \(\vek q\). We call it the mass matrix of the robot (masna matrika).

Proof

We must show that the robot satisfies the assumptions of theorem 8.97 and that the tensor of the link is written with \(\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\).

  1. The joint variables are generalized coordinates of a chain with \(n\) degrees of freedom (lemma 27.4). The constraints do not contain time, because the arm moves only by its motors and not by a prescribed law, so \(\vek b = \vek 0\) and \(T_0 = 0\) in theorem 8.97. The position of the centre of mass \(\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q)\) and the orientation \(\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q)\) are continuously differentiable functions of \(\vek q\) (products and sums of sines and cosines of the joint angles, lemma 27.25).
  2. By step 3 of the proof of theorem 8.97, \(\mat M = \sum_{\mathrm{k}}\big(m_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat J_{\mathrm{k}}\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\big)\), where \(\mat J_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the inertia tensor of link \(k\) in frame 0 and \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) is exactly the matrix \(\partial\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial\vek q\) (step 1 of the same proof).
  3. Let \(\vek r^0\) be the vector from the centre of mass to a point of link \(k\) in frame 0 and \(\vek r^k\) the same vector in frame \(k\). By lemma 27.9, \(\vek r^0 = \mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\vek r^k\). An orthogonal matrix preserves lengths, \(|\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\vek r^k|^2 = |\vek r^k|^2\), and \(\vek r^0(\vek r^0)^\T = \mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\vek r^k(\vek r^k)^\T\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\). Hence \(|\vek r^0|^2\mat I - \vek r^0(\vek r^0)^\T = \mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\big(|\vek r^k|^2\mat I - \vek r^k(\vek r^k)^\T\big)\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\), and by definition 8.89, taking \(\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\) out of the integral, \(\mat J_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\). The tensor \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\) is constant, because the vector \(\vek r^k\) is constant (the link is a rigid body).
  4. Equation (27.34) follows from steps 2 and 3. Symmetry, positive definiteness and continuous differentiability follow from theorem 8.97, since \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\) are continuously differentiable and \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\) is constant. The dependence on \(\vek q\) only is a consequence of step 1.

Source: SPONG (6.50)-(6.53) (PDF pp. 202-203), where \(\mat M\) is denoted \(D\) and positive definiteness is left as an exercise (problem 6-6, PDF p. 203). Here they follow from theorem 8.97. The proof by steps is not from the source.

The name mass matrix has a reason. For one point of mass \(m\) on a line \(T = \tfrac12 m\dot q^2\), so \(\mat M = m\) and the equation we shall derive has \(m\ddot q\) on the left, which is the force by Newton. For a robot the mass is a matrix because the accelerations of different joints are not independent: an acceleration of the first joint in general requires a torque also on the second.

We test the theorem on arm A. For a planar arm the angular velocity has only a component along \(z_0\), and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a rotation about this axis, so \(\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\vek\omega_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\vek\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = \omega_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,J_{\mathrm{zz},\mathrm{k}} = I_{\mathrm{k}}\omega_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) with the moment \(I_{\mathrm{k}} = m_{\mathrm{k}}l_{\mathrm{k}}^2/12\). The second part of the sum is therefore \(I_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek w_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\vek w_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the row \(\vek w_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the component \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\).

Example 27.53 Mass matrix of arm A (masna matrika roke A)

Arm A at \(\vek q = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)\), matrices (27.33), \(m_1 = 10\) kg, \(m_2 = 5\) kg, \(I_1 = 0{,}8333\) kg m\(^2\), \(I_2 = 0{,}1042\) kg m\(^2\).

  1. First link, translation: \(m_1\mat A_1^\T\mat A_1 = 10\begin{pmatrix} 0{,}0625 + 0{,}1875 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2{,}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) kg m\(^2\), since \(0{,}25^2 + 0{,}433^2 = 0{,}25\).
  2. Second link, translation: \(m_2\mat A_2^\T\mat A_2 = 5\begin{pmatrix} 0{,}75^2 + 0{,}866^2 & 0{,}75\cdot 0{,}25 \\ 0{,}75\cdot 0{,}25 & 0{,}25^2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6{,}5625 & 0{,}9375 \\ 0{,}9375 & 0{,}3125 \end{pmatrix}\) kg m\(^2\).
  3. Rotation: \(I_1\vek w_1^\T\vek w_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0{,}8333 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(I_2\vek w_2^\T\vek w_2 = 0{,}1042\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), since \(\vek w_1 = (1,\ 0)\) and \(\vek w_2 = (1,\ 1)\).
  4. The sum of the four parts is
    \[\mat M(30^\circ, 60^\circ) = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 1{,}0417 \\ 1{,}0417 & 0{,}4167 \end{pmatrix}\text{ kg m}^2 .\]
  5. For an arbitrary \(\vek q\) the same computation with SymPy (written in num-08.py) gives
    \[\mat M(\vek q) = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{35}{4} + \tfrac52\cos q_2 & \tfrac{5}{12} + \tfrac54\cos q_2 \\ \tfrac{5}{12} + \tfrac54\cos q_2 & \tfrac{5}{12} \end{pmatrix}\text{ kg m}^2 . \tag{27.35}\]

Source: The computation is ours (SymPy). SPONG, equation (6.86) (PDF p. 209) gives the same formula for the same kind of arm in its own notation.

The matrix does not depend on \(q_1\): turning the whole arm about \(O\) changes neither the distances of the centres of mass from the axis nor the moments of inertia. It does depend on \(q_2\), which changes the distance of the centre of mass \(G_2\) from \(O\) (figure 27.74).

The axes show the angle \(q_2\) from \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\) and the values of the elements, the marked values are the three configurations we shall need. The element \(M_{22}\) is constant, \(0{,}4167\) kg m\(^2\): the second link turns about \(o_1\) regardless of the position of the first, and its moment of inertia about \(o_1\) is \(m_2l_{\mathrm{c}2}^2 + I_2\). The element \(M_{11}\) is largest for the stretched arm, \(11{,}25\) kg m\(^2\) at \(q_2 = 0^\circ\), and smallest for the folded one, \(6{,}25\) kg m\(^2\) at \(q_2 = 180^\circ\). The reason is the distance of the centre of mass \(G_2\) from \(O\): \(1{,}25\) m for the stretched and \(0{,}75\) m for the folded arm, the squares are \(1{,}5625\) and \(0{,}5625\) m\(^2\), the difference \(1\) m\(^2\), times \(m_2 = 5\) kg is \(5\) kg m\(^2\), and indeed \(11{,}25 - 6{,}25 = 5\). For the folded arm the second link is closer to the axis and the first link turns more easily with it. By equation (27.34) the element \(M_{12}\) equals \(m_2(\vek c_2 - \vek o_0)\cdot(\vek c_2 - \vek o_1) + I_2\), since the columns of \(\mat A_2\) are the vectors \(\vek z_0\times(\vek c_2 - \vek o_0)\) and \(\vek z_0\times(\vek c_2 - \vek o_1)\), and the scalar product and the length are the same after a rotation by a right angle (lemma 8.38). This is the scalar product of the radii of figure 27.71, and it is negative when they point in opposite directions: for the folded arm \(\vek c_2 - \vek o_0\) is \(0{,}75\) m long in the direction of the first link and \(\vek c_2 - \vek o_1\) is \(0{,}25\) m long in the opposite one, the product is \(5\cdot(-0{,}1875) + 0{,}1042 = -0{,}8333\) kg m\(^2\). It is zero at \(\cos q_2 = -\tfrac13\), that is at \(q_2 = 109{,}47^\circ\) and \(q_2 = 250{,}53^\circ\).

The mass matrix is invertible in every configuration, also in a singular one. At \(q_2 = 0\) we have \(\det\mat J = l_1l_2\sin q_2 = 0\) (lemma 27.48), yet \(\det\mat M = 11{,}25\cdot 0{,}4167 - 1{,}6667^2 = 1{,}9097\) kg\(^2\) m\(^4\). Singularity of the matrix \(\mat J\) and invertibility of the matrix \(\mat M\) are two different things. The first says that some velocity of the tip is impossible. The second says that by theorem 27.52 every motion of the joints is connected with a nonzero kinetic energy.

27.8.2 Potential energy and gravity

The only force with a potential is the weight (idealization 4). Let \(\vek e\) be the unit vector in frame 0 that points upward, against the weight, and \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s\(^2\) the gravitational acceleration. For arm A frame 0 lies so that \(\vek e = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) (figure 27.71).

Lemma 27.54 Gravity of a robot (težnost robota)

Let the robot have links with masses \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) and centres of mass \(\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q)\), and let only the weight act on the links. Its potential energy (definition 8.58) is

\[V(\vek q) = g\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{n} m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek e\cdot\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q) . \tag{27.36}\]

The column \(\vek g(\vek q) = \partial V/\partial\vek q\) equals

\[\vek g(\vek q) = g\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{n} m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\vek e , \tag{27.37}\]

which is the same column as in equation (27.30).

Proof

We must show that the force of gravity has the potential (27.36), and differentiate it.

  1. The weight acts on every part of link \(k\), per unit volume with the force \(-g\rho\,\vek e\). We divide the link into finitely many parts and choose a point in each. The sum of definition 8.51 for the weights of these parts is a Riemann sum, which tends to an integral as the division gets finer, so the generalized force of the weight of link \(k\) is \(Q_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{s}} = -g\int\rho\,\vek e\cdot\dfrac{\partial\vek x}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}}\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. A point of the link is \(\vek x = \vek c_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q) + \mat R_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q)\,\vek r\), where \(\vek r\) is the vector from the centre of mass in the axis of the link and is constant (the link is a rigid body). Hence \(\partial\vek x/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} + (\partial\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}})\,\vek r\), and by linearity of the integral \(Q_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{s}} = -g\,m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek e\cdot\partial\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} - g\,\vek e\cdot(\partial\mat R_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}})\int\rho\,\vek r\,\mathrm{d}V\). The integral \(\int\rho\,\vek r\,\mathrm{d}V\) is zero by the definition of the centre of mass (definition 8.81). Since \(\vek e\) is constant, \(Q_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{s}} = -\partial(g\,m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek e\cdot\vek c_{\mathrm{k}})/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\). The sum over the links is \(-\partial V/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\) with \(V\) from (27.36), which is therefore the potential energy of the weight by definition 8.58.
  3. By step 2, \(\partial V/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = g\sum_{\mathrm{k}} m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek e\cdot\partial\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\), and \(\partial\vek c_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is column \(s\) of the matrix \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) (step 2 of the proof of theorem 27.52). Hence \(\vek e\cdot(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}) = (\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\vek e)_{\mathrm{s}}\) and (27.37) follows.

Source: SPONG (6.54)-(6.55), (6.64) (PDF pp. 203, 205): the potential energy of the chain is the sum of the potential energies of the links, in which all the mass is in the centre of mass. The proof by steps is not from the source.

For arm A, \(\vek c_1\cdot\vek e = l_{\mathrm{c}1}\sin q_1\) and \(\vek c_2\cdot\vek e = l_1\sin q_1 + l_{\mathrm{c}2}\sin(q_1 + q_2)\), so

\[V = (m_1l_{\mathrm{c}1} + m_2l_1)\,g\sin q_1 + m_2l_{\mathrm{c}2}\,g\sin(q_1 + q_2) , \qquad \vek g(\vek q) = \begin{pmatrix} 98{,}1\cos q_1 + 12{,}2625\cos(q_1 + q_2) \\ 12{,}2625\cos(q_1 + q_2) \end{pmatrix}\text{ N m} , \tag{27.38}\]

since \((m_1l_{\mathrm{c}1} + m_2l_1)g = (5 + 5)\cdot 9{,}81 = 98{,}1\) and \(m_2l_{\mathrm{c}2}g = 5\cdot 0{,}25\cdot 9{,}81 = 12{,}2625\). At \((30^\circ, 60^\circ)\), \(\vek g = (84{,}957,\ 0)\) N m, the second torque is zero because the second link points vertically and its centre of mass \(G_2\) lies on the vertical through \(o_1\) (the radius \(o_1G_2\) in figure 27.71), so the lever arm of the weight about \(o_1\) is zero. At \((0^\circ, 60^\circ)\), \(\vek g = (104{,}231,\ 6{,}131)\) N m.

27.8.3 Equations of motion

Now we have \(T\) and \(V\). Lagrange's equation for the \(k\)-th coordinate (theorem 8.101) requires the time derivative of \(\partial T/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the derivative \(\partial T/\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}\). For \(T = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q}\) the first gives \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q}\) and also terms with the derivative of \(\mat M\), that is the derivative with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) multiplied by the velocity \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the second gives terms with the derivatives of \(\mat M\) with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\). All these terms contain a product of two velocities. Since the product \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\) is symmetric in \(i\) and \(j\), we can simplify the coefficient next to it by replacing it with its symmetric part. We obtain numbers that we name.

Definition 27.55 Coefficients of the velocity terms (koeficienti hitrostnih členov)

Let \(\mat M(\vek q) = (d_{\mathrm{kj}})\) be a symmetric matrix of size \(n \times n\) with continuously differentiable elements on an open set in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The coefficients of the velocity terms (Christoffel symbols of the first kind, Christoffelovi simboli) are the numbers

\[c_{\mathrm{ijk}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial d_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}} + \frac{\partial d_{\mathrm{ki}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial d_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}}\Big) , \qquad i, j, k = 1, \dots, n , \tag{27.39}\]

functions of \(\vek q\). For a column \(\dot{\vek q}\) of \(n\) numbers, \(\mat C(\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\) is the matrix of size \(n \times n\) with elements \(C_{\mathrm{kj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{n} c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Source: SPONG (6.63) and (6.67) (PDF p. 205), where the \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) are called Christoffel symbols of the first kind, with no reason for the name.

The source does not explain the name after a person, so we take it only as a label. Our name has a reason: the symbols stand next to the products of velocities in the equation of motion. From equation (27.39) it follows that \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}} = c_{\mathrm{jik}}\), because \(d_{\mathrm{ij}} = d_{\mathrm{ji}}\) and the first two terms are exchanged under \(i \leftrightarrow j\). By the definition the matrix \(\mat C\) depends on \(\vek q\) and is linear in \(\dot{\vek q}\). Two symbols are used elsewhere in the book: \(\mat C\) is here the matrix of the velocity terms, not the damping matrix of chapter 10, and \(g\) without an argument is the gravitational acceleration \(9{,}81\) m/s\(^2\), while \(\vek g(\vek q)\) with an argument is the column of lemma 27.54.

Theorem 27.56 Equations of motion of a robot (gibalne enačbe robota)

Let the robot be as in theorem 27.52 and lemma 27.54, let the motors give the torques and forces \(\boldsymbol\tau\) and let a load \(\vek F\) (possibly \(\vek 0\)) also act on the last link. A twice differentiable motion \(\vek q(t)\) is a motion of the robot if and only if for every time

\[\mat M(\vek q)\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C(\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\,\dot{\vek q} + \vek g(\vek q) = \boldsymbol\tau + \mat J(\vek q)^\T\vek F , \tag{27.40}\]

where \(\mat M\) is from theorem 27.52, \(\mat C\) from definition 27.55 with the elements \(d_{\mathrm{kj}}\) of the matrix \(\mat M\), and \(\vek g\) from lemma 27.54. The matrix \(\mat M\) is invertible, so \(\ddot{\vek q} = \mat M^{-1}(\boldsymbol\tau + \mat J^\T\vek F - \mat C\dot{\vek q} - \vek g)\).

Proof

We must show that the \(k\)-th Lagrange equation is exactly the \(k\)-th row of equation (27.40). For the \(k\)-th coordinate we compute both derivatives of the energy.

  1. The robot satisfies the assumptions of theorem 8.101: the joint variables are generalized coordinates (lemma 27.4), the joints are ideal, \(T = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q}\) (theorem 27.52) and the force of gravity has the potential \(V\) (lemma 27.54).
  2. Motor \(i\) acts with the moment \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}}\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) on link \(i\) and with the opposite moment on link \(i - 1\). The virtual rotation of link \(k\) is \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta\vek q\) (definition 8.51), where column \(s\) of the matrix \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(\vek z_{\mathrm{s}-1}\) for a revolute joint \(s \le k\) and \(\vek 0\) otherwise. For a revolute joint \(i\) the matrices \(\mat W_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) differ only in column \(i\), which is \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\), so \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} - \delta\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{i}-1} = \vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\delta q_{\mathrm{i}}\). The work of the pair is \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}}\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\cdot(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} - \delta\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{i}-1}) = \tau_{\mathrm{i}}\,\delta q_{\mathrm{i}}\). For a prismatic joint the forces \(\pm\tau_{\mathrm{i}}\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) act at the same point of both links, which separate by \(\vek z_{\mathrm{i}-1}\delta q_{\mathrm{i}}\) along the coordinate \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the work is again \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}}\,\delta q_{\mathrm{i}}\). The generalized force of motor \(i\) (definition 8.51) is therefore \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the generalized force of the load is \((\mat J^\T\vek F)_{\mathrm{k}}\) (steps 2 to 4 of the proof of theorem 27.50). The nonconservative generalized force is thus \(Q^{\mathrm{nc}}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tau_{\mathrm{k}} + (\mat J^\T\vek F)_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. By theorem 8.101, and since \(V\) does not depend on \(\dot q_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{k}}} - \dfrac{\partial T}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}} = \tau_{\mathrm{k}} + (\mat J^\T\vek F)_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. The derivative with respect to velocity is \(\partial T/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{kj}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\), since \(\mat M\) is symmetric. By the product rule and the chain rule (lemma 8.30) its time derivative is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{kj}}\ddot q_{\mathrm{j}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}\dfrac{\partial d_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  5. The derivative with respect to position is \(\partial T/\partial q_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}\dfrac{\partial d_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\), because \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\) does not depend on \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) (\(T\) is a function of the \(2n\) variables \(\vek q\) and \(\dot{\vek q}\) as in section 8.9, where we differentiate with respect to one and hold the others).
  6. Their difference is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{kj}}\ddot q_{\mathrm{j}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}a_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\) with \(a_{\mathrm{ij}} = \dfrac{\partial d_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}} - \tfrac12\dfrac{\partial d_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}}\).
  7. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}a_{\mathrm{ij}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\) does not change if \(a_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is replaced by \(\tfrac12(a_{\mathrm{ij}} + a_{\mathrm{ji}})\): by renaming indices, \(\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}a_{\mathrm{ji}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}a_{\mathrm{ij}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\), and the sum of both is twice the wanted one. Since \(d_{\mathrm{ij}} = d_{\mathrm{ji}}\), \(\tfrac12(a_{\mathrm{ij}} + a_{\mathrm{ji}}) = \tfrac12\big(\frac{\partial d_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}} + \frac{\partial d_{\mathrm{ki}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial d_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}}\big) = c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\).
  8. So \(\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\dot q_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{kj}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\). Insert into step 3 and \(\partial V/\partial q_{\mathrm{k}} = g_{\mathrm{k}}\) (lemma 27.54): \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{kj}}\ddot q_{\mathrm{j}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{kj}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}} + g_{\mathrm{k}} = \tau_{\mathrm{k}} + (\mat J^\T\vek F)_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(k = 1, \dots, n\), which is (27.40).
  9. The steps are equalities, so the converse holds as well. The matrix \(\mat M\) is invertible: \(\mat M\vek x = \vek 0\) implies \(\vek x^\T\mat M\vek x = 0\), and by positive definiteness \(\vek x = \vek 0\).

Source: SPONG (6.56)-(6.68) (PDF pp. 203-205): the same derivation, in which equality (6.62) is left as an exercise (problem 6-7, PDF p. 204). The proof by steps 1, 2, 7 and 9 is ours.

What did the theorem say? The term \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q}\) is the part of the torque that is linear in the acceleration, and \(\vek g\) says what the arm needs for holding. The remaining term \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\) contains only velocities and arises because the mass matrix changes with the configuration: the coefficients \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) are made of derivatives of \(\mat M\). If \(\dot{\vek q} = \vek 0\) it vanishes, and for \(\ddot{\vek q} = \vek 0\) what remains is \(\vek g = \boldsymbol\tau + \mat J^\T\vek F\), which is exactly theorem 27.50. The terms with a squared velocity, \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}^2\), are according to SPONG (PDF p. 205) called centrifugal, from the Latin centrum and fugere, to flee from the centre: a body that moves in a circle departs from the circle by inertia. The terms with a product of two different velocities are according to the same source called Coriolis. They are named after a person, the reason for the name SPONG does not give, so we call them mixed terms.

27.8.4 Tests and use

Example 27.57 Equations of motion of arm A (gibalne enačbe roke A)

Arm A, \(\mat M\) from equation (27.35) and \(\vek g\) from equation (27.38).

  1. The matrix \(\mat M\) depends only on \(q_2\), so all derivatives with respect to \(q_1\) are zero. The derivatives with respect to \(q_2\) are \(\partial d_{11}/\partial q_2 = -\tfrac52\sin q_2 = 2h\), \(\partial d_{12}/\partial q_2 = -\tfrac54\sin q_2 = h\) and \(\partial d_{22}/\partial q_2 = 0\) with \(h = -m_2l_1l_{\mathrm{c}2}\sin q_2 = -1{,}25\sin q_2\) kg m\(^2\).
  2. By equation (27.39) the nonzero symbols are \(c_{121} = c_{211} = c_{221} = h\) and \(c_{112} = -h\). For example \(c_{112} = \tfrac12(\partial d_{21}/\partial q_1 + \partial d_{21}/\partial q_1 - \partial d_{11}/\partial q_2) = -\tfrac12\cdot 2h = -h\) and \(c_{221} = \tfrac12(\partial d_{12}/\partial q_2 + \partial d_{12}/\partial q_2 - \partial d_{22}/\partial q_1) = h\).
  3. The matrix \(C_{\mathrm{kj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\) is
    \[\mat C(\vek q, \dot{\vek q}) = h\begin{pmatrix} \dot q_2 & \dot q_1 + \dot q_2 \\ -\dot q_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{27.41}\]
  4. The equations by components, with \(\vek F = \vek 0\):
