    \[\begin{aligned} \tau_1 &= \big(\tfrac{35}{4} + \tfrac52\cos q_2\big)\ddot q_1 + \big(\tfrac5{12} + \tfrac54\cos q_2\big)\ddot q_2 + h\,(2\dot q_1\dot q_2 + \dot q_2^2) + 98{,}1\cos q_1 + 12{,}2625\cos(q_1 + q_2) , \\ \tau_2 &= \big(\tfrac5{12} + \tfrac54\cos q_2\big)\ddot q_1 + \tfrac5{12}\ddot q_2 - h\,\dot q_1^2 + 12{,}2625\cos(q_1 + q_2) . \end{aligned} \tag{27.42}\]

Source: The computation is ours (SymPy, num-08.py). SPONG (6.90)-(6.91) (PDF p. 210) gives the same equations in its own notation.

In the second equation stands \(-h\dot q_1^2 = 1{,}25\sin q_2\,\dot q_1^2\), the centrifugal term: when the first link turns with \(\dot q_1\), the mass of the second link moves away from \(O\) by inertia and would turn the second link about \(o_1\), so the torque of the motor of the second joint must balance this moment. In the first equation are the mixed term \(2h\dot q_1\dot q_2\) and the centrifugal term \(h\dot q_2^2\).

A test with the double pendulum of chapter 8. The equations contain more terms than can be checked by hand, so we compare the computation with an independent computation of the same system. The geometry is the same as in figure 27.71, except that frame 0 is turned and the masses are in the joint and at the tip. Take point masses on light rods with \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m as in example 8.50, \(m_1 = 10\) kg in the joint and \(m_2 = 5\) kg at the tip (the masses are ours, the example does not give them). Turn frame 0 so that the axis \(x_0\) points downward, and take \(q_1 = \theta_1\) and \(q_2 = \theta_2 - \theta_1\) (the relative angle, step 3 of example 8.50). At \(\theta_1 = 30^\circ\) and \(\theta_2 = 60^\circ\), so \(\vek q = (30^\circ, 30^\circ)\), the points are \(P_1 = (0{,}866,\ 0{,}5)\) m and \(P_2 = (1{,}116,\ 0{,}933)\) m in these axes, that is \((0{,}5000,\ -0{,}8660)\) m and \((0{,}9330,\ -1{,}1160)\) m in the axes of the example. The centres of mass are now in the joint and at the tip, \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}} = \mat 0\), \(\vek e = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}_0}\). Theorem 27.52 gives

\[\mat M = \begin{pmatrix} 16{,}25 + 5\cos q_2 & 1{,}25 + 2{,}5\cos q_2 \\ 1{,}25 + 2{,}5\cos q_2 & 1{,}25 \end{pmatrix}\text{ kg m}^2 , \qquad \vek g = \begin{pmatrix} 147{,}15\sin q_1 + 24{,}525\sin(q_1 + q_2) \\ 24{,}525\sin(q_1 + q_2) \end{pmatrix}\text{ N m} .\]

At \(q_2 = 30^\circ\), \(\mat M = \begin{pmatrix} 20{,}580 & 3{,}415 \\ 3{,}415 & 1{,}25 \end{pmatrix}\), \(\vek g = (94{,}814,\ 21{,}239)\) N m and with \(h = -m_2l_1l_2\sin q_2 = -1{,}25\) kg m\(^2\) equation (27.41) (the same form) at \(\dot{\vek q} = (1,\ 0{,}5)\) rad/s gives \(\mat C = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}625 & -1{,}875 \\ 1{,}25 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) kg m\(^2\)/s. For \(\boldsymbol\tau = \vek 0\) equation (27.40) gives the accelerations \(\ddot{\vek q} = (-2{,}8275,\ -10{,}2664)\) rad/s\(^2\). The same system in the angles \(\theta_1\), \(\theta_2\) of chapter 8: from \(T\) and \(V\) by theorem 8.101, without equation (27.40), the equations are (SymPy)

\[\begin{aligned} 15\ddot\theta_1 + 2{,}5\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\ddot\theta_2 + 2{,}5\sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\dot\theta_2^2 + 147{,}15\sin\theta_1 &= 0 , \\ 2{,}5\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\ddot\theta_1 + 1{,}25\,\ddot\theta_2 - 2{,}5\sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\dot\theta_1^2 + 24{,}525\sin\theta_2 &= 0 . \end{aligned}\]

At \(\dot\theta = (1,\ 1{,}5)\) rad/s and accelerations \(\ddot\theta_1 = \ddot q_1 = -2{,}8275\) and \(\ddot\theta_2 = \ddot q_1 + \ddot q_2 = -13{,}0940\) rad/s\(^2\) (from \(\theta_2 = q_1 + q_2\)) the left sides are \(0{,}0007\) and \(0{,}0001\), so zero within rounding, and in SymPy to \(10^{-8}\). The matrices \(\mat M\), \(\mat C\) and \(\vek g\) of the theorem therefore give a motion that the independently derived equation in other coordinates confirms.

A case without the term \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\). Arm A shows that the velocity terms exist. Does every robot have them? Look at a robot whose links only slide, each along its own line. In figure 27.79 the guide is vertical and link 1 of mass \(m_1 = 10\) kg is threaded on it and slides up and down. Along it slides link 2 of mass \(m_2 = 5\) kg horizontally. The displacements \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) are the joint variables. The motors act with the forces \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) along the guides, and on both centres of mass acts the weight. Both joints are prismatic, so \(\mat W_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat 0\) (the angular velocity is zero for a prismatic joint), and the columns of the matrices \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the joint axes: \(\vek z_0\) vertically upward and \(\vek z_1\) horizontal. So \(\mat A_1 = (\vek z_0,\ \vek 0)\) (the first link moves only vertically) and \(\mat A_2 = (\vek z_0,\ \vek z_1)\). Since \(\vek z_0\) and \(\vek z_1\) are perpendicular unit vectors, \(\mat A_1^\T\mat A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mat A_2^\T\mat A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\). Theorem 27.52 gives a constant matrix

\[\mat M = m_1\mat A_1^\T\mat A_1 + m_2\mat A_2^\T\mat A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} m_1 + m_2 & 0 \\ 0 & m_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\text{ kg} .\]

All derivatives of \(\mat M\) are zero, so by equation (27.39) all \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}} = 0\) and \(\mat C = \mat 0\). By equation (27.37) with \(\vek e = \vek z_0\) the weight is \(\vek g = ((m_1 + m_2)g,\ 0) = (147{,}15,\ 0)\) N. The equations are \((m_1 + m_2)(\ddot q_1 + g) = f_1\) and \(m_2\ddot q_2 = f_2\). At \(\ddot{\vek q} = (2,\ -1)\) m/s\(^2\) we get \(f_1 = 177{,}15\) N and \(f_2 = -5\) N, which is exactly Newton. For this robot a forgotten term \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\) would go unnoticed, because there is none. The reason is written in the formula: the \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) are made of derivatives of \(\mat M\). Here \(\mat M\) is constant because the velocity of the centre of mass for each \(\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the same in every configuration, so the \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) are constant. For a revolute joint the direction of the velocity turns with the configuration and \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) depends on \(\vek q\): for arm A the matrix \(\mat M\) is a function of \(q_2\) (figure 27.74).

The error that a forgotten term brings. Arm A at \(\vek q = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)\), \(\dot{\vek q} = (1,\ 0{,}5)\) rad/s, \(\ddot{\vek q} = (2,\ -1)\) rad/s\(^2\) (inverse dynamics, SymPy).

Example 27.58 Inverse dynamics of arm A (obratna dinamika roke A)

We look for the torques that give the stated motion, without a load.

  1. The mass matrix from example 27.53: \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 1{,}0417 \\ 1{,}0417 & 0{,}4167 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = (18{,}958,\ 1{,}667)\) N m.
  2. The velocity term: \(h = -1{,}25\sin 60^\circ = -1{,}0825\) kg m\(^2\), \(\mat C = h\begin{pmatrix} 0{,}5 & 1{,}5 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mat C\dot{\vek q} = h\,(0{,}5 + 0{,}75,\ -1) = (-1{,}353,\ 1{,}083)\) N m.
  3. The weight from equation (27.38): \(\vek g = (84{,}957,\ 0)\) N m.
  4. The sum: \(\boldsymbol\tau = (18{,}958 - 1{,}353 + 84{,}957,\ 1{,}667 + 1{,}083 + 0) = (102{,}562,\ 2{,}749)\) N m. If the arm rests in the same configuration, \(\boldsymbol\tau = \vek g = (84{,}957,\ 0)\) N m.
  5. The error if we leave out the term \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\) is exactly this term, \((-1{,}353,\ 1{,}083)\) N m, on the second motor \(1{,}083\) of \(2{,}749\) N m, that is \(39\) %. The matrix \(\mat C\) is linear in the velocity, so at \(s\) times the velocities \(\mat C(\vek q, s\dot{\vek q})\,s\dot{\vek q} = s^2\,\mat C\dot{\vek q}\): at twice the velocities the error is four times larger, at four times sixteen times larger: the length of the error, \(1{,}733\) N m, grows to \(1{,}733\cdot 16 = 27{,}7\) N m.

Source: The computation is ours (SymPy, num-08.py).

The velocity term is thus small in slow motion and grows quickly with the square of the velocity. So in fast motions we must not leave it out.

Let us also test a motion along a long path (figure 27.81). We turn the first link of arm A from \(0\) to \(90^\circ\) in one second and stop it at the start and at the end, and hold the second link at \(q_2 = 60^\circ\). A polynomial that goes from \(0\) to \(\tfrac\pi2\) in one second with zero velocity at both ends must satisfy four conditions. A quadratic cannot, because its velocity is linear and is zero at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\) only if it is zero everywhere. The lowest degree is therefore three, \(q_1(t) = \tfrac\pi2\,(3t^2 - 2t^3)\) with \(t\) in seconds. Its velocity is \(\dot q_1 = 3\pi\,t(1 - t)\) and its acceleration \(\ddot q_1 = 3\pi(1 - 2t)\) rad/s\(^2\). We compute the torques from equation (27.42) with \(\dot q_2 = \ddot q_2 = 0\) (SymPy, num-08.py).

The upper axes show time and the torque of the first motor. The blue curve shows \(\tau_1\), the dashed one the gravity part \(g_1\). At \(t = 0\), \(\tau_1 = 198{,}479\) N m: the arm is still at rest, so the velocity term is zero, and this is \(10\cdot 3\pi + 104{,}231\) (\(M_{11}\ddot q_1\) and \(g_1(0^\circ, 60^\circ)\)). The gravity part is thus only a good half. At the end \(\tau_1 = -104{,}87\) N m: the motor brakes, \(-94{,}25\) N m for the acceleration \(-3\pi\) rad/s\(^2\) and \(-10{,}62\) N m the gravity part at \(q_1 = 90^\circ\). The lower axes show time and the torque of the second motor. The second link does not turn, yet \(\tau_2\) is not zero, because the first one turns: \(\tau_2\) contains \(M_{21}\ddot q_1\), \(g_2\) and the centrifugal term \(-h\dot q_1^2\). The full curve is \(\tau_2\), highest \(15{,}949\) N m at \(t = 0\) and lowest \(-20{,}437\) N m at \(t = 1\). The dashed orange curve is \(\tau_2'\) without the term \(-h\dot q_1^2\). They differ most at \(t = 0{,}5\), where \(\ddot q_1 = 0\), \(\dot q_1 = 2{,}356\) rad/s, and \(\tau_2 = 2{,}84\) N m, \(\tau_2' = -3{,}17\) N m: the difference is \(-h\dot q_1^2 = 1{,}0825\cdot 5{,}55 = 6{,}01\) N m. So at \(t = 0{,}5\) the torques \(\tau_2\) and \(\tau_2'\) have opposite signs. A model that omitted the term would give the wrong direction.

The torques obtained in this way are exactly those that the motors must give if the model holds (idealizations 1 to 4). For direct dynamics we would solve from equation (27.40) the linear system for \(\ddot{\vek q}\) at a given \(\boldsymbol\tau\) (theorem 27.56) and integrate it step by step, which will serve us in section 27.9 for checking the equations at the free fall of the arm. By theorem 8.108 of chapter 8 the equation has for continuously differentiable \(\boldsymbol\tau(t)\) a solution on some interval around \(t_0\) that is unique for given \(\vek q(t_0)\) and \(\dot{\vek q}(t_0)\).

Equation (27.40) is Lagrange's equation. The other way is the Newton-Euler recursion (Newton-Euler formulation): for each link separately it writes the equations of motion of a rigid body (theorem 8.82) and computes the forces in the joints from the tip toward the base (SPONG, section 6.6, PDF pp. 220-230). It does not use the kinetic and potential energy (SPONG, PDF p. 220). That the two methods are equivalent SPONG states without proof (PDF p. 236, reference to source [152]), so we do not prove it.

Two properties of the equation we prove in section 27.9. The first is that the matrix \(\dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C\) is antisymmetric, which holds for \(\mat C\) made of the symbols \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) and not for every matrix with the same column \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\). The second are the bounds of the eigenvalues of the matrix \(\mat M\) for a robot with revolute joints only, because of which the inertia of such an arm never becomes infinite or zero.

27.9 Properties of the equations of motion of a robot

In section 27.8 we obtained for a robot with \(n\) joints the equation of motion (theorem 27.56)

\[\mat M(\vek q)\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C(\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\,\dot{\vek q} + \vek g(\vek q) = \vek\tau ,\]

with the mass matrix \(\mat M\) (theorem 27.52), the matrix \(\mat C\) built from the Christoffel symbols (definition 27.55), the gravity column \(\vek g = \partial V/\partial\vek q\) (lemma 27.54) and the column \(\vek\tau\) of motor torques and forces. Two symbols meet other meanings used elsewhere in the book here: \(\mat C\) is the matrix of the velocity terms and is not the damping matrix of chapter 10, and \(\vek g\) with its argument is a column of \(n\) numbers that depends on the configuration, not the gravitational acceleration \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s². The model is the same as before: rigid links, ideal joints with one degree of freedom, no friction and no inertia of the motors. These are idealizations. A real arm loses energy in its bearings and the motors have inertia of their own, which the equation does not capture. Friction torque \(\vek\tau_{\mathrm{f}}\) would be subtracted from the motor torque, so the derivative of the energy would get one more power \(-\dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau_{\mathrm{f}} \le 0\): friction would make the energy decrease with time, and the bound from passivity would still hold, since friction only takes energy. The inertia of a motor with gear ratio \(r\) adds a term \(r^2 J_{\mathrm{m}}\) on the diagonal of the mass matrix, which raises the eigenvalues and keeps the antisymmetry.

We know how to write the equation. Now we ask what we know about it before solving it, and what these properties are good for. We begin with an experiment that shows the equation does describe falling. Arm A (the planar two-link arm of section 27.1 with lengths \(l_1 = 1\) m and \(l_2 = 0{,}5\) m, masses \(m_1 = 10\) kg and \(m_2 = 5\) kg, which are our values and not from a source, uniform straight bars with the centres of mass at mid-length) is stretched out horizontally, \(\vek q = (0, 0)^\T\), we switch the motors off, \(\vek\tau = \vek 0\), and release it from rest, the result is shown by figure 27.82.

Let us draw what happens. The first link turns about the base \(O\), which stays at rest, and the second is attached to the first at a joint that a small circle shows in every position. At time zero the arm is stretched out in the starting position, dashed, and the tip is \(1{,}5\) m from \(O\). Downwards points the gravitational acceleration \(\vek g\), which pulls on the centres of mass of both links. Why does the arm fall? To hold it in this position the motors would have to give the torques \(\vek g(\vek 0) = (110{,}363,\ 12{,}263)^\T\) N m (statics, section 27.7), and there are no motors. After \(0{,}25\) s the arm is in the position \(\vek q = (-22{,}8^\circ,\ 35{,}3^\circ)^\T\), the first link has turned down and the second has bent against it. After \(0{,}5\) s it is in the blue position \(\vek q = (-69{,}4^\circ,\ 5{,}8^\circ)^\T\), nearly stretched again, now hanging obliquely down. After \(0{,}75\) s it is in the position \((-128{,}8^\circ,\ -5{,}4^\circ)^\T\), already on the other side of the vertical, and after \(1\) s in the position \((-173{,}3^\circ,\ 20{,}6^\circ)^\T\), nearly horizontal on the left. The path of the tip is the thin line below the base and is never farther than \(1{,}5\) m from \(O\), as the workspace of section 27.1 says.

The picture raises three questions, which this section answers.

  1. The arm lost height and gained speed. How much energy is that, and who gives or takes it when the motors work? This is the power of the motors.
  2. The column \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\) appears in the equation, but the matrix \(\mat C\) is not determined by it alone. Why did we choose the one from the Christoffel symbols?
  3. How large can the mass matrix be as the arm moves through all configurations? Can we bound it from above and from below with numbers that do not depend on the configuration?

At the end there is also a short remark on how the equation depends on the masses and inertias.

27.9.1 The matrix \(\mat C\) and antisymmetry

We reach the answer to question 2 through energy. The kinetic energy of the robot is \(T = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q}\) (theorem 8.97), and for the arm after \(0{,}5\) s of the fall \(T = 102{,}822\) J (example 27.62). By the product rule (lemma 1.82) and the symmetry of \(\mat M\) its derivative in time is

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\dot{\mat M}\dot{\vek q} ,\]

where \(\dot{\mat M}\) is the matrix of the time derivatives \(\dot m_{\mathrm{kj}} = \mathrm{d}m_{\mathrm{kj}}(\vek q(t))/\mathrm{d}t\) along the motion. We multiply the equation of motion by \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\) and get \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\ddot{\vek q} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau - \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat C\dot{\vek q} - \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek g\). So

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau - \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek g + \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\big(\dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C\big)\dot{\vek q} .\]

The kinetic energy changes with the power of the motors \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau\) and the power of the weights \(-\dot{\vek q}^\T\vek g\) (definition 8.59), and with nothing else. The last term must therefore be zero. What must the matrix \(\mat C\) be for this to hold, and for which columns?

Let us compare two matrices that give the same column \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\).

Example 27.59 Two matrices with the same column Cq̇ (dve matriki z istim stolpcem Cq̇)

For arm A, \(\mat M = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{35}{4} + \frac52\cos q_2 & \frac{5}{12} + \frac54\cos q_2 \\ \frac{5}{12} + \frac54\cos q_2 & \frac{5}{12} \end{pmatrix}\) kg m² (theorem 27.52). With \(h = -m_2 l_1 l_{\mathrm{c}2}\sin q_2 = -1{,}25\sin q_2\) kg m² the matrix from the Christoffel symbols is \(\mat C = h\begin{pmatrix} \dot q_2 & \dot q_1 + \dot q_2 \\ -\dot q_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and another matrix is \(\mat C' = h\begin{pmatrix} 2\dot q_2 & \dot q_2 \\ -\dot q_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\). Both give

\[\mat C\dot{\vek q} = \mat C'\dot{\vek q} = h\begin{pmatrix} 2\dot q_1\dot q_2 + \dot q_2^2 \\ -\dot q_1^2 \end{pmatrix} ,\]

so the equation with one or the other describes the same motion. Take the position \(q_2 = 60^\circ\) and the velocity \(\dot{\vek q} = (1,\ 0{,}5)^\T\) rad/s, then \(h = -1{,}0825\) kg m². The matrices are

\[\mat C = \begin{pmatrix} -0{,}5413 & -1{,}6238 \\ 1{,}0825 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat C' = \begin{pmatrix} -1{,}0825 & -0{,}5413 \\ 1{,}0825 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat C\dot{\vek q} = \mat C'\dot{\vek q} = \begin{pmatrix} -1{,}3532 \\ 1{,}0825 \end{pmatrix} \text{ N m} .\]

The time derivative of the mass matrix is \(\dot{\mat M} = -1{,}25\,\dot q_2\sin q_2\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and with these numbers \(\dot{\mat M} = \begin{pmatrix} -1{,}0825 & -0{,}5413 \\ -0{,}5413 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) kg m²/s. Hence

\[\dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2{,}7063 \\ -2{,}7063 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C' = \begin{pmatrix} 1{,}0825 & 0{,}5413 \\ -2{,}7063 & 0 \end{pmatrix} .\]

The first matrix is antisymmetric (definition 1.103), the second is not, since it has \(1{,}0825 \ne 0\) on the diagonal. For the velocity of the motion, \(\dot{\vek q}^\T(\dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C)\dot{\vek q} = 0\) in both cases (up to a rounding error of \(10^{-16}\)), as expected, because the columns \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\) are equal. For the column \(\vek z = (1,\ 0)^\T\), however, \(\vek z^\T(\dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C')\vek z = 1{,}0825\) and \(\vek z^\T(\dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C)\vek z = 0\). We tell the two matrices apart only with a column that is not the velocity.

So energy does not tell \(\mat C\) from \(\mat C'\), because we test it only with \(\vek z = \dot{\vek q}\). The matrix from the Christoffel symbols satisfies more: the expression is zero for every column \(\vek z\). SPONG (PDF p. 217) uses this property later in the control of robots, which is outside this book. We prove it because it follows from the formula for \(\mat C\) itself and the symmetry of the mass matrix.

The proof will follow this figure. The grid is the matrix \(\mat N\) with \(n\) rows and \(n\) columns, which is \(4\) in the figure. The indices are the row \(k\) and the column \(j\). The diagonal is dashed because \(j = k\) on it. We choose the element \(n_{\mathrm{kj}}\) below the diagonal and its mirror partner above it, at the place \((j, k)\). The theorem claims that the mirroring across the diagonal is only a change of sign. A matrix with this property is called antisymmetric (skew-symmetric), whereas a symmetric one would have the same number in both fields. Example 27.59 has already shown it with numbers: \(n_{12} = 2{,}7063\) and \(n_{21} = -2{,}7063\) with zeros on the diagonal.

Theorem 27.60 Skew symmetry of Ṁ − 2C (antisimetričnost matrike Ṁ − 2C)

Let \(\mat M(\vek q)\) be the mass matrix of a robot with \(n\) degrees of freedom (theorem 27.52), symmetric with continuously differentiable entries \(m_{\mathrm{kj}}(\vek q)\). Let \(\mat C(\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\) be the matrix with entries \(c_{\mathrm{kj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{n} c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\), where \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) are the Christoffel symbols (definition 27.55)

\[c_{\mathrm{ijk}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial m_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}} + \frac{\partial m_{\mathrm{ki}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial m_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}}\Big) .\]

For a motion \(\vek q(t)\) let \(\dot{\mat M}\) be the matrix of the time derivatives of the entries \(m_{\mathrm{kj}}(\vek q(t))\). Then the matrix \(\mat N = \dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C\) is antisymmetric: \(n_{\mathrm{jk}} = -n_{\mathrm{kj}}\) for all \(j, k\). Therefore \(\vek z^\T\mat N\vek z = 0\) for every column \(\vek z\) of \(n\) numbers.

Proof

We must show that in the entry \(n_{\mathrm{kj}}\) all terms but two cancel, and that swapping \(j \leftrightarrow k\) changes the sign of those two. For this we need the symmetry of the mass matrix.

  1. By the chain rule (lemma 8.30, item 1), the element \(m_{\mathrm{kj}}\) depends on time only through \(\vek q(t)\), so \(\dot m_{\mathrm{kj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{n}\dfrac{\partial m_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  2. By the definition of the matrix \(\mat C\), for the entry \(n_{\mathrm{kj}}\) \(n_{\mathrm{kj}} = \dot m_{\mathrm{kj}} - 2c_{\mathrm{kj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{n}\Big[\dfrac{\partial m_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}} - \Big(\dfrac{\partial m_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}} + \dfrac{\partial m_{\mathrm{ki}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}} - \dfrac{\partial m_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}}\Big)\Big]\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\). The first and second term in the bracket cancel (this is the reason for the factor \(2\) at \(\mat C\)), what remains is
    \[n_{\mathrm{kj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{n}\Big[\frac{\partial m_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial m_{\mathrm{ki}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}}\Big]\dot q_{\mathrm{i}} . \tag{27.43}\]
  3. Look at the place \((j, k)\). We swap the names \(k\) and \(j\) in equation (27.43): \(n_{\mathrm{jk}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\big[\partial m_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial m_{\mathrm{ji}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}\big]\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  4. The mass matrix is symmetric (definition 1.103). This is an assumption of the proof and holds for every kinetic energy, because in the form \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q}\) the antisymmetric part of a matrix contributes nothing and is therefore never taken. So \(m_{\mathrm{ik}} = m_{\mathrm{ki}}\) and \(m_{\mathrm{ji}} = m_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Thus \(n_{\mathrm{jk}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\big[\partial m_{\mathrm{ki}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial m_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}\big]\dot q_{\mathrm{i}} = -n_{\mathrm{kj}}\) by equation (27.43), which is the mirroring with a change of sign. Without the symmetry, \(\partial m_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\partial m_{\mathrm{ki}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\) would differ and the antisymmetry would fail.
  5. For \(j = k\) step 4 gives \(n_{\mathrm{kk}} = -n_{\mathrm{kk}}\), so \(n_{\mathrm{kk}} = 0\): the diagonal is zero. For any column \(\vek z\), \(\vek z^\T\mat N\vek z = \sum_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{j}} z_{\mathrm{k}} n_{\mathrm{kj}} z_{\mathrm{j}}\). The terms \((k, j)\) and \((j, k)\) with \(j \ne k\) are \(z_{\mathrm{k}} n_{\mathrm{kj}} z_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{jk}} z_{\mathrm{k}} = -z_{\mathrm{k}} n_{\mathrm{kj}} z_{\mathrm{j}}\) and cancel, and the diagonal terms are zero.

Source: SPONG, Proposition 6.1 (PDF pp. 216-217) with equations (6.112) to (6.114), in our notation \(\mat M\) for \(D\). The same source stresses that the antisymmetry is guaranteed only by the matrix \(\mat C\) of equation (6.67) (PDF p. 217, which example 27.59 confirms). The proof follows SPONG (PDF pp. 216-217), step 5 is our write-up.

The proof showed that on mirroring the matrix \(\mat N = \dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C\) across the diagonal only the sign changes, so no column \(\vek z\) receives power from it. Example 27.59 is a counterexample here: with the matrix \(\mat C'\) the column \(\mat C'\dot{\vek q}\) is right, but the antisymmetry fails. The matrix \(\mat C\) from here on is therefore always the one from the Christoffel symbols.

A second view, a physical one. The Coriolis and centrifugal terms, \(\mat C\dot{\vek q}\), act on a turning robot like the magnetic force on a charged particle: at every velocity they redirect the motion (so they bend the path of the tip too, together with gravity), but they neither give nor take energy. This is the same as \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat N\dot{\vek q} = 0\). The ground is Newton's work-energy theorem (a force perpendicular to the displacement does no work).

27.9.2 Power of the motors and passivity

Back to question 1. In the derivative of the kinetic energy the last term vanishes by theorem 27.60 with \(\vek z = \dot{\vek q}\). We add the potential \(V(\vek q)\) that the weights of the links produce, and the total energy \(E = T + V\). The property we are going to prove is called passivity, and the name comes from the theory of electrical circuits: a system is passive if it can be built from passive elements, resistors, capacitors and inductors, and a passive mechanical system from masses, springs and dampers (SPONG, PDF p. 217). Such a system cannot give out more energy than it had.

The figure is schematic and shows what the corollary below says. The horizontal axis is time \(t\), the vertical one energy in joules. The dashed line is the lower bound \(V_{\min}\) of the potential that arms with revolute joints have, because a sine is bounded. The potential \(V(\vek q(t))\) changes during the motion but does not go below this line. The total energy \(E\) is the curve above it, and the kinetic energy is the grey area between them, because \(T = E - V\) and \(T \ge 0\). So \(E\) never goes below \(V_{\min}\). The gap \(\beta\) is the vertical distance from \(E(0)\) to \(V_{\min}\): this much energy the motors can take from the robot. The slope of the tangent to \(E\) is at every time the power of the motors.

Corollary 27.61 Power of the motors and passivity (moč motorjev in pasivnost)

Let \(\vek q(t)\) be a twice continuously differentiable motion of the robot that satisfies the equation of motion of theorem 27.56, and \(E = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M(\vek q)\dot{\vek q} + V(\vek q)\) its total energy.

  1. At every time \(t\), \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau\), the power of the motors (definition 8.59).
  2. If there is a number \(V_{\min}\) with \(V(\vek q) \ge V_{\min}\) for every \(\vek q\), then for every \(T > 0\)
    \[\int_0^T \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau\,\mathrm{d}t \ge -\beta , \qquad \beta = E(0) - V_{\min} \ge 0 . \tag{27.44}\]
Proof

We must show that the derivative of the energy equals the power of the motors (item 1), then that the energy is bounded below and that the integral of the power is a difference of energies (item 2).

  1. By the product rule and the symmetry of the mass matrix, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big(\tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q}\big) = \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\dot{\mat M}\dot{\vek q}\) (lemma 1.82, lemma 1.102). By the chain rule (lemma 8.30), \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial\vek q} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek g\) (lemma 27.54).
  2. From the equation of motion, \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} = \vek\tau - \mat C\dot{\vek q} - \vek g\), so \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\ddot{\vek q} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau - \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat C\dot{\vek q} - \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek g\).
  3. We add steps 1 and 2. The terms with \(\vek g\) cancel and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau + \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\big(\dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C\big)\dot{\vek q}\) remains.
  4. By theorem 27.60 the last term, \(\vek z^\T\mat N\vek z\) with \(\vek z = \dot{\vek q}\), is zero. This is item 1.
  5. The matrix \(\mat M\) is positive definite (theorem 27.52), so the kinetic energy \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q} \ge 0\) and \(E(T) \ge V(\vek q(T)) \ge V_{\min}\).
  6. The function \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau\) is continuous, because \(\vek q\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(\mat M\), \(\mat C\), \(\vek g\) are continuous. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.55), \(\int_0^T\dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau\,\mathrm{d}t = E(T) - E(0) \ge V_{\min} - E(0) = -\beta\), and \(\beta \ge 0\) because \(E(0) \ge V_{\min}\) by step 5.

Source: SPONG equations (6.115) to (6.119) (PDF pp. 217-218). In the proof SPONG says that \(H(T)\) is nonnegative, which holds when the potential is chosen so that \(V \ge 0\). We require this explicitly as the condition \(V \ge V_{\min}\), because \(\beta\) does not change if a constant is added to the potential. The proof by steps is ours.

Item 1 is the balance equation that theorem 8.121 also gives for any forces outside the potential, with \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = \tau_{\mathrm{s}}\). Here we reached it in the matrix form of the robot and saw what makes it possible: the antisymmetry of theorem 27.60. Item 2 says that the motors cannot take from the robot more energy than it has at the start above its lowest possible position, \(\beta\).

Let us test item 1 on a motion with motors. We move joint \(q_1\) of arm A cubically from \(0\) to \(90^\circ\) in \(1\) s, \(q_1(t) = \tfrac{\pi}{2}(3t^2 - 2t^3)\), and hold the second joint at \(q_2 = 60^\circ\). The motors must give the torques from the equation of motion for this, and by theorem 27.56 we compute them at every time, the result is shown by figure 27.85.

The upper panel has a time axis and a power axis. The curve in it shows the power \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau\) of the motors. It is positive while the motors accelerate the arm and negative towards the end, when they brake it. The area between the curve and the axis is the work of the motors, above the axis a gain of the arm, below it a loss. At time \(0{,}5\) s the power is \(155{,}96\) W. The lower panel has the same time axis and an energy axis. In it is the energy \(E - E(0)\), which at the same time has a tangent with the slope \(155{,}96\) J/s, the same value as the power has. This is item 1 of the corollary with a number: the power and the derivative of the energy agree to \(3 \cdot 10^{-4}\) W (central differences with step \(0{,}5\) ms). The work of the motors over the whole motion is \(93{,}6116\) J and equals the difference of energies \(E(1) - E(0) = 104{,}2313 - 10{,}6196\) J, as step 6 of the proof says. At \(t \approx 0{,}29\) s the power is largest, \(262{,}36\) W. At \(t = 0{,}84\) s it is smallest, \(-80{,}35\) W: the motors brake the arm, and energy goes from the arm into the motor, which must give out or store this power.

Example 27.62 The most the motors can take (največ, kar motorji lahko vzamejo)

Take arm A from the start of the section, horizontal and at rest. Choose \(V = 0\) in this position. The potential is \(V = g\big[(m_1 l_{\mathrm{c}1} + m_2 l_1)\sin q_1 + m_2 l_{\mathrm{c}2}\sin(q_1 + q_2)\big]\) with \(l_{\mathrm{c}1} = 0{,}5\) m and \(l_{\mathrm{c}2} = 0{,}25\) m, so \(V \ge V_{\min} = -g(m_1 l_{\mathrm{c}1} + m_2 l_1 + m_2 l_{\mathrm{c}2}) = -110{,}3625\) J, because a sine is at least \(-1\). This is the position \(\vek q = (-90^\circ, 0)^\T\), the arm hangs vertically. The energy at the start is \(E(0) = 0\), so \(\beta = 110{,}3625\) J. If the motors brake the arm from the horizontal position to the vertical one, where it is at rest, then by item 1 the work of the motors is \(\int \dot{\vek q}^\T\vek\tau\,\mathrm{d}t = E(T) - E(0) = V_{\min} - 0 = -110{,}3625\) J. The bound of equation (27.44) is reached: the motors take from the arm exactly all the energy it has above its lowest position, and no more. For the freely falling arm of figure 27.82, \(E(0) = 0\) and it stays so, to within \(2 \cdot 10^{-7}\) J in \(2\) s, which is one more check of the equation with \(\vek\tau = \vek 0\): at \(0{,}5\) s, \(T = 102{,}822\) J and \(V = -102{,}822\) J.

Example 27.63 No passivity if the potential has no lower bound (pasivnosti ni, če potencial nima spodnje meje)

The condition \(V \ge V_{\min}\) is necessary. Let a robot carry a weight of \(5\) kg on a vertical prismatic joint with coordinate \(z\), which in the model can be arbitrarily low (\(V = m g z\)). A motor lowering the load by a height difference \(s\) must pull upwards with the force \(m g = 49{,}05\) N, the load moves downwards, so its work is \(-49{,}05\,s\) J: \(-49{,}05\) J for \(s = 1\) m and \(-490{,}5\) J for \(s = 10\) m. The number \(\beta\) of equation (27.44) does not exist, because \(V\) is not bounded below. For arm A with revolute joints only, \(V\) is bounded because a sine is bounded, and \(\beta\) exists (example 27.62).

27.9.3 Bounds on the mass matrix

Now question 3. The mass matrix of arm A at \(q_2 = 60^\circ\) is \(\begin{pmatrix} 10 & 1{,}0417 \\ 1{,}0417 & 0{,}4167 \end{pmatrix}\) kg m², and at \(q_2 = 0\) it is \(\begin{pmatrix} 11{,}25 & 1{,}6667 \\ 1{,}6667 & 0{,}4167 \end{pmatrix}\) kg m². How does it change with the configuration? Its eigenvalues (definition 2.81) are real, because the matrix is symmetric (corollary 10.25), and we compute them for every \(q_2\), the result is shown by figure 27.87.

On the horizontal axis the angle \(q_2\) runs from \(0\) to \(360^\circ\), because after \(360^\circ\) the arm is in the same position again. On the vertical axis are the eigenvalues in kg m². The upper curve is the larger eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\), the lower one the smaller \(\lambda_1\). Both lie everywhere between the bounds. The orange dashed lines are the numbers \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{M}}\), which the lemma below obtains from the smallest and largest value of a quadratic form. The largest eigenvalue is at \(q_2 = 0\), when the arm is stretched out: then \(M_{11} = 11{,}25\) kg m² is the inertia of both links about joint 1 (bar \(1\): \(m_1 l_1^2/3 = 3{,}3333\), bar \(2\): \(m_2(l_1 + l_{\mathrm{c}2})^2 + J_{\mathrm{G}2} = 7{,}9167\) kg m²), since then the second link is farthest from the axis. At \(q_2 = 180^\circ\), when the arm is folded, \(\lambda_2 = 6{,}3667\) kg m². The smallest eigenvalue is also at \(q_2 = 0\), \(0{,}1661\) kg m², with the eigencolumn \(\vek z = (0{,}149,\ -0{,}989)^\T\): the cheapest motion is mostly a turn of the light second link with a small opposite turn of the first. That \(\lambda_1\) does not exceed \(M_{22} = 0{,}4167\) kg m² is given by theorem 10.21, in which we put the mass matrix of the robot in place of \(\mat K\) and the identity matrix \(\mat I\) in place of \(\mat M\) (the smallest value of the quadratic form on unit columns), since at \(\vek z = (0, 1)^\T\) it equals \(M_{22}\).

The bounds of the figure do not hold for arm A only.

Lemma 27.64 Bounds on the mass matrix of a robot with revolute joints (meje masne matrike robota z vrtljivimi sklepi)

Let a robot have \(n\) revolute joints and let \(\mat M(\vek q)\) be its mass matrix (theorem 27.52). Then there are numbers \(0 < \lambda_{\mathrm{m}} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{M}}\), independent of \(\vek q\), such that for every \(\vek q\) and every column \(\vek z\) of \(n\) numbers

\[\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\,|\vek z|^2 \le \vek z^\T\mat M(\vek q)\,\vek z \le \lambda_{\mathrm{M}}\,|\vek z|^2 . \tag{27.45}\]

Every eigenvalue of the matrix \(\mat M(\vek q)\) lies in the interval \([\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}, \lambda_{\mathrm{M}}]\).

Proof

We must show that the quadratic form attains its smallest and largest value on a bounded closed set, that because of periodicity this set covers all configurations, and that the eigenvalues follow from the quadratic form.

  1. For a revolute joint \(i\) the coordinate \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) enters as in the matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{z},\theta_\mathrm{i}}\) with \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}} = q_{\mathrm{i}} + \text{const.}\) (section 27.4, lemma 27.28), and appears only in \(\cos q_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\sin q_{\mathrm{i}}\). By theorem 27.52 the mass matrix is built from these matrices and their products, so its entries are continuous functions (corollary 1.65) with period \(2\pi\) in every \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  2. Let \(S = \{\vek z : |\vek z| = 1\}\) and \(K = [0, 2\pi]^n \times S\). The factor \([0, 2\pi]\) for \(q_2\) of arm A is the horizontal axis of the figure. The set \(K\) is bounded. It is closed, because the length is continuous, so the limit of a sequence of points of length \(1\) has length \(1\) (definition 1.75).
  3. The function \(f(\vek q, \vek z) = \vek z^\T\mat M(\vek q)\vek z\) is continuous on \(K\) by step 1. By theorem 8.27 there are points where \(f\) is smallest and largest: \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = f(\vek q^*, \vek z^*)\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{M}} = f(\vek q^{**}, \vek z^{**})\). The matrix \(\mat M(\vek q^*)\) is positive definite and \(\vek z^* \ne \vek 0\), so \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} > 0\).
  4. For any \(\vek q\) let \(\vek q'\) be the point in \([0, 2\pi]^n\) with \(q_{\mathrm{i}}' = q_{\mathrm{i}} - 2\pi\lfloor q_{\mathrm{i}}/2\pi\rfloor\). By step 1, \(\mat M(\vek q) = \mat M(\vek q')\), so for \(|\vek z| = 1\) the value \(f(\vek q, \vek z) = f(\vek q', \vek z) \in [\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}, \lambda_{\mathrm{M}}]\). For \(\vek z \ne \vek 0\), \(\vek z^\T\mat M\vek z = |\vek z|^2 f(\vek q, \vek z/|\vek z|)\), which gives equation (27.45).
  5. The matrix \(\mat M(\vek q)\) is symmetric, so by corollary 10.25 it has an eigenpair \(\mat M\vek\varphi = \lambda\vek\varphi\) with \(|\vek\varphi| = 1\). Then \(\lambda = \vek\varphi^\T\mat M\vek\varphi \in [\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}, \lambda_{\mathrm{M}}]\) (both curves between the bounds) by equation (27.45).

Source: SPONG, section 6.5.2, equations (6.120) and (6.121) (PDF p. 218). SPONG says that \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{M}}\) can be found because the entries are bounded, since they are sines and cosines. The proof with the extreme value theorem is ours.

For arm A, \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = 0{,}1661\) kg m² and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{M}} = 11{,}5006\) kg m² (figure 27.87, both at \(q_2 = 0\)). The kinetic energy at a velocity of length \(|\dot{\vek q}| = 1\) rad/s is therefore between \(\tfrac12\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = 0{,}083\) J and \(\tfrac12\lambda_{\mathrm{M}} = 5{,}750\) J, whatever the configuration. The largest eigenvalue stays finite, the smallest positive: the mass matrix does not approach infinity or a singular matrix as the configuration changes.

Example 27.65 A prismatic joint breaks the bound (prizmatični sklep razbije mejo)

The hypothesis of revolute joints is necessary. Take a planar robot with a revolute joint \(q_1\) and a prismatic joint \(d\) on a rod that turns with the joint \(q_1\). Our choice (not from a source): the inertia of the rod about the axis is \(0{,}5\) kg m² and a point mass of \(2\) kg sits at distance \(d\) from the axis. The kinetic energy is \(\tfrac12\big(0{,}5 + 2d^2\big)\dot q_1^2 + \tfrac12\cdot 2\,\dot d^2\), so \(\mat M = \mathrm{diag}\big(0{,}5 + 2d^2,\ 2\big)\), the first entry in kg m², since it belongs to a turn, the second in kg, since it belongs to a shift. On the \(d\) axis we take \(d = 0\), \(0{,}5\), \(1\), \(2\), \(5\), \(10\) m. There \(M_{11}\) \(= 0{,}5\), \(1\), \(2{,}5\), \(8{,}5\), \(50{,}5\), \(200{,}5\) kg m². For \(\vek z = (1, 0)^\T\), \(\vek z^\T\mat M\vek z = 0{,}5 + 2d^2\), which grows without bound with \(d\). The bound \(\lambda_{\mathrm{M}}\) does not exist, because \(d\) is not an angle: it is not periodic and we cannot confine it to \([0, 2\pi]\). If the joint has a stroke, say \(0 \le d \le 1\) m, then \(\lambda_{\mathrm{M}}\) is finite, but it depends on the stroke, not only on the robot.

27.9.4 What depends on the parameters, and what follows

The equation of motion depends on the masses and inertias of the links. For arm A the entries of \(\mat M\) and \(\vek g\) are functions of five numbers, which SPONG works out for his planar arm on PDF pp. 219-220 (equations (6.123) to (6.133), in other notation). Let \(a = m_1 l_{\mathrm{c}1}^2 + m_2(l_1^2 + l_{\mathrm{c}2}^2) + J_{\mathrm{G}1} + J_{\mathrm{G}2} = 8{,}75\) kg m², \(b = m_2 l_1 l_{\mathrm{c}2} = 1{,}25\) kg m², \(d = m_2 l_{\mathrm{c}2}^2 + J_{\mathrm{G}2} = 0{,}4167\) kg m², \(p_1 = m_1 l_{\mathrm{c}1} + m_2 l_1 = 10\) kg m and \(p_2 = m_2 l_{\mathrm{c}2} = 1{,}25\) kg m. Then \(\mat M = \begin{pmatrix} a + 2b\cos q_2 & d + b\cos q_2 \\ d + b\cos q_2 & d \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\vek g = g\,(p_1\cos q_1 + p_2\cos(q_1 + q_2),\ p_2\cos(q_1 + q_2))^\T\). Therefore \(\vek\tau = \mat Y(\vek q, \dot{\vek q}, \ddot{\vek q})\,\vek\Theta\) with \(\vek\Theta = (a, b, d, p_1, p_2)^\T\) and

\[\mat Y = \begin{pmatrix} \ddot q_1 & \cos q_2\,(2\ddot q_1 + \ddot q_2) - \sin q_2\,(2\dot q_1\dot q_2 + \dot q_2^2) & \ddot q_2 & g\cos q_1 & g\cos(q_1 + q_2) \\ 0 & \cos q_2\,\ddot q_1 + \sin q_2\,\dot q_1^2 & \ddot q_1 + \ddot q_2 & 0 & g\cos(q_1 + q_2) \end{pmatrix} .\]

For \(\vek q = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)^\T\), \(\dot{\vek q} = (1, 0{,}5)^\T\) rad/s and \(\ddot{\vek q} = (2, -1)^\T\) rad/s², \(\mat Y\vek\Theta\) gives the torques \((102{,}562,\ 2{,}749)^\T\) N m that the direct equation gives. The column \(\vek\Theta\) holds the parameters and the matrix \(\mat Y\) only the motion: the equation is linear in the parameters. Without gravity three parameters, \(a\), \(b\) and \(d\), are enough. SPONG states this property (section 6.5.3, PDF pp. 218-219) for every robot, with the matrix \(\mat Y\) that he calls the regressor, and at most \(10\) parameters per link: the mass, six entries of the inertia tensor and three coordinates of the centre of mass. We do not give the general proof here: for arm A we checked the property by computation, for a general robot we cite it from the source as not proved. A minimal set of independent parameters is hard to find in general (SPONG, PDF p. 219, and the sources on PDF p. 236).

Two more details from the same source, which we only mention. For a planar robot with a parallelogram (SPONG, PDF pp. 215-216), for a chosen ratio of parameters (equation (6.108)) the mass matrix is diagonal and constant, there are no Coriolis and centrifugal terms, and each joint feels gravity separately. The equations of motion are then separate joint by joint, which SPONG gives as the reason for the popularity of the parallelogram in industrial robots. Deriving the equations of motion with the Newton-Euler recursion instead of Lagrange's equations (SPONG, section 6.6, PDF pp. 220-230) is mentioned in section 27.8. That the two ways give the same equation SPONG only states with a reference (PDF pp. 220 and 236) and does not prove.

We have answered the three questions. The matrix \(\mat C\) from the Christoffel symbols is the one for which \(\dot{\mat M} - 2\mat C\) is antisymmetric (theorem 27.60, proved from the symmetry of the mass matrix). Therefore the power of the motors is the derivative of the total energy and the arm cannot give out more energy than it had above its lowest position (corollary 27.61). The mass matrix of an arm with revolute joints is bounded from above and from below by constant numbers (lemma 27.64). What is not proved here is cited: linearity in the parameters for a general robot, the Newton-Euler recursion and its equality with Lagrange's equation. Flexible links, a spinning rotor and closed chains are not part of this section, and the connections to the chapters that treat them are in the last section of the chapter.

27.10 Connections

The course abbreviations are the same as in section 1.19. The chapter followed one path: the pose of the links (sections 27.2 to 27.4), velocity as its derivative (section 27.6), joint forces as the transfer along the same matrix (section 27.7) and the equations of motion from the kinetic energy (sections 27.8 and 27.9). Below, for each notion we say where it comes back and what stays outside.

  • Lagrange's equations and the rigid body of chapter 8 (DSK 13): the equations of motion \(\mat M(\vek q)\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C(\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\dot{\vek q} + \vek g(\vek q) = \vek\tau\) of theorem 27.56 are theorem 8.101 with kinetic energy \(T = \tfrac12 \dot{\vek q}^\mathsf{T}\mat M\dot{\vek q}\), where by theorem 27.52 the mass matrix is the sum of the contributions of the links from theorem 8.97. For arm A in the pose \((30°, 60°)\) with the velocities \(\dot{\vek q} = (1;\ 0{,}5)\) rad/s the contribution of the first link is \(1{,}667\) J, of the second \(3{,}906\) J, and the sum \(5{,}573\) J is exactly \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\mathsf{T}\mat M\dot{\vek q}\) with the mass matrix of section 27.9 (SymPy). On this route only the weight enters, through the potential, and the motor torques, as generalized forces. The force with which the links hold each other at the joint \(o_1\) does not appear, because the joint is an ideal constraint and the sum of the virtual works of its forces is zero (definition 8.3). This keeps the promise of chapter 8 that manipulators are treated with Lagrange's equations. For each link separately, the two equations of theorem 8.82 on the equations of motion of a rigid body would give the same. Since the theorem counts the constraint forces among the forces on the body, we then have to write the force and the torque at the joint on both links with opposite signs. This is the idea of the Newton-Euler procedure. The source derives it link by link and joins it into a recursion (SPONG, section 6.6, PDF pp. 220 to 230), but it only states that it is equivalent to Lagrange's equations (SPONG, PDF p. 236). We do not prove it.
  • Closed chains: lemma 27.4 holds only for a chain in which every joint adds one independent variable. In a closed chain, such as mechanism D in example 8.49 with three joint angles and one degree of freedom, the joint angles are not coordinates and the equations of motion of this chapter cannot be copied. Why not is seen when we open the chain at \(C\) and turn the second angle from \(-60°\) to \(30°\): the end goes to \(C'\), which is \(0{,}683\) m above the guide, and the mechanism cannot go there, because the slider keeps \(C\) on the guide. So the angle cannot be chosen freely, and a coordinate is exactly a number that can. Crank mechanisms, which are closed chains, are treated in chapter 23 (DSK).
  • Rotation matrices and frames: the orientation matrix \(\mat R^i{}_{\mathrm{j}}\) of definition 27.8 is by lemma 27.9 the transpose of the rotation matrix of definition 2.44, because it holds the axes of frame \(j\) in its columns and not in its rows. For a rotation by \(30°\) the first column is the pair of numbers \(0{,}866\) and \(0{,}5\) that the perpendiculars from the tip of the axis \(x_1\) cut off on the axes of frame 0, and the second column is \(-0{,}5\) and \(0{,}866\) for the axis \(y_1\). This is the promise of chapter 1 that matrices describing the rotations of robot links come back. The same matrix for the rotation of a bar and a beam element is in lemma 7.29 and lemma 12.23 (AK, chapters 7 and 12). Letters have several meanings in the book. Bold \(\mat R\) is the orientation here and the polar factor in chapter 2, \(\mat T\) is the homogeneous matrix while the slanted \(T\) stays the kinetic energy. Bold \(\mat J\) is the Jacobian matrix here, and the inertia tensor of a link is written \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{k}}\) with the index \(G\). Bold \(\mat C\) is the matrix of Christoffel symbols here and the damping matrix in chapter 10. Without arguments \(g\) is the gravitational acceleration \(9{,}81\) m/s\(^2\), with an argument \(\vek g(\vek q)\) is the column of gravity torques.
  • Inverting a map: the local inverse of corollary 27.35 is theorem 8.34 applied to the forward map of the arm pose, and holds where the determinant of the Jacobian matrix is not zero. For the two-link arm this determinant is \(l_1 l_2 \sin q_2\) (lemma 27.48). The determinant is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns of the matrix, the velocities of the tip when a single joint turns. In the pose \((30°, 60°)\) the columns point in different directions and the area is \(1 \cdot 0{,}5 \cdot \sin 60° = 0{,}433\) m\(^2\). With the arm stretched out, \(q_2 = 0\), we have \(\vek j_1 = 3\,\vek j_2\), the parallelogram flattens into a segment of area zero, and the tip cannot move along the arm. There is no inverse there, because it would have to assign a turn of the joints to a small move of the tip in this direction, and no such turn exists. The general inverse, the arm with a spherical wrist and the pseudoinverse for redundant arms stay cited (SPONG, sections 5.2 to 5.4, PDF pp. 165 to 177, and section 4.11, PDF pp. 153 and 154).
  • Flexible links: chapter 28 (DSK) takes from this chapter the matrices \(\mat T^{i-1}{}_{\mathrm{i}}\) of section 27.4, the link Jacobian matrices of section 27.6, the equations of theorem 27.56 and the skew symmetry of theorem 27.60. Here the links are rigid (definition 1.11), the first idealization of the robot model: a tube that sags by \(1{,}9\) mm under a load of \(50\) N stays straight in the model, and the gripper is that far from where the model puts it. What changes when a link is not rigid is answered in that chapter.
  • Mass matrix and eigenvalues: lemma 27.64 applies theorems 10.21 and 8.27 to a mass matrix that is symmetric and positive definite at every configuration. For arm A both eigenvalues lie at every angle \(q_2\) between the bounds \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = 0{,}1661\) kg m\(^2\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{M}} = 11{,}5006\) kg m\(^2\). For a small oscillation about a rest configuration \(\vek q^*\) we would also need a stiffness, which we do not derive here, and the resulting system of chapter 10 is shortened by modes in chapter 21 (DSK).
  • Spinning bodies: the rotation of a body about its own axis and gyroscopic forces are treated in chapter 24 (DSK). In this chapter every link turns about the joint axis and is a rigid body. The term \(\mat C(\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\dot{\vek q}\) alone does work in general, since by theorem 27.60 its power is \(\dot{\vek q}^\mathsf{T}\mat C\dot{\vek q} = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\mathsf{T}\dot{\mat M}\dot{\vek q}\). Only the difference \(\big(\mat C - \tfrac12\dot{\mat M}\big)\dot{\vek q}\) does no work, and so by corollary 27.61 the power of the motors is exactly the derivative of the total energy. For arm A this is read off the figure: the power at time \(0{,}5\) s is \(155{,}96\) W, and the tangent to the energy curve at the same time has slope \(155{,}96\) J/s. In a rotor the same property is simpler: the gyroscopic matrix itself is skew symmetric, so the gyroscopic forces do no work (lemma 24.19).
  • Damping and friction: the model contains no joint friction and no inertia of the motor behind its gear, which with a ratio of \(100 : 1\) would add \(10^4\,J_{\mathrm{m}}\) to the inertia of the link (section 27.1). Damping models are treated in chapter 20 (DSK), the joint stiffness with an elastic transmission is in the source (SPONG, example 6.2 in section 6.1.1, PDF p. 191).
  • Control and path planning: from theorem 27.56 we get the torques for a given motion (inverse dynamics, the example of arm A in section 27.8). How to choose the motion and how to provide the torques is covered by the chapters of the source from the seventh on (SPONG) and not by this book. Corollary 27.61 is the property on which the passivity rests that the source uses in control (SPONG, section 6.5, PDF p. 217): the motors cannot take more energy from the robot than \(\beta\), the energy it has at the start above the lower bound of the potential.
  • Limits of the chapter: proved are the existence and uniqueness of the DH parameters, the columns of the Jacobian matrix, joint forces from virtual work, the equations of motion, skew symmetry and the bounds of the mass matrix. Cited without proof are the roll-pitch-yaw and axis-angle formulas, the general inverse kinematics, the analytical Jacobian, the pseudoinverse, manipulability ellipsoids, linearity in the inertia parameters and the Newton-Euler procedure with its equivalence. The masses of the links in the examples (10 kg and 5 kg) are ours and not from the source.
